items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/End Term 2024-25 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: Calculate the quantity of lime and soda required for softening 50,000 liters of water containing the following salts per litre : $Ca(HCO_3)_2$ – 9.2 mg/l, $Mg(HCO_3)_2$ – 7.9 mg/l, $CaSO_4$ – 15.3 mg/l, $MgSO_4$ – 15.0 mg/l, $MgCl_2$ – 3.0 mg/l, $NaCl$ – 4.3 mg/l.
items.answer_md:
**Given:** volume of water $V$ = 50,000 L; lime purity = 100%, soda purity = 100%.

Purity is not stated, so lime and soda are taken as 100% pure.

**To find:** mass of lime $\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2}$ (molar mass 74) and soda $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}$ (molar mass 106) required.

**Step 1: Convert each constituent to $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ equivalent**

$$\text{ppm as CaCO}_3 = \frac{\text{mg/L of salt}\times 100}{\text{molar mass of salt}}$$

| Constituent | Amount (mg/L) | Molar mass | Factor | ppm as $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ | Type | Needs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\mathrm{Ca(HCO_3)_2}$ | 9.2 | 162 | 100/162 | 5.679 | Temporary Ca | L |
| $\mathrm{Mg(HCO_3)_2}$ | 7.9 | 146 | 100/146 | 5.411 | Temporary Mg | 2L |
| $\mathrm{CaSO_4}$ | 15.3 | 136 | 100/136 | 11.25 | Permanent Ca | S |
| $\mathrm{MgSO_4}$ | 15 | 120 | 100/120 | 12.5 | Permanent Mg | L + S |
| $\mathrm{MgCl_2}$ | 3 | 95 | 100/95 | 3.158 | Permanent Mg | L + S |
| $\mathrm{NaCl}$ | 4.3 | 58.5 | - | - | No hardness | none |

(L = lime, S = soda. Temporary Mg takes 2 lime; permanent Mg takes lime and then soda for the $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ it releases; Na, K salts and $\mathrm{SiO_2}$ cause no hardness and are ignored.)

**Step 2: Formulae**

$$\text{Lime} = \frac{74}{100}\left[\text{Temp Ca}\ (\mathrm{Ca(HCO_3)_2}) + 2\times\text{Temp Mg}\ (\mathrm{Mg(HCO_3)_2}) + \text{Perm Mg}\ (\mathrm{MgSO_4}) + \text{Perm Mg}\ (\mathrm{MgCl_2})\right]\times\frac{V}{10^6}\times\frac{100}{\%\text{ purity}}\ \text{kg}$$

$$\text{Soda} = \frac{106}{100}\left[\text{Perm Ca}\ (\mathrm{CaSO_4}) + \text{Perm Mg}\ (\mathrm{MgSO_4}) + \text{Perm Mg}\ (\mathrm{MgCl_2})\right]\times\frac{V}{10^6}\times\frac{100}{\%\text{ purity}}\ \text{kg}$$

**Step 3: Substitution**

Lime (100% pure) per litre $= \frac{74}{100}[5.679 + 2(5.411) + 12.5 + 3.158] = \frac{74}{100}\times 32.16 = 23.8$ mg/L

Lime (100% pure) for 50,000 L $= 23.8\times 50000 = 1190000$ mg $= 1.19$ kg

Soda (100% pure) per litre $= \frac{106}{100}[11.25 + 12.5 + 3.158] = \frac{106}{100}\times 26.91 = 28.52$ mg/L

Soda (100% pure) for 50,000 L $= 28.52\times 50000 = 1426000$ mg $= 1.426$ kg



**Result:** Lime required = **1.19 kg**; Soda required = **1.426 kg**.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/End Term 2024-25 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md:
Write short notes on any two:

a. Caustic embrittlement
items.answer_md: **Caustic embrittlement** is brittleness and cracking of boiler metal at stressed points (rivets, bends, joints) caused by **concentrated NaOH**. Residual $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}$ in lime-soda softened water hydrolyses at high pressure, $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3 + H_2O \rightarrow 2NaOH + CO_2}$; NaOH concentrates in hair cracks and dissolves the stressed iron as sodium ferroate ($\mathrm{Fe + 2NaOH \rightarrow Na_2FeO_2 + H_2}$). Prevented by softening with sodium phosphate, or adding tannin, lignin or $\mathrm{Na_2SO_4}$.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/End Term 2024-25 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md:
Write short notes on any two:

b. Break Point Chlorination
items.answer_md:
**Break-point chlorination** is the addition of chlorine to water just beyond the dose at which all reducing substances, ammonia (as chloramines) and organic matter are completely oxidised, so that **free residual chlorine** first appears; that dose is the **break point**.

- On a plot of residual chlorine vs chlorine applied, the residual first rises (chloramines), then falls to a minimum (break point), then rises linearly (free chlorine).
- Dosing up to the break point ensures complete disinfection, removes taste, odour and colour, and leaves a free residual (about 0.1-0.2 ppm) that guards against recontamination.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/End Term 2024-25 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md:
Write short notes on any two:

c. Priming and Foaming
items.answer_md:
- **Priming:** carrying over of water droplets with steam (wet steam), caused by high steam velocity, high water level, sudden boiling and poor boiler design. Prevented by steam purifiers, low water level and soft water.
- **Foaming:** formation of persistent bubbles at the water surface, caused by oil and alkalis that lower surface tension. Prevented by antifoams (castor oil) and removing oil with sodium aluminate.
- Together they are called **carry-over**; they deposit salts on turbine blades and upset water-level readings.

items.question_md: Write in detail the De-ionization process to remove all the cations and anions present in hard water. Explain the set up with the help of a diagram.
items.answer_md:
**De-ionization (demineralisation)** removes **all** cations ($\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$, $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$, $\mathrm{Na^+}$ ...) and anions ($\mathrm{Cl^-}$, $\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}$, $\mathrm{HCO_3^-}$ ...) by passing water through ion-exchange resins: long-chain, cross-linked, insoluble styrene-divinylbenzene copolymers carrying exchangeable groups.

**Set-up**

```
        Acid (HCl)                       Alkali (NaOH)
      regenerant tank                   regenerant tank
            |                                 |
 Hard  ---> +-----------+       ---->   +-----------+         +----------+
 water      | CATION    |   (acidic     | ANION     |  ---->  | DEGASSER |---> Demineralised
 (pump)     | EXCHANGER |    water)     | EXCHANGER |         | (removes |     (soft) water
            |  R-H+     |               |  R'-OH-   |         |   CO2)   |
            | resin bed |               | resin bed |         +----------+
            | on gravel |               | on gravel |
            +-----+-----+               +-----+-----+
                  |                           |
           Washings to sink            Washings to sink
```

**Working**
1. Hard water is first passed through the **cation exchange column**, which exchanges all cations for $\mathrm{H^+}$; the water leaving it is acidic.
2. It then passes through the **anion exchange column**, which exchanges all anions for $\mathrm{OH^-}$.
3. $\mathrm{H^+}$ and $\mathrm{OH^-}$ combine to form water, so the outlet is ion-free (deionised) water. A **degasser** removes $\mathrm{CO_2}$ formed from bicarbonates.

**Reactions in the cation exchanger** ($\mathrm{RH^+}$, sulphonic acid resin):
$$\mathrm{2RH^+ + Ca^{2+} \rightarrow R_2Ca^{2+} + 2H^+}$$
$$\mathrm{2RH^+ + Mg^{2+} \rightarrow R_2Mg^{2+} + 2H^+}$$
$$\mathrm{RH^+ + Na^+ \rightarrow RNa^+ + H^+}$$

**Reactions in the anion exchanger** ($\mathrm{R'OH^-}$, quaternary ammonium resin):
$$\mathrm{R'OH^- + Cl^- \rightarrow R'Cl^- + OH^-}$$
$$\mathrm{2R'OH^- + SO_4^{2-} \rightarrow R'_2SO_4^{2-} + 2OH^-}$$
$$\mathrm{2R'OH^- + CO_3^{2-} \rightarrow R'_2CO_3^{2-} + 2OH^-}$$

The $\mathrm{H^+}$ and $\mathrm{OH^-}$ released combine: $\mathrm{H^+ + OH^- \rightarrow H_2O}$.

**Regeneration** (when exhausted):
$$\mathrm{R_2Ca^{2+} + 2HCl \rightarrow 2RH^+ + CaCl_2}\quad(\text{dil. HCl or } \mathrm{H_2SO_4})$$
$$\mathrm{R'Cl^- + NaOH \rightarrow R'OH^- + NaCl}\quad(\text{dil. NaOH})$$

After regeneration the columns are washed with water to remove $\mathrm{CaCl_2}$, $\mathrm{NaCl}$ to the sink.

**Advantages:** residual hardness as low as 0-2 ppm; works for acidic or alkaline water; product is fit for high-pressure boilers. **Disadvantages:** costly equipment and resins; turbid water must be filtered first, as turbidity fouls the resin.

items.topic: Numericals on calorific value and ultimate analysis
items.question_md:
A Sample of coal contains: C = 93 %, H = 6 % and ash = 1 %. The following data were obtained when the above coal was tested in bomb calorimeter:

(i) Weight of coal burnt = 0.92 g

(ii) Weight of water taken = 550 g

(iii) Water equivalent of bomb and calorimeter = 2,200 g

(iv) Raise in temperature = $2.42^\circ C$

(v) Fuse wire correction = 10.0 cal

(vi) Acid correction = 50.0 cal

Calculate gross and net calorific value of the coal, assuming the latent heat of condensation of steam as 580 cal/g.
items.answer_md:
**Given**: $x = 0.92$ g, $W = 550$ g, $w = 2200$ g, $\Delta t = 2.42\ ^\circ$C, $t_F = 10.0$ cal, $t_A = 50.0$ cal, H = 6%, $L = 580$ cal/g.

**To find**: GCV and NCV.

**Formulae**
$$\mathrm{GCV} = \frac{(W+w)\,\Delta t - (t_A + t_F)}{x}, \qquad \mathrm{NCV} = \mathrm{GCV} - 0.09\,H \times L$$

**GCV**
$$\mathrm{GCV} = \frac{(550 + 2200)(2.42) - (50 + 10)}{0.92} = \frac{6655 - 60}{0.92} = \frac{6595}{0.92}$$
$$\mathbf{GCV = 7168.48\ cal/g\ (kcal/kg)}$$

**NCV**
$$0.09 \times 6 \times 580 = 313.20\ \text{cal/g}$$
$$\mathrm{NCV} = 7168.48 - 313.20 = \mathbf{6855.28\ cal/g}$$

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/End Term 2024-25 Sem 1.pdf
items.topic: Calorific value and characteristics of a good fuel
items.question_md:
Write short notes on any two:

a. Gross and Net calorific value
items.answer_md:
**Gross (higher) calorific value (GCV):** total heat liberated when unit mass/volume of fuel is burnt completely and the combustion products are cooled to room temperature, so it includes the latent heat of condensation of steam. Measured by a bomb calorimeter.

**Net (lower) calorific value (NCV):** heat liberated when the products are allowed to escape uncondensed.

$$\mathrm{NCV = GCV - 0.09\,H \times 587\ kcal/kg}$$
(H = % hydrogen; 1 part of H gives 9 parts of water; 587 kcal/kg = latent heat of steam).

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/End Term 2024-25 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md:
Write short notes on any two:

b. Octane and cetane number.
items.answer_md:
**Octane number (ON)**: the percentage by volume of **iso-octane** (2,2,4-trimethylpentane, ON = 100) in a mixture with **n-heptane** (ON = 0) which has the same knocking characteristics as the petrol under test. E.g. ON 80 means the fuel knocks like a mixture of 80% iso-octane and 20% n-heptane.

**Cetane number (CN)**: the percentage by volume of **cetane** (n-hexadecane, CN = 100) in a mixture with **α-methylnaphthalene** (CN = 0) which has the same ignition quality as the diesel fuel under test.

High ON means good antiknock petrol; high CN means good diesel. Good petrol is a poor diesel and vice versa.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/End Term 2024-25 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md:
Write short notes on any two:

c. Producer gas
items.answer_md:
**Producer gas** is a mixture of mainly **CO (22-30%) and $\mathrm{N_2}$ (50-56%)** with some $\mathrm{H_2}$ (8-12%), and little $\mathrm{CO_2}$ and $\mathrm{CH_4}$. It is made by passing air (with a little steam) over red-hot coke at about 1100 °C in a gas producer: $\mathrm{C + O_2 \rightarrow CO_2}$, $\mathrm{CO_2 + C \rightarrow 2CO}$, $\mathrm{C + H_2O \rightarrow CO + H_2}$.
Its calorific value is low (about 1300 kcal/m³) because about half of it is $\mathrm{N_2}$. **Uses:** heating open-hearth and muffle furnaces, glass furnaces, and as a reducing atmosphere in metallurgy.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/End Term 2024-25 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: What are the differences between Proximate analysis and Ultimate analysis of coal? How will you calculate the amount of Nitrogen by ultimate analysis?
items.answer_md:
**Proximate vs ultimate analysis**

| Point | Proximate analysis | Ultimate analysis |
|---|---|---|
| Determines | Moisture, volatile matter, ash, fixed carbon | C, H, N, S, ash, O (elements) |
| Nature | Practical / commercial, empirical | Scientific, elemental |
| Method | Simple heating and weighing | Combustion, Kjeldahl, $\mathrm{BaSO_4}$ gravimetry |
| Use | Grading coal, judging its behaviour on burning | Calorific value by Dulong's formula, air needed for combustion |

**Nitrogen by Kjeldahl's method:** about 1 g coal is digested with conc. $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$, $\mathrm{K_2SO_4}$ and $\mathrm{CuSO_4}$; N becomes $\mathrm{(NH_4)_2SO_4}$. It is distilled with NaOH, the liberated $\mathrm{NH_3}$ is absorbed in a known volume of standard $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$, and the unused acid is back-titrated with standard NaOH.

$$\%\,\mathrm{N} = \frac{V \times N \times 1.4}{W}$$
$V$ = mL of acid neutralised by $\mathrm{NH_3}$, $N$ = normality of acid, $W$ = weight of coal (g).

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/End Term 2024-25 Sem 1.pdf
items.topic: Mechanisms of lubrication: thick layer, thin layer, extreme pressure
items.question_md: Explain the mechanism of hydrodynamic and boundary lubrication
items.answer_md:
**Hydrodynamic (fluid film / thick film) lubrication**
- The surfaces are completely separated by a continuous lubricant film thicker than the asperities (about 1000 Å); no metal contact.
- In a journal bearing the rotating shaft drags oil into the **converging wedge** between shaft and bearing; the pressure built up lifts the shaft and carries the load.
- Friction is only the internal friction of the oil, so **viscosity** is the key property; coefficient of friction about 0.001-0.03.
- Works at low load and high speed. Lubricant: mineral oils of proper viscosity with antioxidants. Example: shaft in journal bearing, turbines.

**Boundary (thin film) lubrication**
- At high load, low speed, start-stop, or with low-viscosity oil, the full film breaks and asperities nearly touch.
- A film only a few molecules thick is held on each surface by **physical or chemical adsorption** of polar molecules; these layers slide over each other and prevent welding of asperities.
- **Oiliness** is the key property; coefficient of friction about 0.05-0.15.
- Lubricants: vegetable/animal oils, their soaps, fatty acids, graphite, $\mathrm{MoS_2}$. Examples: gears, cams, rail wheels.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/End Term 2024-25 Sem 1.pdf
items.topic: Physical and chemical properties of lubricants and their testing
items.question_md:
Describe with their significance of the following :(Any Two)

a. Saponification number
items.answer_md:
**Saponification number:** the number of **milligrams of KOH required to saponify 1 g** of the oil.
**Significance:** vegetable and animal oils (esters) saponify but mineral oils do not, so it is used to **detect and estimate vegetable/animal oil in a blended oil** and to identify the oil. Formula: $\dfrac{(B - S) \times N_{\mathrm{HCl}} \times 56}{W_{\mathrm{oil}}}$ mg KOH/g ($B$ blank, $S$ sample titre).

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/End Term 2024-25 Sem 1.pdf
items.topic: Physical and chemical properties of lubricants and their testing
items.question_md:
Describe with their significance of the following :(Any Two)

b. Steam Emulsification number
items.answer_md:
**Steam emulsion number (SEN):** the time in **seconds** in which a given volume of oil and water emulsion (made by passing steam through the oil at about 90 °C) **separates** into two layers.
**Significance:** a good lubricant should have a **low SEN** (good demulsibility), so any water separates quickly; this is essential for steam turbines and marine engines.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/End Term 2024-25 Sem 1.pdf
items.topic: Physical and chemical properties of lubricants and their testing
items.question_md:
Describe with their significance of the following :(Any Two)

c. Aniline point
items.answer_md:
**Aniline point:** the **lowest temperature at which equal volumes of aniline and the oil are completely miscible**.
**Significance:** aromatic hydrocarbons dissolve in aniline easily, so a **high aniline point** means low aromatic content; such oil does not dissolve or swell **rubber seals and packings**. A good lubricant should have a high aniline point.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/End Term 2024-25 Sem 1.pdf
items.topic: Physical and chemical properties of lubricants and their testing
items.question_md:
Describe with their significance of the following :(Any Two)

d. Carbon residue
items.answer_md:
**Carbon residue:** the percentage of **carbon left** when a weighed oil sample is heated (destructively distilled) in a limited supply of air, as in the **Conradson** apparatus.
**Significance:** carbon deposits foul engine cylinders, piston rings and valves; so a good lubricant, especially for IC engines and air compressors, should have a **low carbon residue**.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/End Term 2024-25 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: What are solid lubricants? Explain the structure of graphite and molybdenum di sulphide.
items.answer_md:
**Solid lubricants** are solids with a layered structure, used as dry powder or dispersed in oil/water, where liquid lubricants fail: very high load or temperature, slow speed, or where oil contamination is not allowed. Examples: graphite, molybdenum disulphide, talc, mica.

**Structure of graphite**
- Each carbon is $sp^2$ hybridised and bonded to three others, forming flat **hexagonal layers** (C-C about 1.42 Å).
- The layers are about 3.35 Å apart and held only by **weak van der Waals forces**.
- So layers slide over each other easily, giving low friction. Graphite is used as powder, **oildag** (in oil) or **aquadag** (in water).

**Structure of molybdenum disulphide ($\mathrm{MoS_2}$)**
- Hexagonal **sandwich layers**: a sheet of Mo atoms between two sheets of S atoms (S-Mo-S), strongly bonded within the layer.
- Adjacent sandwiches are held by **weak van der Waals forces** between S layers, so they shear easily.
- Unlike graphite, it does not need adsorbed moisture to lubricate, so it works even in **vacuum** (space equipment).

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/End Term 2024-25 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: Explain the mechanism of polymerization which is initiated in the presence of benzoyl peroxide.
items.answer_md:
Benzoyl peroxide is a free radical initiator, so the polymerisation is **free radical (addition) polymerisation**. Example: ethylene to polyethylene.

**Free radical polymerisation** (initiator: benzoyl peroxide, monomer: ethylene)

1. **Initiation:** the peroxide splits on heating into free radicals, which add to the monomer.
$$\mathrm{(C_6H_5COO)_2 \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2\,C_6H_5COO^{\bullet} \rightarrow 2\,C_6H_5^{\bullet} + 2\,CO_2}$$
$$\mathrm{R^{\bullet} + CH_2{=}CH_2 \rightarrow R{-}CH_2{-}CH_2^{\bullet}} \quad (\mathrm{R^{\bullet}} = \mathrm{C_6H_5^{\bullet}})$$
2. **Propagation:** the radical adds monomer after monomer.
$$\mathrm{R{-}CH_2{-}CH_2^{\bullet} + n\,CH_2{=}CH_2 \rightarrow R{-}(CH_2{-}CH_2)_n{-}CH_2{-}CH_2^{\bullet}}$$
3. **Termination:** two growing radicals destroy each other.
   - by coupling (combination): $\mathrm{R{-}(CH_2CH_2)_m^{\bullet} + {}^{\bullet}(CH_2CH_2)_n{-}R \rightarrow R{-}(CH_2CH_2)_{m+n}{-}R}$
   - by disproportionation (H-atom transfer): $\mathrm{{\sim}CH_2{-}CH_2^{\bullet} + {}^{\bullet}CH_2{-}CH_2{\sim} \rightarrow {\sim}CH{=}CH_2 + CH_3{-}CH_2{\sim}}$

Benzoyl peroxide is used in small amounts; heat (or light) breaks the weak O-O bond to start the chain.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/End Term 2024-25 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: Write the mathematical formula of number-average molecular weight and weight-average molecular weight of the polymers.
items.answer_md:
**Number average molecular weight:**
$$\overline{M}_n = \frac{\sum N_i M_i}{\sum N_i}$$
**Weight average molecular weight:**
$$\overline{M}_w = \frac{\sum N_i M_i^2}{\sum N_i M_i} = \sum w_i M_i$$
where $N_i$ = number of molecules (or moles) having molar mass $M_i$ and $w_i$ = weight fraction of those molecules ($\sum w_i = 1$). Units: g/mol.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/End Term 2024-25 Sem 1.pdf
items.topic: Manufacture of Portland cement (wet and dry)
items.question_md: Describe the Wet method of preparation (with equations) of Portland cement with the labeled diagram of Rotary kiln.
items.answer_md:
**Raw materials:** calcareous material (limestone, chalk; supplies $\mathrm{CaO}$) and argillaceous material (clay, shale; supplies $\mathrm{SiO_2, Al_2O_3, Fe_2O_3}$) in about **3 : 1** ratio; powdered coal, oil or gas as fuel; 2 to 3% gypsum added at the end.

**Wet process:**
1. Limestone is crushed; clay is washed with water in a **wash mill** to remove flint and organic matter.
2. Both are mixed in about 3 : 1 ratio and ground in a tube mill with water to a **slurry containing 35 to 40% water**.
3. The slurry is corrected for composition in correcting basins and stored in slurry tanks with agitation.
4. It is fed at the upper end of the rotary kiln.

**Reactions in the kiln zones:**

1. **Drying zone (upper end, about 400 $^\circ$C):** water of the slurry (or moisture of the raw meal) is evaporated; clay loses its combined water.
$$\mathrm{Al_2O_3\cdot 2SiO_2\cdot 2H_2O \rightarrow Al_2O_3 + 2SiO_2 + 2H_2O}$$
2. **Calcination zone (middle, 700 to 1000 $^\circ$C):** limestone decomposes.
$$\mathrm{CaCO_3 \xrightarrow{\sim 900^\circ C} CaO + CO_2\uparrow}$$
3. **Clinkering (burning) zone (lower end, 1400 to 1500 $^\circ$C):** lime combines with clay oxides; the mass partly fuses into hard greyish balls called **clinker** (3 to 20 mm).
$$\mathrm{2CaO + SiO_2 \rightarrow 2CaO\cdot SiO_2\ (C_2S)}$$
$$\mathrm{3CaO + SiO_2 \rightarrow 3CaO\cdot SiO_2\ (C_3S)}$$
$$\mathrm{3CaO + Al_2O_3 \rightarrow 3CaO\cdot Al_2O_3\ (C_3A)}$$
$$\mathrm{4CaO + Al_2O_3 + Fe_2O_3 \rightarrow 4CaO\cdot Al_2O_3\cdot Fe_2O_3\ (C_4AF)}$$

**Cooling and grinding:** hot clinker is cooled in a rotary cooler (the heated air is used for combustion), then ground in ball/tube mills with **2 to 3% gypsum** ($\mathrm{CaSO_4\cdot 2H_2O}$), which retards setting. Gypsum is added after the kiln, never inside it (it would decompose). The fine powder is Portland cement, stored in silos and packed.

**Labelled diagram of the rotary kiln (draw as described):**
- A long steel cylinder, about 2.5 to 3 m in diameter and 45 to 150 m long, lined inside with **refractory firebricks**, **inclined** slightly (about 1 in 25) and **rotating slowly** (about 1 rpm) on roller supports driven by a gear.
- **Upper end:** inlet for the slurry (wet process) or raw meal (dry process), feed hopper, and the outlet for hot gases to the **chimney** (via dust collector).
- **Lower end:** **burner** where powdered coal, oil or gas is blown in with hot air, and the outlet for **clinker** to the **rotary cooler**.
- Mark the three zones from the top: **drying zone** (about 400 $^\circ$C), **calcination zone** (700 to 1000 $^\circ$C), **clinkering (burning) zone** (1400 to 1500 $^\circ$C) nearest the burner.
- Arrows: charge moves down, hot gases move up (**counter-current**).

```
 slurry/raw meal --> [hopper]
                        \   <- hot gases to chimney
 ___________________________________________________
|  DRYING ZONE   |  CALCINATION ZONE  |  CLINKERING  |<== burner (coal dust
|   ~400 C       |    700-1000 C      |   1400-1500 C|    + hot air)
|________________|____________________|______________|
   firebrick lining, inclined, rotating ~1 rpm          \
                                                         --> clinker to cooler
                                                             --> grind + 2-3% gypsum
```

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/End Term 2024-25 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: What is the effect of nature of oxide film on metal during corrosion?
items.answer_md:
In dry corrosion the metal first forms a surface film of oxide; further attack is possible only if $\mathrm{M^{n+}}$ ions or $\mathrm{O^{2-}}$ ions can diffuse through it. Hence the **nature of the oxide film decides the rate**:

1. **Stable (protective) film:** fine-grained, tightly adhering, non-porous; it acts as a barrier and stops further oxidation. e.g. Al, Sn, Pb, Cu, Cr ($\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$, $\mathrm{Cr_2O_3}$).
2. **Unstable film:** the oxide decomposes back to metal and oxygen ($\mathrm{2M_2O \rightleftharpoons 4M + O_2}$), so no lasting corrosion. e.g. Ag, Au, Pt.
3. **Volatile film:** the oxide evaporates as it forms, exposing fresh metal, so corrosion is rapid and continuous. e.g. $\mathrm{MoO_3}$ on molybdenum.
4. **Porous film:** has pores or cracks through which oxygen reaches the metal, so oxidation continues till the metal is consumed. e.g. alkali and alkaline earth metals (Na, K, Mg, Ca).

**Pilling-Bedworth rule:** $\mathrm{PBR} = \dfrac{V_{oxide}}{V_{metal}}$. If PBR < 1 the film is porous and non-protective (Na 0.58, Mg 0.81); if PBR is about 1 to 2 it is compact and protective (Al 1.29, Cu 1.68); if PBR is much greater than 2 the film is strained, cracks and spalls off (W about 3.4).

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/End Term 2024-25 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md:
Write short notes on any two:

a. Mechanism of wet corrosion by oxygen absorption
items.answer_md:
**Oxygen absorption** is the cathodic reaction of wet corrosion in **neutral or alkaline, aerated** solution (e.g. iron in moist air, sea water).

- Anode (metal, e.g. a scratch in the oxide film): $\mathrm{Fe \rightarrow Fe^{2+} + 2e^-}$
- Electrons flow through the metal to the cathode (the oxide-covered or more aerated area): $\mathrm{\tfrac12 O_2 + H_2O + 2e^- \rightarrow 2OH^-}$
- $\mathrm{Fe^{2+} + 2OH^- \rightarrow Fe(OH)_2}$; with excess oxygen $\mathrm{4Fe(OH)_2 + O_2 + 2H_2O \rightarrow 4Fe(OH)_3}$, i.e. yellow rust $\mathrm{Fe_2O_3\cdot xH_2O}$; with limited oxygen, black $\mathrm{Fe_3O_4}$.

Small anode, large cathode: the metal is eaten at the anode, rust deposits near the cathode (between the two).

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/End Term 2024-25 Sem 1.pdf
items.topic: Soil, pitting, intergranular, waterline and stress corrosion
items.question_md:
Write short notes on any two:

b. Pitting corrosion
items.answer_md:
**Pitting corrosion** is localised, accelerated attack that produces small but deep holes (pits, cavities) in the metal while the rest of the surface remains largely unaffected.

- **Cause:** breakdown of the protective film (scratch, $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ attack, inclusions) or a deposit (sand, dust, water drop) on the surface, giving **differential aeration**: the area under the deposit is poorly aerated and becomes a **small anode**; the large surrounding surface is the cathode.
- Anode (inside the pit): $\mathrm{Fe \rightarrow Fe^{2+} + 2e^-}$; cathode (surrounding surface): $\mathrm{O_2 + 2H_2O + 4e^- \rightarrow 4OH^-}$.
- Small anode / large cathode makes the attack intense and self-accelerating; e.g. stainless steel in chloride solutions.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/End Term 2024-25 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md:
Write short notes on any two:

c. Sacrificial anodic protection method
items.answer_md:
**Sacrificial anodic protection** (a cathodic protection method): the metal structure to be protected is connected by a wire to a **more active (anodic) metal** such as **Mg, Zn or Al** (or their alloys). The active metal acts as the anode and corrodes ("sacrificed"), while the structure becomes the cathode and is protected.

- Anode reaction: $\mathrm{Mg \rightarrow Mg^{2+} + 2e^-}$; electrons flow to the steel, which acts as cathode: $\mathrm{O_2 + 2H_2O + 4e^- \rightarrow 4OH^-}$.
- The consumed anode is replaced periodically.
- Uses: buried pipelines and cables, ship hulls, water tanks, boilers, marine structures; magnesium blocks in domestic water heaters.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/End Term 2024-25 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: Discuss how the following factors influences corrosion: (i) Nature of metal, (ii) Nature of corroding environment.
items.answer_md:
**(i) Nature of metal**
1. **Galvanic position:** more active metals (higher in series) corrode faster; larger potential difference in a couple gives faster attack on the anode.
2. **Area ratio:** small anode with large cathode gives intense corrosion, rate $\propto A_{cathode}/A_{anode}$.
3. **Purity:** impurities set up local cells, so impure metals corrode faster.
4. **Oxide film / passivity:** a protective film (Al, Cr; PBR about 1 to 2) stops corrosion; porous films (Mg, Na) do not.
5. **Overvoltage:** higher $\mathrm{H_2}$ overvoltage reduces corrosion rate.

**(ii) Nature of corroding environment**
1. **Temperature:** rate increases with temperature.
2. **Humidity:** above critical humidity (about 60 to 80%) corrosion is rapid.
3. **Atmospheric impurities:** $\mathrm{SO_2}$, $\mathrm{H_2S}$, $\mathrm{CO_2}$, NaCl increase acidity and conductivity.
4. **pH:** low pH (acidic) accelerates corrosion of Fe; strongly alkaline medium passivates Fe.
5. **Oxygen / differential aeration and conductivity:** more dissolved $\mathrm{O_2}$ and more conducting electrolyte (sea water) give faster corrosion; the less aerated part becomes anodic.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/End Term 2024-25 Sem 2.pdf
items.question_md: Analyze advantages and disadvantages of Friction and explain the role of lubricants in managing friction using appropriate schematic presentation.
items.answer_md:
### Friction
**Friction** is the resistance to relative motion between two surfaces in contact, caused by the interlocking and momentary welding of their surface irregularities (asperities). Coefficient of friction $\mu = F/N$, where $F$ is the frictional force and $N$ the normal load.

### Advantages (useful friction)
- Makes walking, gripping and road traction of tyres possible.
- Brakes, clutches and belt drives work only because of friction.
- Nuts, bolts, screws and nails hold because of friction.

### Disadvantages (harmful friction)
- **Wear** of moving parts and loss of dimensions.
- **Heat** generation, which can cause **seizure** (welding) of parts.
- **Loss of energy** and lower mechanical efficiency; more fuel or power needed.
- Noise and vibration.

### Role of lubricants
A **lubricant** is a substance introduced between two moving surfaces to reduce friction and wear. It keeps the surfaces apart, so the solid (dry) friction between metals is replaced by the much smaller **internal (fluid) friction** of the lubricant. It also cools the parts, prevents corrosion, acts as a seal and carries away dirt.

### Schematic (draw as described)
1. **Dry surfaces:** two jagged metal surfaces with their peaks interlocking; arrow showing direction of motion; label "high friction, wear, heat".
2. **Thin-film (boundary) lubrication:** a layer of lubricant molecules adsorbed on each surface, a few molecules thick; some peaks still touch; label "reduced friction" (used at high load, low speed; oils with fatty additives, graphite, $\mathrm{MoS_2}$).
3. **Thick-film (hydrodynamic) lubrication:** a continuous film of oil thicker than the height of the asperities completely separates the surfaces; label "fluid friction only, minimum wear" (high speed, low load; e.g. journal bearings).

Thus lubricants keep the useful work of machines while removing most of the harmful effects of friction.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/End Term 2024-25 Sem 2.pdf
items.topic: Physical and chemical properties of lubricants and their testing
items.question_md: What are the characteristics of a *good lubricant*? Discuss **any four** reasons why water is not usually used as a lubricant despite being liquid.
items.answer_md:
**Characteristics of a good lubricant**
1. **Adequate viscosity** at working temperature to keep a film, and a **high viscosity index**.
2. **High oiliness** (sticks to metal under boundary conditions).
3. **High flash and fire points** (above working temperature).
4. **Low cloud and pour points** (flows in cold).
5. **High oxidation stability:** low Sligh oxidation number, low carbon residue, does not gum.
6. **Low acid value** (non-corrosive) and **low steam emulsion number** (separates from water).
7. **High aniline point** (does not attack rubber seals); low volatility.

**Why water is not used as a lubricant (any four)**
1. **Very low viscosity** (about 1 cP): its film is squeezed out under load, so metal-to-metal contact occurs.
2. **Causes corrosion/rusting** of iron and steel parts, since it dissolves oxygen and salts.
3. **Narrow liquid range:** it **boils at 100 °C** (evaporates from hot bearings) and **freezes at 0 °C** (fails in cold).
4. **Poor oiliness:** it does not adsorb on metal surfaces to form a boundary film.
5. Its viscosity drops sharply on heating, and it dissolves impurities and supports microbial growth.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/End Term 2024-25 Sem 2.pdf
items.question_md: Define emulsion and its types. Illustrate how such emulsion functions as lubricants using **any two** specific industrial applications.
items.answer_md:
**Emulsion:** a stable dispersion of one liquid as fine droplets in another immiscible liquid, stabilised by an **emulsifying agent** (soaps, sulphonated oils). In lubrication the two liquids are oil and water.

**Types**
1. **Oil-in-water (O/W):** oil droplets dispersed in water. Water gives cooling, oil gives lubrication.
2. **Water-in-oil (W/O):** water droplets dispersed in oil. Oil is the continuous phase, so lubrication is better, and the water reduces flammability.

**How they work as lubricants (two applications)**

**(a) Cutting fluids in metal machining (O/W)**
- **Soluble oil** (mineral oil + emulsifier) is diluted with water to give a milky O/W emulsion, sprayed at the tool-workpiece interface.
- Water, with its high specific heat, **cools** the tool and work, increasing tool life and keeping dimensions accurate.
- Oil droplets **lubricate** the tool-chip interface, reduce friction, prevent chip welding (built-up edge) and give good surface finish; the flow also washes away chips and the oil film prevents rusting.

**(b) Fire-resistant hydraulic fluids (W/O, invert emulsions)**
- Used in coal mines, steel mills and die-casting machines, near flames or hot metal.
- Oil (continuous phase) lubricates pumps and valves; the dispersed water (about 40%) absorbs heat and turns to steam if the fluid leaks onto a hot surface, smothering the fire.

(Other example: O/W emulsions as **rolling oils** in cold rolling of steel, which cool the rolls and lubricate the strip.)

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/End Term 2024-25 Sem 2.pdf
items.question_md: Compare and contrast knocking in petrol/gasoline and diesel engines. Is it feasible to employ the same anti-knocking additives for both engine types? Justify your answer.
items.answer_md:
### Knocking in petrol (SI) and diesel (CI) engines

| Point | Petrol engine | Diesel engine |
|---|---|---|
| Ignition | Fuel-air mixture ignited by a **spark** | Fuel injected into hot compressed air; **self-ignites** |
| Cause of knock | Unburnt end gas **self-ignites too early**, before the flame front reaches it (peroxide formation at high compression ratio) | **Long ignition delay**: injected fuel accumulates, then burns all at once |
| Fuel that knocks | One that ignites **too easily** (straight-chain alkanes) | One that ignites **with difficulty** (aromatics, branched) |
| Rating | Octane number (iso-octane 100, n-heptane 0) | Cetane number (cetane 100, α-methylnaphthalene 0) |
| Remedy | Raise ON: branched/aromatic fuels, antiknock (TEL, MTBE) | Raise CN: straight-chain fuels, cetane improvers (ethyl nitrite) |

**Similarity**: both give a sudden pressure rise, a metallic knocking sound, loss of power, overheating and mechanical damage.

### Can the same additives be used? **No.**
- The two problems are **opposite** in nature. In a petrol engine knock is due to **premature** ignition, so the additive must **delay/suppress** self-ignition. TEL does this by forming PbO that destroys the peroxide and free-radical chains.
- In a diesel engine knock is due to **delayed** ignition, so the additive must **promote** self-ignition. Cetane improvers (ethyl nitrite, isoamyl nitrite, acetone peroxide) decompose easily to give radicals that start combustion sooner.
- Adding TEL to diesel would lengthen the ignition delay and **increase** diesel knock; adding a cetane improver to petrol would increase petrol knock.

Hence antiknock agents for petrol and diesel must be different, just as good petrol (high ON) is bad diesel (low CN).

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/End Term 2024-25 Sem 2.pdf
items.topic: Numericals on calorific value and ultimate analysis
items.question_md: A Biogas sample by weight has $CH_4 = 64\%$, $CO = 2.8\%$, $H_2S = 3.4\%$, $CO_2 = 22\%$ and rest is $N_2$, calculate amount of air required for complete combustion of 500 L when 30% excess air is supplied. Also calculate the % of dry product obtained.
items.answer_md:
**Given** (by weight): $\mathrm{CH_4}$ 64%, CO 2.8%, $\mathrm{H_2S}$ 3.4%, $\mathrm{CO_2}$ 22%, $\mathrm{N_2}$ = 100 - 92.2 = 7.8%; volume of gas = 500 L; excess air 30%; air has 21% $\mathrm{O_2}$ by volume.

**To find**: volume of air supplied; % composition of dry products.

### Step 1: weight % to volume (mole) %
Per 100 g gas (moles = mass/molar mass):

| Gas | Mass (g) | M | Moles | Volume in 500 L (L) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\mathrm{CH_4}$ | 64 | 16 | 4.000 | 401.72 |
| CO | 2.8 | 28 | 0.100 | 10.04 |
| $\mathrm{H_2S}$ | 3.4 | 34 | 0.100 | 10.04 |
| $\mathrm{CO_2}$ | 22 | 44 | 0.500 | 50.22 |
| $\mathrm{N_2}$ | 7.8 | 28 | 0.279 | 27.98 |
| Total | 100 | | 4.979 | 500.00 |

(Volume of each gas = $500 \times$ moles/4.979, since equal moles occupy equal volumes.)

### Step 2: oxygen required
| Reaction | $\mathrm{O_2}$ needed (L) |
|---|---|
| $\mathrm{CH_4 + 2O_2 \rightarrow CO_2 + 2H_2O}$ | $2 \times 401.72 = 803.44$ |
| $\mathrm{CO + \tfrac12 O_2 \rightarrow CO_2}$ | $0.5 \times 10.04 = 5.02$ |
| $\mathrm{H_2S + \tfrac32 O_2 \rightarrow SO_2 + H_2O}$ | $1.5 \times 10.04 = 15.06$ |
| Total | **823.53** |

$\mathrm{CO_2}$ and $\mathrm{N_2}$ need no oxygen.

### Step 3: air
$$\text{Minimum air} = 823.53 \times \frac{100}{21} = 3921.57\ \text{L}$$
$$\text{Air supplied (30\% excess)} = 3921.57 \times 1.30 = \mathbf{5098.04\ L}\ (\approx 5.10\ \mathrm{m^3})$$

### Step 4: dry products (water condensed)
| Product | Source | Volume (L) | % |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\mathrm{CO_2}$ | $401.72 + 10.04 + 50.22$ | 461.98 | **9.68** |
| $\mathrm{SO_2}$ | from $\mathrm{H_2S}$ | 10.04 | **0.21** |
| $\mathrm{O_2}$ (excess) | $0.30 \times 823.53$ | 247.06 | **5.17** |
| $\mathrm{N_2}$ | $27.98 + 0.79 \times 5098.04$ | 4055.43 | **84.94** |
| Total | | 4774.51 | 100.00 |

**Result**: air supplied = **5098.04 L**; dry products: $\mathrm{CO_2}$ 9.68%, $\mathrm{SO_2}$ 0.21%, $\mathrm{O_2}$ 5.17%, $\mathrm{N_2}$ 84.94% by volume.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/End Term 2024-25 Sem 2.pdf
items.topic: Gross and net calorific value by bomb calorimeter
items.question_md:
A 1.50 g sample of fuel with a gross calorific value (GCV) of 20 kJ/g is combusted in a Bomb calorimeter containing 1000 g of water at an initial temperature of 24.5°C. The water equivalent of the calorimeter is 250 g; Cooling correction = 0.05°C; Acid correction ($t_A$) = 8.5 J; Fuse wire correction ($t_F$) = 4.0 J; Thread correction ($t_T$) = 1.5 J

Calculate the ***final temperature of the system***, assuming all the heat is absorbed by the water and the calorimeter body. *(Specific heat capacity of water: $c = 4.18\ J/g^\circ C$)*.
items.answer_md:
**Given**: $x = 1.50$ g, GCV = 20 kJ/g, $W = 1000$ g, $w = 250$ g, $t_1 = 24.5\ ^\circ$C, $t_c = 0.05\ ^\circ$C, $t_A = 8.5$ J, $t_F = 4.0$ J, $t_T = 1.5$ J, $c = 4.18$ J/g °C.

**To find**: final temperature $t_2$.

**Formula** (bomb calorimeter with corrections, in joules)
$$\mathrm{GCV} = \frac{(W+w)\,c\,(t_2 - t_1 + t_c) - (t_A + t_F + t_T)}{x}$$
$$\Rightarrow (W+w)\,c\,(t_2 - t_1 + t_c) = x \cdot \mathrm{GCV} + (t_A + t_F + t_T)$$

**Substitution**
- Heat from fuel: $x \cdot \mathrm{GCV} = 1.50 \times 20 = 30\ \text{kJ} = 30000$ J
- Corrections: $8.5 + 4.0 + 1.5 = 14$ J
- Total heat absorbed $= 30014$ J
- Heat capacity of system: $(1000 + 250) \times 4.18 = 5225$ J/°C

$$t_2 - t_1 + t_c = \frac{30014}{5225} = 5.744\ ^\circ\text{C}$$
$$t_2 - t_1 = 5.744 - 0.05 = 5.694\ ^\circ\text{C}$$

**Result**
$$t_2 = 24.5 + 5.694 = \mathbf{30.19\ ^\circ C}$$

(The cooling correction is the heat lost to the surroundings; the observed final reading is therefore 30.19 °C. If no heat at all were lost, the temperature would reach $24.5 + 5.744 = 30.24$ °C.)

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/End Term 2024-25 Sem 2.pdf
items.topic: Purification of water step by step
items.question_md: Illustrate coagulation and flocculation process with suitable diagram. How do these processes aid in sedimentation during water treatment?
items.answer_md:
Fine clay, silica and organic colloids in water (size about 1 nm - 1 µm) carry a **negative charge**; mutual repulsion keeps them dispersed and they never settle by plain sedimentation.

```
 Raw water          Coagulant (alum)
     |                    |
     v                    v
 +-----------+      +----------------+      +-----------------------+
 |  FLASH    |      |  FLOCCULATOR   |      |  SEDIMENTATION TANK   |
 |  MIXER    |----->|  slow paddles  |----->|  flocs settle,        |----> Clarified water
 |  (rapid   |      |  micro-flocs   |      |  clear water overflows|      to sand filter
 |  stirring)|      |  grow to large |      |                       |
 +-----------+      |  flocs         |      \___________ __________/
  COAGULATION       +----------------+                  |
  (charge                FLOCCULATION              Sludge outlet
  neutralisation)
```

**1. Coagulation (rapid mixing)**
A coagulant such as alum is added and mixed vigorously in a flash mixer for a few seconds. The trivalent $\mathrm{Al^{3+}}$ ions neutralise the negative charge on the colloids (destabilisation), and the coagulant hydrolyses to gelatinous $\mathrm{Al(OH)_3}$:
$$\mathrm{Al_2(SO_4)_3 + 3Ca(HCO_3)_2 \rightarrow 2Al(OH)_3\downarrow + 3CaSO_4 + 6CO_2}$$

**2. Flocculation (slow mixing)**
The water is stirred gently with slow paddles for 20-30 minutes. The destabilised particles and $\mathrm{Al(OH)_3}$ micro-flocs collide and stick together (bridging), growing into large, heavy **flocs** that also sweep up and entrap bacteria and colour.

**How they aid sedimentation**
1. Settling velocity rises sharply with particle size and density (Stokes' law, $v \propto d^2$), so the large flocs settle in hours, whereas the original colloids would stay suspended indefinitely.
2. Charge neutralisation removes the repulsion that kept particles apart, so they can aggregate.
3. The sweeping floc carries down fine silt, colloidal matter, colour and many bacteria, so turbidity is greatly reduced and the load on the sand filter is lowered.
4. The clear water overflowing from the sedimentation tank goes to filtration; the sludge is removed from the bottom.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/End Term 2024-25 Sem 2.pdf
items.question_md: A water sample contains following impurities: $Mg(HCO_3)_2$ = 146 mg/L; $Ca(HCO_3)_2$ = 81 mg/L, $MgSO_4$ = 80 mg/L; $MgCl_2$ = 9.5 mg/L; $Na_2SO_4$ = 15 mg/L. Calculate (i) Temporary (ii) Permanent and (iii) Total hardness.
items.answer_md:
**Given:** $\mathrm{Mg(HCO_3)_2}$ = 146, $\mathrm{Ca(HCO_3)_2}$ = 81, $\mathrm{MgSO_4}$ = 80, $\mathrm{MgCl_2}$ = 9.5, $\mathrm{Na_2SO_4}$ = 15 mg/L.

**To find:** temporary, permanent and total hardness.

**Formula:**
$$\text{Hardness (mg/L as CaCO}_3) = \frac{\text{mass of salt (mg/L)}\times 100}{\text{molar mass of salt}}$$

| Salt | Amount (mg/L) | Molar mass | ppm as $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ | Type |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\mathrm{Mg(HCO_3)_2}$ | 146 | 146 | 146 $\times$ 100/146 = 100 | temporary |
| $\mathrm{Ca(HCO_3)_2}$ | 81 | 162 | 81 $\times$ 100/162 = 50 | temporary |
| $\mathrm{MgSO_4}$ | 80 | 120 | 80 $\times$ 100/120 = 66.67 | permanent |
| $\mathrm{MgCl_2}$ | 9.5 | 95 | 9.5 $\times$ 100/95 = 10 | permanent |
| $\mathrm{Na_2SO_4}$ | 15 | 142 | - | no hardness |

Bicarbonates of Ca and Mg give **temporary** hardness; chlorides and sulphates of Ca and Mg give **permanent** hardness; $\mathrm{Na_2SO_4}$ is a sodium salt and causes **no hardness**.

**Temporary hardness** $= 100 + 50 = $ **150 mg/L as $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$**

**Permanent hardness** $= 66.67 + 10 = $ **76.67 mg/L as $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$**

**Total hardness** $= 150 + 76.67 = $ **226.67 mg/L (ppm) as $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$**

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/End Term 2024-25 Sem 2.pdf
items.question_md: Compare disinfection and sterilization in terms of effectiveness, applications and level of microbial control. List any **two methods** for each.
items.answer_md:
| Basis | Disinfection | Sterilization |
|---|---|---|
| Meaning | Destruction of **pathogenic** (disease-causing) micro-organisms only | Destruction of **all** micro-organisms, pathogenic or not, including spores |
| Level of microbial control | Partial; harmless microbes and spores may survive | Complete; the product is free of all living organisms |
| Effectiveness | Makes water safe to drink | Absolute kill; more drastic |
| Agents / conditions | Mild chemicals at low dose: $\mathrm{Cl_2}$, bleaching powder, chloramine, $\mathrm{O_3}$, UV | Severe conditions: boiling / autoclaving (steam at 121 °C), dry heat, high dose of chemicals, irradiation |
| Residual effect | Chlorination leaves a residual that protects water in the mains | Usually no residual protection |
| Applications | Municipal and domestic drinking water, swimming pools | Surgical instruments, hospital and laboratory media, pharmaceuticals, injection water |
| Cost / scale | Cheap; suited to large volumes of water | Costly; not practical for large volumes of municipal water |

**Two methods of disinfection**
1. **Chlorination** (liquid chlorine or bleaching powder): $\mathrm{Cl_2 + H_2O \rightarrow HOCl + HCl}$; HOCl inactivates the enzymes of pathogens.
2. **Ozonation / UV treatment**: $\mathrm{O_3 \rightarrow O_2 + [O]}$; nascent oxygen oxidises the microbes. UV light destroys their DNA.

**Two methods of sterilization**
1. **Moist heat (autoclaving / boiling)**: steam at 121 °C, 15 psi for 15-20 min kills all organisms including spores.
2. **Dry heat or radiation**: hot-air oven at 160-180 °C for 1-2 h, or gamma irradiation, for instruments and glassware.

Water treatment uses **disinfection**, since only pathogens need to be killed and sterilization of huge volumes is uneconomic.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/End Term 2024-25 Sem 2.pdf
items.question_md: Why are vulcanized rubber and thermoset plastics so different in flexibility, despite both having cross-linking? Illustrate.
items.answer_md:
Both are cross-linked, but they differ in **how many** cross-links there are and **what lies between them**.

**1. Vulcanised rubber: few cross-links (low cross-link density)**
- Only about 3-5% S is used, so a $\mathrm{-S-S-}$ bridge occurs only every few hundred chain atoms.
- Between cross-links are **long, flexible, coiled polyisoprene segments** whose $T_g$ (about -70 °C) is far below room temperature, so the segments rotate freely.
- On stretching, the coils straighten; the few cross-links stop chains slipping past each other and **pull them back** when the force is removed. Result: high **elasticity and flexibility**.

**2. Thermoset plastic (e.g. bakelite): dense 3-D network**
- Every monomer is polyfunctional (phenol reacts at 3 positions), so cross-links occur **every few atoms** through short $\mathrm{-CH_2-}$ bridges and rigid benzene rings.
- No long free segments exist; the network is effectively one giant molecule, $T_g$ is above service temperature, so no segment can move. Result: **hard, rigid and brittle**; it breaks rather than stretches.

**Illustration**
```
Vulcanised rubber              Thermoset (bakelite)
 ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~            -Ar-CH2-Ar-CH2-Ar-
        |S-S|                     |       |      |
 ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~             CH2     CH2    CH2
 (long coils, rare bridges)       |       |      |
                                -Ar-CH2-Ar-CH2-Ar-
                                (bridge at every unit)
```

**Proof:** if rubber is vulcanised with about 30% S, cross-link density rises sharply and it becomes **ebonite**, a hard, rigid, thermoset-like material. So flexibility is decided by **cross-link density and chain-segment mobility**, not by the mere presence of cross-links.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/End Term 2024-25 Sem 2.pdf
items.question_md: Explain the concepts of number average molecular weight ($M_n$) and weight average molecular weight ($M_w$) in polymers. Why is $M_w$ always equal to or greater than $M_n$ and what it signifies in terms of polymer properties.
items.answer_md:
### Why an average
A polymer sample contains chains of many different lengths (it is **polydisperse**), so its molecular weight can only be expressed as an average.

### Definitions
**Number average molecular weight:** total weight of the polymer divided by the total number of molecules; every molecule counts equally.
$$\overline{M}_n = \frac{\sum N_i M_i}{\sum N_i}$$
**Weight average molecular weight:** each molecule is weighted by its mass (weight fraction), so heavier molecules contribute more.
$$\overline{M}_w = \frac{\sum N_i M_i^2}{\sum N_i M_i} = \sum w_i M_i$$
Here $N_i$ = number of molecules of molar mass $M_i$, and $w_i = N_iM_i/\sum N_iM_i$ is the weight fraction.

$\overline{M}_n$ is measured by osmometry or end-group analysis; $\overline{M}_w$ by light scattering.

### Why $\overline{M}_w \ge \overline{M}_n$
Write $\langle M\rangle = \sum N_iM_i/\sum N_i = \overline{M}_n$ and $\langle M^2\rangle = \sum N_iM_i^2/\sum N_i$. Then
$$\overline{M}_w = \frac{\langle M^2\rangle}{\langle M\rangle} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \overline{M}_w - \overline{M}_n = \frac{\langle M^2\rangle - \langle M\rangle^2}{\langle M\rangle} = \frac{\sigma^2}{\overline{M}_n} \ge 0$$
since the variance $\sigma^2$ of the distribution cannot be negative. Physically, $\overline{M}_w$ gives extra weight to the heavier chains, so it is pulled above $\overline{M}_n$. Equality holds only when $\sigma = 0$, i.e. all chains have the same length (**monodisperse**).

**Example:** equal numbers of chains of 10 000 and 30 000 g/mol give $\overline{M}_n = 20\,000$ and $\overline{M}_w = (10^8 + 9\times10^8)/(4\times10^4) = 25\,000$ g/mol.

### Significance: polydispersity index
$$\mathrm{PDI} = \overline{M}_w/\overline{M}_n \ge 1$$
- PDI close to 1: narrow distribution, uniform properties, sharp melting (e.g. living anionic polymers).
- Large PDI: broad distribution; the low-mass chains act as plasticiser (lower strength, easier flow), the high-mass chains raise melt viscosity and toughness.
- Mechanical strength, toughness and melt viscosity correlate mainly with $\overline{M}_w$; colligative properties with $\overline{M}_n$.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/End Term 2024-25 Sem 2.pdf
items.question_md: *Raja Bhoj Setu* in Bhopal faces constant moisture and mechanical stress. Suggest a suitable RCC and cement composition for long-term durability of such structures. State how it helps to resist environmental damage.
items.answer_md:
A bridge over a lake is exposed to **moisture, wet-dry cycles, dissolved salts, $\mathrm{CO_2}$ and repeated traffic loads**, which cause corrosion of steel and cracking of concrete.

### Suggested RCC and cement composition
1. **Cement:** **Portland Pozzolana Cement (PPC, with fly ash)** or **Portland Slag Cement**, or OPC with low $\mathrm{C_3A}$ (sulphate-resisting, $\mathrm{C_3A}$ below about 5%). Pozzolana reacts with the free lime to form extra C-S-H gel, making concrete denser and less permeable:
$$\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2 + SiO_2 + H_2O \rightarrow CaO\cdot SiO_2\cdot H_2O\ (C\text{-}S\text{-}H)}$$
2. **Concrete:** high grade (M30 to M40 or above) with **low water-cement ratio (about 0.40 to 0.45)**, plasticiser for workability, well-graded clean aggregates, thorough compaction and **curing for at least 7 to 14 days**.
3. **Reinforcement:** adequate **cover (about 45 to 50 mm)**, epoxy-coated or galvanised bars, and corrosion inhibitors in the mix.
4. **Surface protection:** waterproof or epoxy coating/sealant on exposed faces; cathodic protection for critical members.

### How it resists environmental damage
- Low permeability keeps water, chlorides and $\mathrm{CO_2}$ away from the steel, so the steel stays in the alkaline, **passive** state.
- It slows **carbonation**, which otherwise lowers the pH and depassivates steel: $\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2 + CO_2 \rightarrow CaCO_3 + H_2O}$.
- Preventing rust avoids the volume expansion of rust that cracks and spalls concrete.
- Low $\mathrm{C_3A}$ and less free $\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2}$ resist **sulphate attack** and leaching.
- Steel carries tension and dense concrete resists fatigue and cracking under repeated mechanical stress.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/End Term 2024-25 Sem 2.pdf
items.question_md: How does concentration cell corrosion occur in metals and what is the underlying electrochemical mechanism that drives this process? Illustrate.
items.answer_md:
**Concentration cell corrosion** occurs on a **single metal** when different parts of its surface are in contact with electrolyte of **different concentration** or **different aeration**. The difference sets up a potential difference, so one part becomes anode and the other cathode.

**1. Metal-ion concentration cell:** the part in the more dilute solution of its own ions is the anode. From the Nernst equation, $E = E^\circ + \frac{0.0591}{n}\log[\mathrm{M^{n+}}]$, so the lower $[\mathrm{M^{n+}}]$ gives the more negative potential, i.e. the anode. Cell EMF at 25 °C: $E = \dfrac{0.0591}{n}\log\dfrac{C_2}{C_1}$ ($C_2 > C_1$).

**2. Differential aeration corrosion (most common):** the part exposed to **less oxygen becomes the anode** and corrodes; the well-aerated part is the cathode.
- Anode (poorly aerated): $\mathrm{M \rightarrow M^{n+} + n e^-}$ (e.g. $\mathrm{Zn \rightarrow Zn^{2+} + 2e^-}$)
- Cathode (well aerated): $\mathrm{O_2 + 2H_2O + 4e^- \rightarrow 4OH^-}$
- Product: $\mathrm{M^{n+} + n OH^- \rightarrow M(OH)_n}$

**Illustration:** a zinc rod partly dipped in dilute NaCl: the part deep in the solution (less $\mathrm{O_2}$) corrodes, while the part near the surface (more $\mathrm{O_2}$) is cathodic and protected. *Diagram in words:* vertical Zn rod in NaCl solution; upper zone near the water surface labelled "more aerated, cathode, $\mathrm{O_2 + 2H_2O + 4e^- \rightarrow 4OH^-}$"; lower immersed zone labelled "less aerated, anode, $\mathrm{Zn \rightarrow Zn^{2+} + 2e^-}$, corroded"; $e^-$ arrow up through the rod.

**Examples:** waterline corrosion (just below the waterline), pitting under dirt or drops, crevice corrosion under bolts and washers, corrosion of buried pipes passing through clay (less aerated) and sand (more aerated).

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/End Term 2024-25 Sem 2.pdf
items.topic: Soil, pitting, intergranular, waterline and stress corrosion
items.question_md:
Write explanatory note on ***any two*** of the following three:

(i) Soil Corrosion and its prevention.
items.answer_md:
**Soil corrosion** is the corrosion of buried metal structures (pipelines, cables, tank bottoms) by the soil, which acts as the electrolyte. Factors: moisture, aeration (clay is less aerated than sand, so a pipe passing through both corrodes in the clay by differential aeration), pH and acidity, dissolved salts and low soil resistivity, stray currents, and **sulphate-reducing bacteria** in anaerobic, waterlogged soils ($\mathrm{SO_4^{2-} + 8H^+ + 8e^- \rightarrow S^{2-} + 4H_2O}$; $\mathrm{Fe^{2+} + S^{2-} \rightarrow FeS}$, black).

**Prevention:** protective coatings (coal-tar/bitumen wrapping, epoxy, polyethylene sleeves); cathodic protection by sacrificial Mg/Zn anodes or impressed current; uniform backfill (sand/limestone) around pipes; proper drainage; insulation against stray currents.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/End Term 2024-25 Sem 2.pdf
items.question_md:
Write explanatory note on ***any two*** of the following three:

(ii) Passivity and Corrosion Resistance.
items.answer_md:
**Passivity** is the phenomenon by which a metal or alloy, though active in the electrochemical series, shows high corrosion resistance because a very thin (about 0.0004 mm), highly protective, non-porous and invisible oxide film forms on its surface in an oxidising environment.

- The film is adherent and **self-healing**: if scratched, it re-forms in the presence of oxygen.
- Examples: Al ($\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$), Cr, Ti, Ni, stainless steel (at least 11 to 12% Cr gives $\mathrm{Cr_2O_3}$ film), Fe in conc. $\mathrm{HNO_3}$.
- Hence Al and Ti resist corrosion although their $E^\circ$ is very negative.
- Passivity breaks down in $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ media or reducing conditions, leading to pitting; it is used in anodising and anodic protection.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/End Term 2024-25 Sem 2.pdf
items.question_md:
Write explanatory note on ***any two*** of the following three:

(iii) Factors influencing Metal Corrosion
items.answer_md:
**Factors influencing corrosion:**

*Nature of metal:* position in galvanic series (more active corrodes faster); relative areas of anode and cathode (small anode, large cathode is worst); purity (impurities create local cells); nature of oxide film (protective if PBR about 1 to 2); overvoltage (higher $\mathrm{H_2}$ overvoltage slows corrosion); physical state (stressed, fine-grained parts corrode faster); solubility and volatility of products.

*Nature of environment:* temperature (rate rises with temperature); humidity above critical value (60 to 80%); impurities in air ($\mathrm{SO_2}$, $\mathrm{H_2S}$, $\mathrm{CO_2}$, NaCl near sea); pH (acidic below about 4 is severe for Fe); conductivity of electrolyte; differential aeration and dissolved oxygen.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/Mid Term 2024-25 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: Define and Explain the preparation, properties and uses of Addition and Condensation polymers (2Examples).
items.answer_md:
**Addition polymers** are formed by repeated addition of unsaturated monomers **without loss of any atom**, so polymer molecular mass $= n \times$ monomer mass. **Condensation polymers** are formed by reaction between two different functional groups with **elimination of a small molecule** ($\mathrm{H_2O}$, HCl).

**Addition polymers**
1. **Polyethylene:** $\mathrm{n\,CH_2=CH_2 \xrightarrow{\text{peroxide, 1000-2000 atm, 200 °C}} -[CH_2-CH_2]_n-}$ (LDPE; Ziegler-Natta catalyst at low pressure gives HDPE). Properties: tough, flexible, chemically inert, good insulator. Uses: films, bags, bottles, cable insulation.
2. **PVC:** $\mathrm{n\,CH_2=CHCl \xrightarrow{\text{peroxide}} -[CH_2-CHCl]_n-}$. Properties: rigid, made flexible with plasticizer, flame retardant, good insulator. Uses: pipes, wire insulation, raincoats, floor tiles.

**Condensation polymers**
1. **Nylon-66:** $\mathrm{n\,H_2N(CH_2)_6NH_2 + n\,HOOC(CH_2)_4COOH \rightarrow -[NH(CH_2)_6NHCO(CH_2)_4CO]_n- + 2n\,H_2O}$. Properties: strong, tough, abrasion resistant, high m.p. (H-bonds). Uses: fibres, ropes, tyre cords, gears.
2. **Bakelite:** phenol + HCHO $\rightarrow$ methylol phenol $\rightarrow$ novolac (loss of $\mathrm{H_2O}$) $\rightarrow$ cross-linked with hexamethylenetetramine. Properties: hard, rigid, heat resistant, electrical insulator. Uses: switches, plugs, handles.

| | Addition polymerisation | Condensation polymerisation |
|---|---|---|
| Monomer | Unsaturated (C=C) | Two functional groups each |
| By-product | None | Small molecule ($\mathrm{H_2O}$, HCl, $\mathrm{CH_3OH}$) |
| Formula | Polymer = $n\times$ monomer | Repeat unit differs from monomers |
| Growth | Chain growth, fast, needs initiator | Step growth, slow |
