items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/Supplementary End Term 2024-25.pdf
items.question_md:
A sample of water on analysis was found to contain following impurities in mg/liter:

$Ca(HCO_3)_2$ = 10.0; $Mg(HCO_3)_2$ = 8.5; $CaSO_4$ = 12.0; $MgSO_4$ = 14.0

Calculate the temporary, permanent and total hardness of water in mg/liter. (At.wts Ca = 40; Mg = 24; C = 12; S = 32; O = 16; H = 1)
items.answer_md:
**Given:** $\mathrm{Ca(HCO_3)_2}$ = 10.0, $\mathrm{Mg(HCO_3)_2}$ = 8.5, $\mathrm{CaSO_4}$ = 12.0, $\mathrm{MgSO_4}$ = 14.0 mg/L. From the atomic weights: $\mathrm{Ca(HCO_3)_2}$ = 162, $\mathrm{Mg(HCO_3)_2}$ = 146, $\mathrm{CaSO_4}$ = 136, $\mathrm{MgSO_4}$ = 120, $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ = 100.

**To find:** temporary, permanent and total hardness.

**Formula:**
$$\text{Hardness (mg/L as CaCO}_3) = \frac{\text{mass of salt (mg/L)}\times 100}{\text{molar mass of salt}}$$

| Salt | Amount (mg/L) | Molar mass | ppm as $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ | Type |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\mathrm{Ca(HCO_3)_2}$ | 10 | 162 | 10 $\times$ 100/162 = 6.173 | temporary |
| $\mathrm{Mg(HCO_3)_2}$ | 8.5 | 146 | 8.5 $\times$ 100/146 = 5.822 | temporary |
| $\mathrm{CaSO_4}$ | 12 | 136 | 12 $\times$ 100/136 = 8.824 | permanent |
| $\mathrm{MgSO_4}$ | 14 | 120 | 14 $\times$ 100/120 = 11.67 | permanent |

Bicarbonates of Ca and Mg give **temporary** hardness; chlorides and sulphates of Ca and Mg give **permanent** hardness.

**Temporary hardness** $= 6.173 + 5.822 = $ **11.99 mg/L as $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$**

**Permanent hardness** $= 8.824 + 11.67 = $ **20.49 mg/L as $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$**

**Total hardness** $= 11.99 + 20.49 = $ **32.48 mg/L (ppm) as $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$**

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/Supplementary End Term 2024-25.pdf
items.question_md: Write short notes on: Temporary and permanent hardness
items.answer_md:
**Temporary (carbonate) hardness** is caused by the dissolved **bicarbonates** of calcium and magnesium (and carbonate of Fe). It is removed simply by **boiling**, which precipitates insoluble carbonate / hydroxide:
$$\mathrm{Ca(HCO_3)_2 \xrightarrow{\Delta} CaCO_3\downarrow + H_2O + CO_2\uparrow}$$
$$\mathrm{Mg(HCO_3)_2 \xrightarrow{\Delta} Mg(OH)_2\downarrow + 2CO_2\uparrow}$$

**Permanent (non-carbonate) hardness** is caused by the **chlorides, sulphates and nitrates** of calcium and magnesium (e.g. $\mathrm{CaCl_2}$, $\mathrm{CaSO_4}$, $\mathrm{MgCl_2}$, $\mathrm{MgSO_4}$). It is **not removed by boiling**; it needs chemical treatment (lime-soda, zeolite or ion-exchange process).

Total hardness = temporary hardness + permanent hardness (both expressed as ppm $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ equivalent).

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/Supplementary End Term 2024-25.pdf
items.topic: Scale and sludge: internal and external treatment
items.question_md: Write short notes on: Scale and sludge
items.answer_md:
In a boiler, water evaporates continuously, so dissolved salts concentrate and precipitate.

- **Sludge**: a soft, loose, slimy precipitate formed in the colder parts of the boiler by salts more soluble in hot water ($\mathrm{MgCO_3}$, $\mathrm{MgCl_2}$, $\mathrm{CaCl_2}$, $\mathrm{MgSO_4}$); poor conductor of heat; removed by **blow-down**.
- **Scale**: a hard, adherent coating on the hot surfaces, formed by $\mathrm{CaSO_4}$ (less soluble when hot), $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ from $\mathrm{Ca(HCO_3)_2 \rightarrow CaCO_3 + H_2O + CO_2}$, $\mathrm{Mg(OH)_2}$ and silicates; wastes fuel, overheats plates and may cause explosion; removed only by scraping, thermal shocks or chemicals (HCl, EDTA).

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/Supplementary End Term 2024-25.pdf
items.question_md: What is Lime soda method of softening of water? Explain cold lime soda method by suitable diagram.
items.answer_md:
**Lime-soda process** is an external (chemical) method of softening in which lime $\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2}$ and soda $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}$ are added in calculated amounts so that all soluble hardness salts are converted into insoluble $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ and $\mathrm{Mg(OH)_2}$, which settle and are removed by filtration. Lime removes temporary hardness, Mg salts, free acids, $\mathrm{CO_2}$, Fe and Al salts; soda removes calcium permanent hardness.
$$\mathrm{Mg(HCO_3)_2 + 2Ca(OH)_2 \rightarrow 2CaCO_3\downarrow + Mg(OH)_2\downarrow + 2H_2O}$$
$$\mathrm{MgSO_4 + Ca(OH)_2 \rightarrow Mg(OH)_2\downarrow + CaSO_4};\quad \mathrm{CaSO_4 + Na_2CO_3 \rightarrow CaCO_3\downarrow + Na_2SO_4}$$

**Cold lime-soda process (room temperature)**

```
             Raw water        Chemicals (lime + soda + coagulant)
                 |                 |
                 v                 v          Motor
          +------+-----------------+------+     |
          |      |  inner chamber  |      |  stirrer shaft
          |      |   (paddles,     |      |-----+
 Softened |  ====|=== wood-fibre ==|====  |  <- filter
 water <--|      |   stirring)     |      |
 outlet   |      |                 |      |  outer chamber
          |      +-------+---------+      |  (settling zone,
           \             v               /    water rises up)
            \     sludge settles        /
             \_________________________/
                         |
                   Sludge outlet
```

1. Raw water and calculated quantities of lime, soda and a **coagulant** (alum, $\mathrm{FeSO_4}$ or sodium aluminate) are fed into the **inner vertical chamber**.
2. A motor-driven stirrer with paddles mixes them thoroughly; the softening reactions occur at room temperature.
3. At room temperature the precipitates are very fine, so the coagulant forms a floc that helps them settle.
4. The water moves to the **outer conical chamber**; the sludge settles to the bottom and is removed through the sludge outlet.
5. Softened water rises through a **wood-fibre filter** that retains remaining particles, and leaves from the top outlet.

Residual hardness of cold-process water is about **50-60 ppm**.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/Supplementary End Term 2024-25.pdf
items.question_md: 2.5 g of coal was heated for 1 hr at 110 °C and the residue was found to be 2.415 g. The crucible was then covered and heated to $925 \pm 20$ °C and residue found to be 1.528 g. The crucible was again heated without lid until a constant weight is obtained. The last residue weighs 0.245 g. Calculate the percentage results of the above analysis.
items.answer_md:
**Given**: mass of coal = 2.5 g; after 1 h at 110 °C = 2.415 g; after covered heating at 925 ± 20 °C = 1.528 g; ash (final residue) = 0.245 g.

**To find**: % moisture, % volatile matter, % ash, % fixed carbon (proximate analysis).

**Moisture**
$$\%M = \frac{2.5 - 2.415}{2.5} \times 100 = \frac{0.085}{2.5} \times 100 = \mathbf{3.40\%}$$

**Volatile matter**
$$\%VM = \frac{2.415 - 1.528}{2.5} \times 100 = \frac{0.887}{2.5} \times 100 = \mathbf{35.48\%}$$

**Ash**
$$\%\text{Ash} = \frac{0.245}{2.5} \times 100 = \mathbf{9.80\%}$$

**Fixed carbon**
$$\%FC = 100 - (3.40 + 35.48 + 9.80) = 100 - 48.68 = \mathbf{51.32\%}$$

All percentages are on the original 2.5 g sample.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/Supplementary End Term 2024-25.pdf
items.question_md: Write short notes on: Cracking
items.answer_md:
**Cracking** is the decomposition of bigger, high-boiling hydrocarbon molecules into smaller, low-boiling ones (alkanes + alkenes), e.g.
$$\mathrm{C_{10}H_{22} \xrightarrow{\Delta} C_5H_{12} + C_5H_{10}}$$
It increases the yield and quality of petrol from heavy oils.

**Types**: (i) **Thermal cracking**: heat and pressure only; liquid phase (475-530 °C, 30-100 kg/cm²) or vapour phase (600-650 °C, 10-20 kg/cm²). (ii) **Catalytic cracking**: catalyst such as alumina-silica or zeolite at 300-450 °C and low pressure; fixed-bed or fluidised (moving) bed; gives higher yield and higher octane petrol.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/Supplementary End Term 2024-25.pdf
items.topic: Gross and net calorific value by bomb calorimeter
items.question_md: Write short notes on: Higher and lower calorific value
items.answer_md:
**Higher (gross) calorific value, HCV**: total heat liberated when unit mass of fuel is burnt completely and the products are cooled to room temperature, so the steam formed **condenses** and its latent heat is **included**. Measured in the bomb calorimeter.

**Lower (net) calorific value, LCV**: heat liberated when the products of combustion **escape** as hot gases, so the latent heat of steam is **lost**.

Since 1 part H gives 9 parts water:
$$\mathrm{LCV} = \mathrm{HCV} - 0.09\,H \times 587\ \text{cal/g}\quad(H = \%\ \text{hydrogen})$$

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/Supplementary End Term 2024-25.pdf
items.topic: Gross and net calorific value by bomb calorimeter
items.question_md: Describe the construction, working and calculations of Bomb Calorimeter.
items.answer_md:
## Bomb calorimeter

### Principle
A known mass of fuel is burnt completely in excess oxygen in a closed vessel; the heat liberated is absorbed by a known mass of water and the calorimeter. From the rise in temperature the **gross (higher) calorific value** is calculated. (Used for solid and non-volatile liquid fuels.)

### Construction (labelled diagram described)
1. **Bomb**: a strong, cylindrical **stainless-steel** vessel with an air-tight screw cap, able to withstand about 25-50 atm. The lid carries an **oxygen inlet valve** and **two stainless-steel electrodes**.
2. **Crucible**: a small Ni or Pt crucible held by a ring on one electrode, containing the weighed fuel pellet.
3. **Fuse wire**: a fine Mg (or Pt) wire stretched between the two electrodes and touching the fuel.
4. **Calorimeter**: a copper vessel holding a known mass of water in which the bomb is immersed.
5. **Stirrer**: electrically driven, keeps the water temperature uniform.
6. **Beckmann thermometer**: reads temperature to 0.01 °C.
7. **Air jacket and water jacket**: surround the calorimeter to prevent heat loss by radiation and convection.
8. Electrodes connected to a **6 V battery** through a switch for ignition.

*Diagram*: outer water jacket, inside it an air jacket, inside that the copper calorimeter with water; the steel bomb stands in the water with the crucible and fuse wire inside it between the electrodes; the $\mathrm{O_2}$ valve and electrode terminals on the lid; the Beckmann thermometer and stirrer dip into the water; leads go to the battery.

### Working
1. About 0.5-1 g of the fuel is weighed ($x$ g) as a pellet into the crucible; the fuse wire is placed touching it.
2. The bomb is closed and filled with **oxygen at about 25 atm**.
3. It is placed in the calorimeter containing a known mass of water ($W$ g); stirring is started and the initial temperature $t_1$ is noted.
4. The circuit is closed; the fuse wire glows and ignites the fuel, which burns completely: $\mathrm{C \rightarrow CO_2}$, $\mathrm{H \rightarrow H_2O}$.
5. The heat raises the temperature of water and calorimeter; the **maximum temperature $t_2$** is recorded.

### Calculations
Let $w$ = water equivalent of calorimeter, bomb, stirrer and thermometer (g).

Heat liberated by fuel = heat absorbed by water and calorimeter:
$$x \times \mathrm{GCV} = (W + w)(t_2 - t_1)$$
$$\mathrm{GCV} = \frac{(W+w)(t_2 - t_1)}{x}\ \text{cal/g}$$

**Corrections** for accurate results:
- **Fuse wire correction** $t_F$: heat from burning the fuse wire (subtracted).
- **Acid correction** $t_A$: S and N form $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$ and $\mathrm{HNO_3}$ exothermically (subtracted). Determined by titrating the bomb washings.
- **Cotton thread correction** $t_T$ (subtracted).
- **Cooling correction** $t_c$ = rate of cooling × time taken to cool from $t_2$ to room temperature (**added** to the temperature rise).

$$\boxed{\mathrm{GCV} = \frac{(W+w)(t_2 - t_1 + t_c) - (t_A + t_F + t_T)}{x}}$$

**Net calorific value**: the steam formed condenses inside the bomb, so the value found is the **GCV**. Since 1 part H gives 9 parts water ($\mathrm{H_2 + \tfrac12 O_2 \rightarrow H_2O}$, 2 g H gives 18 g), mass of water per g fuel $= 0.09H$:
$$\boxed{\mathrm{NCV} = \mathrm{GCV} - 0.09\,H \times 587\ \text{cal/g}}$$
where H = % hydrogen and 587 cal/g is the latent heat of condensation of steam.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/Supplementary End Term 2024-25.pdf
items.topic: Mechanisms of lubrication: thick layer, thin layer, extreme pressure
items.question_md: Explain the Thick and Thin layer mechanisms of Lubricating oils.
items.answer_md:
**Thick layer (fluid film) mechanism:** the moving surfaces are completely separated by an oil film thicker than the surface irregularities (about 1000 Å), so there is no metal contact; friction comes only from the oil's **viscosity**. It works at low load and high speed, e.g. journal bearings.

**Thin layer (boundary) mechanism:** at high load or low speed a full film cannot form; a film only a few molecules thick is **adsorbed** on the metal surfaces. **Oiliness** matters here; vegetable/animal oils, graphite and $\mathrm{MoS_2}$ are used, e.g. gears and cams.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/Supplementary End Term 2024-25.pdf
items.topic: Physical and chemical properties of lubricants and their testing
items.question_md: Write short notes on: Flash and fire point
items.answer_md:
**Flash point:** the lowest temperature at which an oil gives off enough vapour to **ignite for a moment** (flash) when a small flame is brought near it.
**Fire point:** the lowest temperature at which the vapours **burn continuously for at least 5 seconds**. Fire point is usually 5-40 °C above flash point.

Both are found with the **Pensky-Martens** (closed cup) or Cleveland (open cup) apparatus. A good lubricant must have flash and fire points **well above its working temperature**, so it does not catch fire during use.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/Supplementary End Term 2024-25.pdf
items.question_md: Write short notes on: Functions of lubricants
items.answer_md:
A **lubricant** is a substance put between moving surfaces to reduce friction. Its functions:

1. **Reduces friction** and so power loss; improves efficiency.
2. **Reduces wear and tear** of moving parts.
3. **Acts as a coolant**, carrying away frictional heat; prevents expansion and seizure.
4. **Prevents corrosion** by keeping air and moisture off the metal.
5. **Acts as a seal**, e.g. between piston rings and cylinder in IC engines.
6. Reduces **noise**, flushes away dirt and debris, transmits pressure in hydraulic systems, and lowers maintenance cost.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/Supplementary End Term 2024-25.pdf
items.question_md: Give detailed classification of lubricants as liquid, solid and semi-solid with suitable examples.
items.answer_md:
Lubricants are classified by physical state into three classes.

**1. Liquid lubricants (lubricating oils)**
- **Animal and vegetable oils:** tallow, lard oil, whale oil, neatsfoot oil; castor, palm, olive, coconut, rapeseed oil. Good oiliness but oxidise, gum and are costly.
- **Mineral (petroleum) oils:** fractions from distillation of crude oil (paraffinic, naphthenic). Cheap and stable but poor oiliness.
- **Blended (compounded) oils:** mineral oil + additives such as oiliness agents (fatty oils), VI improvers, pour-point depressants, antioxidants, EP additives.
- **Synthetic oils:** silicones, polyglycols, esters, polyalphaolefins; for extreme temperatures.

**2. Semi-solid lubricants (greases)**
Oil thickened with metallic soap: calcium (cup) grease, sodium grease, lithium grease, axle grease. Used at slow speed and heavy load, intermittent working, and where the bearing must be sealed against dust and moisture.

**3. Solid lubricants**
Graphite, molybdenum disulphide ($\mathrm{MoS_2}$), talc, mica, soapstone, PTFE. Layered structures with weak interlayer forces. Used at very high load or temperature and where oil contamination is not allowed (food, textile machinery). Graphite is also used as oildag (in oil) and aquadag (in water).

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/Supplementary End Term 2024-25.pdf
items.topic: Manufacture of Portland cement (wet and dry)
items.question_md: Describe the method of preparation (with equations) of Portland cement with the labeled diagram of Rotary kiln.
items.answer_md:
**Raw materials:** calcareous material (limestone, chalk; supplies $\mathrm{CaO}$) and argillaceous material (clay, shale; supplies $\mathrm{SiO_2, Al_2O_3, Fe_2O_3}$) in about **3 : 1** ratio; powdered coal, oil or gas as fuel; 2 to 3% gypsum added at the end.

**Wet process:**
1. Limestone is crushed; clay is washed with water in a **wash mill** to remove flint and organic matter.
2. Both are mixed in about 3 : 1 ratio and ground in a tube mill with water to a **slurry containing 35 to 40% water**.
3. The slurry is corrected for composition in correcting basins and stored in slurry tanks with agitation.
4. It is fed at the upper end of the rotary kiln.

**Dry process:**
1. Limestone and clay are dried, crushed and finely ground separately.
2. They are mixed in the correct proportion (about 3 : 1) as a **dry powder called raw meal**, homogenised by compressed air in blending silos.
3. The raw meal (often made into nodules/pellets with about 12% water, or preheated in a suspension preheater) is fed into the rotary kiln.

**Reactions in the kiln zones:**

1. **Drying zone (upper end, about 400 $^\circ$C):** water of the slurry (or moisture of the raw meal) is evaporated; clay loses its combined water.
$$\mathrm{Al_2O_3\cdot 2SiO_2\cdot 2H_2O \rightarrow Al_2O_3 + 2SiO_2 + 2H_2O}$$
2. **Calcination zone (middle, 700 to 1000 $^\circ$C):** limestone decomposes.
$$\mathrm{CaCO_3 \xrightarrow{\sim 900^\circ C} CaO + CO_2\uparrow}$$
3. **Clinkering (burning) zone (lower end, 1400 to 1500 $^\circ$C):** lime combines with clay oxides; the mass partly fuses into hard greyish balls called **clinker** (3 to 20 mm).
$$\mathrm{2CaO + SiO_2 \rightarrow 2CaO\cdot SiO_2\ (C_2S)}$$
$$\mathrm{3CaO + SiO_2 \rightarrow 3CaO\cdot SiO_2\ (C_3S)}$$
$$\mathrm{3CaO + Al_2O_3 \rightarrow 3CaO\cdot Al_2O_3\ (C_3A)}$$
$$\mathrm{4CaO + Al_2O_3 + Fe_2O_3 \rightarrow 4CaO\cdot Al_2O_3\cdot Fe_2O_3\ (C_4AF)}$$

**Cooling and grinding:** hot clinker is cooled in a rotary cooler (the heated air is used for combustion), then ground in ball/tube mills with **2 to 3% gypsum** ($\mathrm{CaSO_4\cdot 2H_2O}$), which retards setting. Gypsum is added after the kiln, never inside it (it would decompose). The fine powder is Portland cement, stored in silos and packed.

**Labelled diagram of the rotary kiln (draw as described):**
- A long steel cylinder, about 2.5 to 3 m in diameter and 45 to 150 m long, lined inside with **refractory firebricks**, **inclined** slightly (about 1 in 25) and **rotating slowly** (about 1 rpm) on roller supports driven by a gear.
- **Upper end:** inlet for the slurry (wet process) or raw meal (dry process), feed hopper, and the outlet for hot gases to the **chimney** (via dust collector).
- **Lower end:** **burner** where powdered coal, oil or gas is blown in with hot air, and the outlet for **clinker** to the **rotary cooler**.
- Mark the three zones from the top: **drying zone** (about 400 $^\circ$C), **calcination zone** (700 to 1000 $^\circ$C), **clinkering (burning) zone** (1400 to 1500 $^\circ$C) nearest the burner.
- Arrows: charge moves down, hot gases move up (**counter-current**).

```
 slurry/raw meal --> [hopper]
                        \   <- hot gases to chimney
 ___________________________________________________
|  DRYING ZONE   |  CALCINATION ZONE  |  CLINKERING  |<== burner (coal dust
|   ~400 C       |    700-1000 C      |   1400-1500 C|    + hot air)
|________________|____________________|______________|
   firebrick lining, inclined, rotating ~1 rpm          \
                                                         --> clinker to cooler
                                                             --> grind + 2-3% gypsum
```

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/Supplementary End Term 2024-25.pdf
items.question_md: Write short notes on: Bakelite
items.answer_md:
**Bakelite** (phenol-formaldehyde resin) is a **thermosetting** condensation polymer.

**Preparation**
1. Phenol + HCHO (acid or base catalyst) give **o- and p-methylol phenol**:
$$\mathrm{C_6H_5OH + HCHO \rightarrow HO-C_6H_4-CH_2OH}$$
2. Methylol phenols condense with phenol, eliminating water, to give linear **novolac** (acid, excess phenol) chains linked by $\mathrm{-CH_2-}$ bridges.
3. On heating with **hexamethylenetetramine** (source of extra $\mathrm{CH_2}$), the novolac **cross-links** at o- and p-positions into a hard 3-D network, bakelite.

**Properties:** hard, rigid, scratch resistant; excellent electrical insulator; resistant to heat, water and most chemicals; cannot be remelted (thermoset).

**Uses:** electrical switches, plugs, switchboards, handles of cookers and utensils, telephone parts, ion-exchange resins.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/Supplementary End Term 2024-25.pdf
items.topic: Composition, setting and hardening of cement
items.question_md: Write short notes on: Setting and hardening
items.answer_md:
**Setting** is the stiffening of cement paste (loss of plasticity) within hours; **hardening** is the subsequent gain of strength over days and weeks. Both result from exothermic hydration of the Bogue compounds.

**Setting:** $\mathrm{C_3A}$ and $\mathrm{C_4AF}$ hydrate first (gypsum forms ettringite and prevents flash set):
$$\mathrm{3CaO\cdot Al_2O_3 + 6H_2O \rightarrow 3CaO\cdot Al_2O_3\cdot 6H_2O} + 880\ \mathrm{kJ/kg}$$
$$\mathrm{4CaO\cdot Al_2O_3\cdot Fe_2O_3 + 7H_2O \rightarrow 3CaO\cdot Al_2O_3\cdot 6H_2O + CaO\cdot Fe_2O_3\cdot H_2O} + 420\ \mathrm{kJ/kg}$$
**Hardening:** $\mathrm{C_3S}$ gives early strength (1 to 7 days), $\mathrm{C_2S}$ later strength (7 to 28 days), forming tobermorite gel (C-S-H) and $\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2}$:
$$\mathrm{2(3CaO\cdot SiO_2) + 6H_2O \rightarrow 3CaO\cdot 2SiO_2\cdot 3H_2O + 3Ca(OH)_2} \quad (+500\ \mathrm{kJ/kg})$$
$$\mathrm{2(2CaO\cdot SiO_2) + 4H_2O \rightarrow 3CaO\cdot 2SiO_2\cdot 3H_2O + Ca(OH)_2} \quad (+250\ \mathrm{kJ/kg})$$

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/Supplementary End Term 2024-25.pdf
items.question_md: Discuss the mechanism of free radical, cationic and coordination polymerization.
items.answer_md:
All three are chain-growth (addition) polymerisations with initiation, propagation and termination.

**Free radical polymerisation** (initiator: benzoyl peroxide, monomer: ethylene)

1. **Initiation:** the peroxide splits on heating into free radicals, which add to the monomer.
$$\mathrm{(C_6H_5COO)_2 \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2\,C_6H_5COO^{\bullet} \rightarrow 2\,C_6H_5^{\bullet} + 2\,CO_2}$$
$$\mathrm{R^{\bullet} + CH_2{=}CH_2 \rightarrow R{-}CH_2{-}CH_2^{\bullet}} \quad (\mathrm{R^{\bullet}} = \mathrm{C_6H_5^{\bullet}})$$
2. **Propagation:** the radical adds monomer after monomer.
$$\mathrm{R{-}CH_2{-}CH_2^{\bullet} + n\,CH_2{=}CH_2 \rightarrow R{-}(CH_2{-}CH_2)_n{-}CH_2{-}CH_2^{\bullet}}$$
3. **Termination:** two growing radicals destroy each other.
   - by coupling (combination): $\mathrm{R{-}(CH_2CH_2)_m^{\bullet} + {}^{\bullet}(CH_2CH_2)_n{-}R \rightarrow R{-}(CH_2CH_2)_{m+n}{-}R}$
   - by disproportionation (H-atom transfer): $\mathrm{{\sim}CH_2{-}CH_2^{\bullet} + {}^{\bullet}CH_2{-}CH_2{\sim} \rightarrow {\sim}CH{=}CH_2 + CH_3{-}CH_2{\sim}}$

**Cationic polymerisation** (catalyst: $\mathrm{BF_3}$ with co-catalyst $\mathrm{H_2O}$, monomer: isobutylene; favoured by electron-donating groups, low temperature about $-80$ to $-100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$)

1. **Initiation:** the Lewis acid and water give a proton, which adds to the monomer to form a carbocation.
$$\mathrm{BF_3 + H_2O \rightarrow H^+[BF_3OH]^-}$$
$$\mathrm{H^+ + CH_2{=}C(CH_3)_2 \rightarrow (CH_3)_3C^+\,[BF_3OH]^-}$$
2. **Propagation:** the carbocation adds monomer at its positive end.
$$\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C^+ + n\,CH_2{=}C(CH_3)_2 \rightarrow (CH_3)_3C{-}[CH_2{-}C(CH_3)_2]_{n-1}{-}CH_2{-}C^+(CH_3)_2}$$
3. **Termination:** the chain end loses a proton to the counter-ion, giving a terminal double bond and regenerating the catalyst.
$$\mathrm{{\sim}CH_2{-}C^+(CH_3)_2\,[BF_3OH]^- \rightarrow {\sim}CH{=}C(CH_3)_2 + H^+[BF_3OH]^-}$$
Product: polyisobutylene (with a little isoprene, butyl rubber).

**Coordination (Ziegler-Natta) polymerisation** (catalyst: $\mathrm{TiCl_4}$ + $\mathrm{Al(C_2H_5)_3}$, monomer: propylene)

1. **Formation of the active site:** the aluminium alkyl alkylates titanium, leaving a Ti atom with a Ti-C bond and a vacant coordination site ($\square$).
$$\mathrm{TiCl_4 + Al(C_2H_5)_3 \rightarrow Cl_3Ti{-}C_2H_5\,(\square) + Al(C_2H_5)_2Cl}$$
2. **Coordination:** the monomer double bond donates its $\pi$ electrons to the vacant site of Ti ($\pi$-complex).
3. **Insertion (propagation):** the monomer is inserted between Ti and the alkyl group; the vacant site is regenerated and the cycle repeats.
$$\mathrm{[Ti]{-}C_2H_5 + CH_2{=}CHCH_3 \rightarrow [Ti]{-}CH_2{-}CH(CH_3){-}C_2H_5}$$
$$\mathrm{[Ti]{-}CH_2{-}CH(CH_3){-}C_2H_5 + n\,CH_2{=}CHCH_3 \rightarrow [Ti]{-}[CH_2{-}CH(CH_3)]_{n+1}{-}C_2H_5}$$
4. **Termination:** by chain transfer with hydrogen (or by $\beta$-hydride elimination).
$$\mathrm{[Ti]{-}CH_2{-}CH(CH_3){\sim} + H_2 \rightarrow [Ti]{-}H + CH_3{-}CH(CH_3){\sim}}$$
Because each monomer is placed in the same orientation on the solid catalyst surface, the product is stereoregular (isotactic polypropylene, linear HDPE) at low pressure and temperature.

| Feature | Free radical | Cationic | Coordination |
|---|---|---|---|
| Active centre | free radical | carbocation | metal-carbon bond |
| Initiator | benzoyl peroxide, AIBN | $\mathrm{BF_3/H_2O}$, $\mathrm{AlCl_3}$ | $\mathrm{TiCl_4 + Al(C_2H_5)_3}$ |
| Product | branched, atactic (e.g. LDPE) | polyisobutylene | stereoregular, linear (isotactic PP, HDPE) |

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/Supplementary End Term 2024-25.pdf
items.question_md: What are factors which effect corrosion?
items.answer_md:
**Factors influencing corrosion:**

*Nature of metal:* position in galvanic series (more active corrodes faster); relative areas of anode and cathode (small anode, large cathode is worst); purity (impurities create local cells); nature of oxide film (protective if PBR about 1 to 2); overvoltage (higher $\mathrm{H_2}$ overvoltage slows corrosion); physical state (stressed, fine-grained parts corrode faster); solubility and volatility of products.

*Nature of environment:* temperature (rate rises with temperature); humidity above critical value (60 to 80%); impurities in air ($\mathrm{SO_2}$, $\mathrm{H_2S}$, $\mathrm{CO_2}$, NaCl near sea); pH (acidic below about 4 is severe for Fe); conductivity of electrolyte; differential aeration and dissolved oxygen.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/Supplementary End Term 2024-25.pdf
items.question_md: Write short notes on: Concentration cell corrosion.
items.answer_md:
**Concentration cell corrosion** occurs on a single metal when its parts are exposed to electrolyte of different concentration or different aeration, which creates a potential difference between them.

- **Differential aeration (most common):** the **less aerated part is anodic** and corrodes: $\mathrm{M \rightarrow M^{n+} + ne^-}$; the more aerated part is cathodic: $\mathrm{O_2 + 2H_2O + 4e^- \rightarrow 4OH^-}$.
- **Metal-ion concentration cell:** the part in the more dilute solution of its own ions is anodic ($E = \frac{0.0591}{n}\log\frac{C_2}{C_1}$).

Examples: Zn rod partly immersed in NaCl (immersed portion corrodes), waterline corrosion, pitting under dust/drops, crevice corrosion under bolts, buried pipes passing through clay and sand.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/Supplementary End Term 2024-25.pdf
items.question_md: Write short notes on: Requisites of a good paint
items.answer_md:
**Requisites of a good paint:**
1. Should form a tough, uniform, adherent film that does not crack on drying.
2. Should have good spreading power (covers large area) and hiding (covering) power.
3. Should dry quickly and give a glossy, smooth finish.
4. Should be resistant to corrosion, moisture, weathering and chemicals.
5. Colour should be stable (not fade) under light and atmosphere.
6. Film should be elastic and not peel off on temperature change; should be washable.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/2024-2025 PYQs/Supplementary End Term 2024-25.pdf
items.question_md: Discuss both oxidation and electrochemical mechanism of corrosion with proper diagram.
items.answer_md:
### 1. Oxidation (dry/chemical) mechanism

Direct attack of the metal by oxygen in the absence of moisture, usually at high temperature.

$$\mathrm{2M \rightarrow 2M^{n+} + 2n\,e^-}\ \text{(oxidation, at metal surface)}$$
$$\mathrm{\tfrac{n}{2}O_2 + 2n\,e^- \rightarrow n\,O^{2-}}\ \text{(reduction)}$$
$$\mathrm{2M + \tfrac{n}{2}O_2 \rightarrow M_2O_n}\ \text{(metal oxide)}$$

A thin oxide layer forms at the surface; growth continues by outward diffusion of $\mathrm{M^{n+}}$ (smaller, faster) and inward diffusion of $\mathrm{O^{2-}}$. The rate depends on the oxide film: **stable** (Al, Cr, Cu: protective), **unstable** (Ag, Au: decomposes back), **volatile** ($\mathrm{MoO_3}$: rapid attack), **porous** (Na, K, Mg: continued attack). Pilling-Bedworth ratio $V_{oxide}/V_{metal}$ about 1 to 2 means protective; < 1 porous; >> 2 cracks.

*Diagram (in words):* metal at the bottom, oxide film $\mathrm{M_2O_n}$ in the middle, $\mathrm{O_2}$ gas at the top; arrow "$\mathrm{M^{n+}}$ outward" and arrow "$\mathrm{O^{2-}}$ inward" through the film; $\mathrm{M \rightarrow M^{n+} + ne^-}$ at the metal/oxide interface, $\mathrm{\tfrac12 O_2 + 2e^- \rightarrow O^{2-}}$ at the oxide/gas interface.

### 2. Electrochemical (wet) mechanism

Occurs when a conducting liquid is in contact with the metal; anodic and cathodic areas form and current flows.

- **Anode:** $\mathrm{M \rightarrow M^{n+} + ne^-}$ (e.g. $\mathrm{Fe \rightarrow Fe^{2+} + 2e^-}$)
- **Cathode, (a) hydrogen evolution** (acidic, no $\mathrm{O_2}$): $\mathrm{2H^+ + 2e^- \rightarrow H_2\uparrow}$; large anode, small cathode.
- **Cathode, (b) oxygen absorption** (neutral/alkaline, aerated): $\mathrm{\tfrac12O_2 + H_2O + 2e^- \rightarrow 2OH^-}$; small anode, large cathode.
- **Product:** $\mathrm{Fe^{2+} + 2OH^- \rightarrow Fe(OH)_2}$; $\mathrm{4Fe(OH)_2 + O_2 + 2H_2O \rightarrow 4Fe(OH)_3 \rightarrow Fe_2O_3\cdot xH_2O}$ (rust).

*Diagram (in words):* iron covered with oxide film under NaCl solution; a crack in the film labelled **anode** ($\mathrm{Fe \rightarrow Fe^{2+}}$); the surrounding film-covered surface labelled **cathode** ($\mathrm{O_2 \rightarrow OH^-}$); rust deposited between them; $e^-$ arrow through the metal from anode to cathode.

Metal is corroded at the anode; corrosion product forms near the cathode.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2021-22 Sem 1.pdf
items.topic: Purification of water step by step
items.question_md: Name the steps followed to convert raw water into drinking water. Give importance of each step.
items.answer_md:
Raw water is converted to drinking (municipal) water by the following steps, in this order:

| Step | Importance (what it removes) |
|---|---|
| 1. **Screening** | Removes large floating matter (leaves, wood, plastics) that would damage pumps and choke later units |
| 2. **Plain sedimentation** | Removes heavy suspended particles (sand, silt) by gravity settling in 2-6 h, about 70-75% of suspended matter |
| 3. **Coagulation** | Alum etc. forms $\mathrm{Al(OH)_3}$ floc that neutralises and entraps fine colloidal particles, which do not settle by themselves; reduces turbidity and colour |
| 4. **Filtration** | Sand-gravel filter removes remaining floc, colloids and many bacteria, giving clear water |
| 5. **Disinfection** (sterilisation) | Chlorine / bleaching powder / ozone / UV kills pathogenic organisms; residual chlorine protects water in the mains |

Coagulation reaction: $\mathrm{Al_2(SO_4)_3 + 3Ca(HCO_3)_2 \rightarrow 2Al(OH)_3 + 3CaSO_4 + 6CO_2}$; disinfection: $\mathrm{Cl_2 + H_2O \rightarrow HOCl + HCl}$, HOCl kills germs.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2021-22 Sem 1.pdf
items.topic: Scale and sludge: internal and external treatment
items.question_md: Explain following: a. Scale and Sludge formation
items.answer_md:
In a boiler, water is continuously evaporated, so the concentration of dissolved salts rises. When their concentration exceeds the solubility limit they precipitate. A **soft, loose** precipitate is **sludge**; a **hard, adherent** one is **scale**.

**1. Sludge formation**

**Sludge** is a soft, loose, slimy precipitate formed in the colder parts of the boiler when water evaporates and salts that are **more soluble in hot water than in cold water** ($\mathrm{MgCO_3}$, $\mathrm{MgCl_2}$, $\mathrm{CaCl_2}$, $\mathrm{MgSO_4}$) reach saturation. It is a poor conductor of heat and can choke pipes, but is removed easily by **blow-down** (draining off a part of the concentrated boiler water and replacing it with fresh feed water).

**2. Scale formation**

**Scale** is a hard, adherent coating on the inner walls/heating surfaces of the boiler. Causes:

1. **Decomposition of calcium bicarbonate** (main cause in low-pressure boilers):
$$\mathrm{Ca(HCO_3)_2 \xrightarrow{\Delta} CaCO_3\downarrow + H_2O + CO_2\uparrow}$$
2. **Deposition of calcium sulphate** (main cause in high-pressure boilers): the solubility of $\mathrm{CaSO_4}$ **decreases** as temperature rises, so it separates as a hard scale on the hot surfaces.
3. **Hydrolysis of magnesium salts**:
$$\mathrm{MgCl_2 + 2H_2O \rightarrow Mg(OH)_2\downarrow + 2HCl}$$
4. **Silica** ($\mathrm{SiO_2}$) deposits as calcium or magnesium silicate ($\mathrm{CaSiO_3}$, $\mathrm{MgSiO_3}$), a very hard scale.

**Disadvantages of scale**:
1. **Wastage of fuel**: scale is a poor conductor of heat (e.g. 0.325 mm scale wastes about 10% fuel).
2. **Lowering of boiler safety**: overheating weakens the plates.
3. **Danger of explosion**: if the scale cracks, water suddenly meets the red-hot metal, forms steam at high pressure and may burst the boiler.
4. **Decrease in efficiency**: deposits in valves and condensers choke them.

**3. Comparison**

| Point | Sludge | Scale |
|---|---|---|
| Nature | Soft, loose, slimy, non-adherent precipitate | Hard, adherent coating on boiler walls |
| Where formed | Colder parts of the boiler, where flow is slow (bends, bottom) | Hot heating surfaces |
| Formed by | Salts more soluble in hot than cold water: $\mathrm{MgCO_3}$, $\mathrm{MgCl_2}$, $\mathrm{CaCl_2}$, $\mathrm{MgSO_4}$ | $\mathrm{CaSO_4}$, $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$, $\mathrm{Mg(OH)_2}$, $\mathrm{CaSiO_3}$ / $\mathrm{MgSiO_3}$ |
| Removal | Easily removed by scraping or **blow-down** | Difficult: scraping, thermal shocks, or chemicals (5-10% HCl for $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$, EDTA for $\mathrm{CaSO_4}$) |
| Harm | Poor conductor of heat, chokes pipes; less harmful | Wastes fuel, overheats plates, can cause explosion; more harmful |

**Prevention**: external treatment (lime-soda, zeolite, ion exchange) before feeding, or internal treatment (phosphate, carbonate, calgon conditioning) inside the boiler.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2021-22 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: Explain following: b. Priming and Foaming
items.answer_md:
**Priming** is the carrying over of water droplets with the steam from a boiler, so the steam becomes **wet**. It occurs when steam is produced rapidly and violently.

**Foaming** is the formation of small, **persistent bubbles** (foam) at the water surface in the boiler, which do not break easily. It is caused by oils, grease and alkalis that lower the surface tension of water.

Priming and foaming usually occur together and are jointly called **carry-over**.

**Causes of priming**
1. High steam velocity (sudden increase in steam demand).
2. Very high water level in the boiler.
3. Sudden boiling.
4. Faulty boiler design (inadequate steam space).
5. High concentration of dissolved and suspended solids.

**Causes of foaming:** presence of oil, grease and alkalis (and finely divided suspended matter) that reduce the surface tension of water.

**Ill effects**
1. Dissolved salts in the carried-over droplets deposit on superheater tubes and **turbine blades**, reducing their efficiency.
2. Wet steam reduces the heat content and efficiency of the steam; the dissolved salts may corrode the machinery.
3. Foam makes the **water-level reading** in the gauge glass unreliable, risking overheating or damage to the boiler.
4. Machinery parts that use the steam are damaged and their life is shortened.

**Prevention**
- *Priming:* fit mechanical steam purifiers (anti-priming pipes, baffles); keep a low water level; avoid rapid change in steam rate; use softened, low-TDS water; blow down concentrated water.
- *Foaming:* add antifoaming agents such as castor oil (in moderation; excess itself causes foaming); remove oil by adding sodium aluminate or alum; replace concentrated boiler water with fresh water (blow-down).

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2021-22 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: What is the difference between Disinfection and Sterilization? Explain 'Break-Point Chlorination' with necessary graph.
items.answer_md:
**Disinfection vs Sterilization**

| Disinfection | Sterilization |
|---|---|
| Kills only **pathogenic** micro-organisms | Kills **all** micro-organisms including spores |
| Partial microbial control | Complete microbial control |
| Mild agents: $\mathrm{Cl_2}$, bleaching powder, chloramine, $\mathrm{O_3}$, UV | Drastic agents: autoclaving, boiling, dry heat, irradiation |
| Used for drinking water | Used for surgical instruments, lab media, medicines |

**Break-point chlorination.** When chlorine is added to water in increasing doses and the residual chlorine is measured, the curve (residual chlorine vs chlorine applied) shows four zones:

```
Residual
chlorine |                                   /
         |                                  /  free residual
         |            combined             /   (rises linearly)
         |           /\ (chloramines)     /
         |          /  \                 /
         |         /    \               /
         |        /      \_____________/
         |_______/              ^
         |  A       B       C   |  D
         +-----------------------+----------> Chlorine applied
                          break point
```
- **A:** chlorine is used up by reducing agents ($\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$, $\mathrm{H_2S}$, $\mathrm{NO_2^-}$); no residual.
- **B:** chlorine forms chloramines and chloro-organic compounds; combined residual rises.
- **C:** further chlorine oxidises chloramines and organic matter; residual falls to a minimum, the **break point**.
- **D:** beyond the break point all added chlorine stays as **free residual chlorine**, which rises in proportion to the dose.

Chlorine is dosed just past the break point, so the water carries a small free residual (about 0.1-0.2 ppm) that kills pathogens and protects against recontamination in the mains.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2021-22 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: Calculate the amount of Lime (90% pure) and Soda (98% pure) for the treatment of 1 million litres of water containing impurities $Ca(HCO_3)_2$ = 8.1 ppm, $Mg(HCO_3)_2$ = 7.3 ppm, $CaCl_2$ = 11.1 ppm and $MgCl_2$ = 19 ppm [Molecular weights of $Ca(HCO_3)_2$ = 162, $Mg(HCO_3)_2$ = 146, $CaCl_2$ = 111 and $MgCl_2$ = 95 ppm]
items.answer_md:
**Given:** volume of water $V$ = 1 million L ($10^6$ L); lime purity = 90%, soda purity = 98%.

**To find:** mass of lime $\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2}$ (molar mass 74) and soda $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}$ (molar mass 106) required.

**Step 1: Convert each constituent to $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ equivalent**

$$\text{ppm as CaCO}_3 = \frac{\text{mg/L of salt}\times 100}{\text{molar mass of salt}}$$

| Constituent | Amount (mg/L) | Molar mass | Factor | ppm as $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ | Type | Needs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\mathrm{Ca(HCO_3)_2}$ | 8.1 | 162 | 100/162 | 5 | Temporary Ca | L |
| $\mathrm{Mg(HCO_3)_2}$ | 7.3 | 146 | 100/146 | 5 | Temporary Mg | 2L |
| $\mathrm{CaCl_2}$ | 11.1 | 111 | 100/111 | 10 | Permanent Ca | S |
| $\mathrm{MgCl_2}$ | 19 | 95 | 100/95 | 20 | Permanent Mg | L + S |

(L = lime, S = soda. Temporary Mg takes 2 lime; permanent Mg takes lime and then soda for the $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ it releases; Na, K salts and $\mathrm{SiO_2}$ cause no hardness and are ignored.)

**Step 2: Formulae**

$$\text{Lime} = \frac{74}{100}\left[\text{Temp Ca}\ (\mathrm{Ca(HCO_3)_2}) + 2\times\text{Temp Mg}\ (\mathrm{Mg(HCO_3)_2}) + \text{Perm Mg}\ (\mathrm{MgCl_2})\right]\times\frac{V}{10^6}\times\frac{100}{\%\text{ purity}}\ \text{kg}$$

$$\text{Soda} = \frac{106}{100}\left[\text{Perm Ca}\ (\mathrm{CaCl_2}) + \text{Perm Mg}\ (\mathrm{MgCl_2})\right]\times\frac{V}{10^6}\times\frac{100}{\%\text{ purity}}\ \text{kg}$$

**Step 3: Substitution**

Lime (100% pure) per litre $= \frac{74}{100}[5 + 2(5) + 20] = \frac{74}{100}\times 35 = 25.9$ mg/L

Lime (100% pure) for 1 million L ($10^6$ L) $= 25.9\times 1000000 = 25900000$ mg $= 25.9$ kg

Lime (90% pure) $= 25.9\times\frac{100}{90} = 28.78$ kg

Soda (100% pure) per litre $= \frac{106}{100}[10 + 20] = \frac{106}{100}\times 30 = 31.8$ mg/L

Soda (100% pure) for 1 million L ($10^6$ L) $= 31.8\times 1000000 = 31800000$ mg $= 31.8$ kg

Soda (98% pure) $= 31.8\times\frac{100}{98} = 32.45$ kg

**Result:** Lime required = **28.78 kg**; Soda required = **32.45 kg**.

**Reactions involved**
$$\mathrm{Ca(HCO_3)_2 + Ca(OH)_2 \rightarrow 2CaCO_3\downarrow + 2H_2O}$$
$$\mathrm{Mg(HCO_3)_2 + 2Ca(OH)_2 \rightarrow 2CaCO_3\downarrow + Mg(OH)_2\downarrow + 2H_2O}$$
$$\mathrm{MgCl_2 + Ca(OH)_2 \rightarrow Mg(OH)_2\downarrow + CaCl_2};\quad \mathrm{CaCl_2 + Na_2CO_3 \rightarrow CaCO_3\downarrow + 2NaCl}$$

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2021-22 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: What are 'Anti-knocking Agents'? Explain their mechanism by taking suitable example.
items.answer_md:
**Antiknocking agents** are substances which, added in small amounts to petrol, **reduce its knocking tendency** (raise its octane number). Examples: tetraethyl lead (TEL), $\mathrm{Pb(C_2H_5)_4}$; MTBE, $\mathrm{CH_3\text{-}O\text{-}C(CH_3)_3}$.

**Mechanism (TEL)**
Knocking proceeds by a free-radical chain through **peroxides** that decompose explosively. TEL breaks this chain:
1. $\mathrm{Pb(C_2H_5)_4 \rightarrow Pb + 4\,\dot{C}_2H_5}$ (ethyl radicals)
2. $\mathrm{Pb + O_2 \rightarrow PbO_2}$; Pb/PbO react with peroxides and radicals, deactivating them, so the chain stops and combustion is smooth.
3. To prevent PbO deposits, **ethylene dibromide** is added: $\mathrm{Pb + C_2H_4Br_2 \rightarrow PbBr_2 + C_2H_4}$; volatile $\mathrm{PbBr_2}$ leaves with the exhaust.

Because lead is toxic and poisons catalytic converters, **MTBE** is used in unleaded petrol; it supplies oxygen for complete combustion and suppresses peroxide formation.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2021-22 Sem 1.pdf
items.topic: Numericals on calorific value and ultimate analysis
items.question_md: Calculate the 'Gross Calorific Value' and 'Percentage of Hydrogen' in a coal sample having following composition: C = 90%; O = 3 %; N = 0.5%; S = 0.5% and Ash = 2.5%.
items.answer_md:
**Given**: C = 90%, O = 3%, N = 0.5%, S = 0.5%, ash = 2.5%.

**To find**: % H and GCV.

### Percentage of hydrogen (by difference)
$$\%H = 100 - (90 + 3 + 0.5 + 0.5 + 2.5) = 100 - 96.5 = \mathbf{3.5\%}$$

### GCV by Dulong's formula
$$\mathrm{GCV} = \frac{1}{100}\left[8080\,C + 34500\left(H - \frac{O}{8}\right) + 2240\,S\right]\ \text{kcal/kg}$$
- $8080 \times 90 = 727200$
- $34500 \times \left(3.5 - \frac{3}{8}\right) = 34500 \times 3.125 = 107812.5$
- $2240 \times 0.5 = 1120$

$$\mathrm{GCV} = \frac{727200 + 107812.5 + 1120}{100} = \mathbf{8361.33\ kcal/kg}$$

(N and ash contribute no heat; $O/8$ is subtracted because the fuel oxygen is already combined with hydrogen. If asked, $\mathrm{NCV} = 8361.33 - 0.09 \times 3.5 \times 587 = 8176.42$ kcal/kg.)

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2021-22 Sem 1.pdf
items.topic: Gross and net calorific value by bomb calorimeter
items.question_md: Why Lower Calorific Value (LCV) is lesser than Higher Calorific Value (HCV)? Describe the estimation of HCV and LCV in Bomb Calorimeter with suitable equations.
items.answer_md:
### Why LCV < HCV
The hydrogen of the fuel burns to water: $\mathrm{H_2 + \tfrac12 O_2 \rightarrow H_2O}$ (2 g H gives 18 g water, i.e. 1 part H gives 9 parts water). In **HCV** the products are cooled to room temperature, so this steam condenses and its **latent heat is included**. In **LCV** the steam escapes with the hot gases, so its latent heat is **lost**. Therefore
$$\mathrm{LCV} = \mathrm{HCV} - \text{latent heat of water vapour formed}$$

### Estimation in the bomb calorimeter
1. A weighed pellet of fuel ($x$ g) is placed in the Ni/Pt crucible inside a stainless-steel **bomb**, with a fuse wire touching it between two electrodes.
2. The bomb is filled with $\mathrm{O_2}$ at about **25 atm** and immersed in a copper calorimeter holding $W$ g of water, fitted with a **stirrer** and **Beckmann thermometer**, and surrounded by air and water jackets.
3. Initial temperature $t_1$ is noted; the fuel is ignited electrically and burns completely; the maximum temperature $t_2$ is noted.

**HCV** (the steam condenses inside the bomb, so the measured value is HCV):
$$\mathrm{HCV} = \frac{(W + w)(t_2 - t_1 + t_c) - (t_A + t_F + t_T)}{x}\ \text{cal/g}$$
where $w$ = water equivalent of calorimeter, $t_c$ = cooling correction (added), $t_A$, $t_F$, $t_T$ = acid, fuse wire and cotton thread corrections (subtracted).

**LCV**: mass of water formed per g of fuel $= \dfrac{9H}{100} = 0.09H$, with H = % hydrogen; latent heat of steam = 587 cal/g:
$$\mathrm{LCV} = \mathrm{HCV} - 0.09\,H \times 587\ \text{cal/g}$$

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2021-22 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: Discuss the concept of cracking and its importance? Also explain, how 'Thermal Cracking' is different than 'Catalytic Cracking'.
items.answer_md:
### Concept of cracking
**Cracking** is the decomposition of bigger, high-boiling hydrocarbon molecules into simpler, low-boiling hydrocarbons (a mixture of alkanes and alkenes):
$$\mathrm{C_{10}H_{22} \rightarrow C_5H_{12} + C_5H_{10}}\quad(\text{decane} \rightarrow \text{pentane} + \text{pentene})$$
$$\mathrm{C_{16}H_{34} \rightarrow C_8H_{18} + C_8H_{16}}$$

### Importance
1. Straight-run petrol from fractional distillation is only about 20% of the crude, while demand for petrol is much higher; cracking converts **heavy oils** (gas oil, fuel oil) into petrol, **increasing its yield**.
2. Cracked petrol (especially catalytic) has a **higher octane number** than straight-run petrol, so it knocks less.
3. Gives olefins (ethylene, propylene) as raw material for the **petrochemical and polymer** industry.

### Thermal vs catalytic cracking
| Thermal cracking | Catalytic cracking |
|---|---|
| Heat and pressure only, no catalyst | Catalyst: artificial clay, zeolite, $\mathrm{Al_2O_3 + SiO_2}$ |
| High temperature: 475-530 °C (liquid phase), 600-650 °C (vapour phase) | Lower temperature: 300-450 °C |
| High pressure: 30-100 kg/cm² (liquid phase), 10-20 kg/cm² (vapour phase) | Low pressure: 1-5 kg/cm² |
| Free-radical mechanism | Carbocation mechanism (isomerisation to branched chains) |
| Lower yield; petrol ON about 65-70 | Higher yield; petrol ON about 80-90 |
| More gum, gas and coke; sulphur stays in product | Less gum and coke; S removed as $\mathrm{H_2S}$ |
| Product control poor | Better control; fixed-bed or continuous fluidised-bed with catalyst regeneration |

Hence catalytic cracking has largely replaced thermal cracking.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2021-22 Sem 1.pdf
items.topic: Physical and chemical properties of lubricants and their testing
items.question_md: Why should good lubricating oil possess low Steam Emulsification Number (SEN)?
items.answer_md:
**Steam emulsion number (SEN)** is the time in seconds in which an oil and water emulsion (made by passing steam through the oil at about 90 $^\circ$C) separates into two layers.

A good lubricating oil should have a **low SEN** because:
1. In machines such as **steam turbines** and some engines, the oil comes in contact with water or steam. If oil forms a stable emulsion with water, the emulsion has poor lubricating properties and the oil film breaks.
2. Emulsions trap dirt and promote **sludge** formation, **corrosion** of parts and choking of oil lines.
3. A low SEN means the oil separates from water quickly (good demulsibility), so water can be drained off and the oil keeps lubricating effectively.

Highly refined oils have low SEN; impurities and oxidation products raise it.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2021-22 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: What is Grease? What are the conditions in which usage of Grease is preferred over lubricating oils?
items.answer_md:
**Grease** is a **semi-solid lubricant** made by thickening a lubricating oil with a **metallic soap** (Ca, Na, Li or Al soap), sometimes with fillers such as graphite or talc. Examples: calcium (cup) grease, sodium grease, lithium grease, axle grease.

**Grease is preferred over oils when:**
1. The machine runs at **slow speed and heavy load**, where an oil film would be squeezed out.
2. Operation is **intermittent** (start-stop), and oil would drain away when idle.
3. The bearing must be **sealed against dust, dirt and moisture** (grease acts as a seal).
4. **Dripping or splashing of oil** is undesirable, e.g. textile, paper and food machinery.
5. The part is **inaccessible** or relubricated rarely, e.g. sealed ball/roller bearings, rail axle boxes, open gears.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2021-22 Sem 1.pdf
items.topic: Mechanisms of lubrication: thick layer, thin layer, extreme pressure
items.question_md: Differentiate between Thick and Thin layer mechanisms of Lubrication.
items.answer_md:
| Point | Thick layer (fluid film) | Thin layer (boundary) |
|---|---|---|
| Film thickness | At least about 1000 Å, more than asperities | A few molecules thick |
| Metal contact | None | Asperities nearly touch |
| Film held by | Pressure developed by motion (hydrodynamic wedge) | **Adsorption** of polar molecules on metal |
| Operating conditions | Low load, high speed | High load, low speed, start-stop |
| Key property | **Viscosity** | **Oiliness** |
| Coefficient of friction | About 0.001-0.03 | About 0.05-0.15 |
| Lubricants | Mineral oils of correct viscosity | Vegetable/animal oils, fatty acids, graphite, $\mathrm{MoS_2}$ |
| Examples | Journal bearings, turbines | Gears, cams, rail axles |

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2021-22 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: Give detailed classification of liquid lubricants (oils), with suitable examples.
items.answer_md:
**Classification of liquid lubricants (lubricating oils)**

**1. Animal and vegetable oils**
- Animal: tallow oil, lard oil, whale oil, neatsfoot oil. Vegetable: castor, palm, olive, coconut, rapeseed, cottonseed oil.
- Triglycerides with good **oiliness**; but oxidise, become gummy and are costly. Now used mainly as blending agents.

**2. Mineral (petroleum) oils**
- Obtained by fractional distillation of crude oil residues: paraffinic (high VI, e.g. Pennsylvanian) and naphthenic (low VI).
- Cheap, abundant and chemically stable, but poor oiliness. Most widely used: engine oils, spindle oils, turbine oils.

**3. Blended (compounded) oils**
- Mineral oil + additives: oiliness agents (fatty oils), VI improvers (polyisobutylene), pour-point depressants, antioxidants, EP additives (sulphurised/chlorinated compounds), detergents.
- Examples: multigrade engine oils (SAE 20W-40), EP gear oils.

**4. Synthetic oils**
- Silicones, polyglycols, esters, polyalphaolefins, phosphate esters.
- High VI, wide temperature range, oxidation and fire resistance; costly. Used in jet engines and extreme conditions.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2021-22 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: Write short notes on (i) Silicones resins
items.answer_md:
**Silicones** are polymers with an alternating **Si-O-Si (siloxane)** backbone and organic groups on Si, $\mathrm{-[R_2Si-O]_n-}$.

**Preparation:** alkyl chlorosilanes are hydrolysed and the silanols condense:
$$\mathrm{R_2SiCl_2 + 2H_2O \rightarrow R_2Si(OH)_2 + 2HCl}$$
$$\mathrm{n\,R_2Si(OH)_2 \rightarrow -[R_2Si-O]_n- + n\,H_2O}$$
$\mathrm{R_3SiCl}$ caps the chain ends; **$\mathrm{RSiCl_3}$** (trifunctional) gives cross-links, so a mixture of $\mathrm{R_2SiCl_2}$ and $\mathrm{RSiCl_3}$ gives **silicone resins** (cross-linked).

**Properties:** stable from about -90 to 250 °C; water repellent; excellent electrical insulators; chemically inert; non-toxic.

**Uses:** high-temperature paints and varnishes, electrical insulation, water-proofing of fabrics and masonry, laminates, non-stick coatings.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2021-22 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: Write short notes on (ii) Kevlar
items.answer_md:
**Kevlar** is an aromatic polyamide (**aramid**): poly(p-phenylene terephthalamide).

**Preparation** (condensation polymerisation): p-phenylenediamine + terephthaloyl chloride, with elimination of HCl:
$$\mathrm{n\,H_2N-C_6H_4-NH_2 + n\,ClOC-C_6H_4-COCl \rightarrow -[NH-C_6H_4-NH-CO-C_6H_4-CO]_n- + 2n\,HCl}$$

**Structure and properties**
- Rigid, linear, rod-like chains with para-linked benzene rings; chains are held in sheets by strong **H-bonds** between $\mathrm{C=O}$ and $\mathrm{N-H}$, so it is highly crystalline.
- Very high tensile strength (about 5 times steel on a weight basis), light, high modulus.
- Heat and flame resistant (does not melt; decomposes above about 450 °C), chemically resistant.

**Uses:** bulletproof vests and helmets, tyre cords, ropes and cables, aircraft and boat composites, protective gloves.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2021-22 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: What is the necessity of vulcanizing the rubber? Explain it by the help of structure of vulcanized rubber.
items.answer_md:
**Why raw rubber must be vulcanised (defects of raw rubber)**
1. Soft and **sticky when hot**, hard and **brittle when cold**; useful only over about 10-60 °C.
2. Low tensile strength; on stretching the chains slip, so it shows **permanent set** (does not fully regain shape).
3. High water absorption; swells/dissolves in organic solvents (petrol, benzene).
4. Easily attacked by oxygen, ozone and oxidising agents; poor abrasion resistance.

These arise because the linear cis-polyisoprene chains are held only by weak van der Waals forces.

**Vulcanisation and the structure of vulcanised rubber.** Heating with about 3-5% sulphur (100-140 °C, accelerator + ZnO) forms **-S-S- bridges** between neighbouring chains:

$$\begin{array}{c}
\mathrm{-CH_2-\overset{CH_3}{\overset{|}{C}}H-CH-CH_2-}\\
\mathrm{|}\\
\mathrm{S-S}\\
\mathrm{|}\\
\mathrm{-CH_2-\underset{CH_3}{\underset{|}{C}}H-CH-CH_2-}
\end{array}$$

The cross-links tie the chains into a loose 3-D network:
- chains can no longer slip, so **tensile strength rises about 10 times** and there is no permanent set;
- the coils between cross-links can stretch and the links pull them back, so rubber becomes **elastic**;
- it is non-sticky, works over about -40 to 100 °C, and resists solvents, oxidation and abrasion better.

Hence vulcanised rubber is used for tyres, tubes, belts, hoses and shoe soles.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2021-22 Sem 1.pdf
items.topic: Manufacture of Portland cement (wet and dry)
items.question_md: Describe manufacturing of Portland Cement by Wet process in Rotary Kiln with a well-labelled diagram and reactions taking place at various levels.
items.answer_md:
**Raw materials:** calcareous material (limestone, chalk; supplies $\mathrm{CaO}$) and argillaceous material (clay, shale; supplies $\mathrm{SiO_2, Al_2O_3, Fe_2O_3}$) in about **3 : 1** ratio; powdered coal, oil or gas as fuel; 2 to 3% gypsum added at the end.

**Wet process:**
1. Limestone is crushed; clay is washed with water in a **wash mill** to remove flint and organic matter.
2. Both are mixed in about 3 : 1 ratio and ground in a tube mill with water to a **slurry containing 35 to 40% water**.
3. The slurry is corrected for composition in correcting basins and stored in slurry tanks with agitation.
4. It is fed at the upper end of the rotary kiln.

**Reactions in the kiln zones:**

1. **Drying zone (upper end, about 400 $^\circ$C):** water of the slurry (or moisture of the raw meal) is evaporated; clay loses its combined water.
$$\mathrm{Al_2O_3\cdot 2SiO_2\cdot 2H_2O \rightarrow Al_2O_3 + 2SiO_2 + 2H_2O}$$
2. **Calcination zone (middle, 700 to 1000 $^\circ$C):** limestone decomposes.
$$\mathrm{CaCO_3 \xrightarrow{\sim 900^\circ C} CaO + CO_2\uparrow}$$
3. **Clinkering (burning) zone (lower end, 1400 to 1500 $^\circ$C):** lime combines with clay oxides; the mass partly fuses into hard greyish balls called **clinker** (3 to 20 mm).
$$\mathrm{2CaO + SiO_2 \rightarrow 2CaO\cdot SiO_2\ (C_2S)}$$
$$\mathrm{3CaO + SiO_2 \rightarrow 3CaO\cdot SiO_2\ (C_3S)}$$
$$\mathrm{3CaO + Al_2O_3 \rightarrow 3CaO\cdot Al_2O_3\ (C_3A)}$$
$$\mathrm{4CaO + Al_2O_3 + Fe_2O_3 \rightarrow 4CaO\cdot Al_2O_3\cdot Fe_2O_3\ (C_4AF)}$$

**Cooling and grinding:** hot clinker is cooled in a rotary cooler (the heated air is used for combustion), then ground in ball/tube mills with **2 to 3% gypsum** ($\mathrm{CaSO_4\cdot 2H_2O}$), which retards setting. Gypsum is added after the kiln, never inside it (it would decompose). The fine powder is Portland cement, stored in silos and packed.

**Labelled diagram of the rotary kiln (draw as described):**
- A long steel cylinder, about 2.5 to 3 m in diameter and 45 to 150 m long, lined inside with **refractory firebricks**, **inclined** slightly (about 1 in 25) and **rotating slowly** (about 1 rpm) on roller supports driven by a gear.
- **Upper end:** inlet for the slurry (wet process) or raw meal (dry process), feed hopper, and the outlet for hot gases to the **chimney** (via dust collector).
- **Lower end:** **burner** where powdered coal, oil or gas is blown in with hot air, and the outlet for **clinker** to the **rotary cooler**.
- Mark the three zones from the top: **drying zone** (about 400 $^\circ$C), **calcination zone** (700 to 1000 $^\circ$C), **clinkering (burning) zone** (1400 to 1500 $^\circ$C) nearest the burner.
- Arrows: charge moves down, hot gases move up (**counter-current**).

```
 slurry/raw meal --> [hopper]
                        \   <- hot gases to chimney
 ___________________________________________________
|  DRYING ZONE   |  CALCINATION ZONE  |  CLINKERING  |<== burner (coal dust
|   ~400 C       |    700-1000 C      |   1400-1500 C|    + hot air)
|________________|____________________|______________|
   firebrick lining, inclined, rotating ~1 rpm          \
                                                         --> clinker to cooler
                                                             --> grind + 2-3% gypsum
```

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2021-22 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md:
Explain the following, with at least two examples of each:

(a) Addition polymerization

(b) Condensation polymerization

(c) Co- polymerization

Also provide detailed mechanism of 'Addition Polymerization'.
items.answer_md:
**(a) Addition (chain-growth) polymerisation**: unsaturated monomers join by opening the C=C bond **without loss of any atom**; polymer mass $= n\times$ monomer mass.
- Polyethylene: $\mathrm{n\,CH_2=CH_2 \rightarrow -[CH_2-CH_2]_n-}$
- PVC: $\mathrm{n\,CH_2=CHCl \rightarrow -[CH_2-CHCl]_n-}$
- Polystyrene: $\mathrm{n\,CH_2=CH(C_6H_5) \rightarrow -[CH_2-CH(C_6H_5)]_n-}$

**(b) Condensation (step-growth) polymerisation**: monomers with two (or more) functional groups react with **elimination of small molecules** ($\mathrm{H_2O}$, HCl).
- Nylon-66: $\mathrm{n\,H_2N(CH_2)_6NH_2 + n\,HOOC(CH_2)_4COOH \rightarrow -[NH(CH_2)_6NHCO(CH_2)_4CO]_n- + 2n\,H_2O}$
- Terylene: $\mathrm{n\,HOCH_2CH_2OH + n\,HOOC-C_6H_4-COOH \rightarrow -[OCH_2CH_2O-CO-C_6H_4-CO]_n- + 2n\,H_2O}$
- Bakelite: phenol + HCHO, with loss of $\mathrm{H_2O}$.

**(c) Copolymerisation**: polymerisation of **two or more different monomers** together so that both units appear in the **same chain** (not a mixture of two polymers). Types: random, alternating, block, graft.
- **Buna-S (SBR)**: $\mathrm{n\,CH_2=CH-CH=CH_2 + n\,CH_2=CH(C_6H_5) \rightarrow -[CH_2-CH=CH-CH_2-CH_2-CH(C_6H_5)]_n-}$
- **Buna-N (NBR)**: butadiene + acrylonitrile $\rightarrow$ $\mathrm{-[CH_2-CH=CH-CH_2-CH_2-CH(CN)]_n-}$
- (Nylon-66 is also formed from two different monomers, by condensation.)

**Mechanism of addition (free radical) polymerisation**, e.g. ethylene / vinyl monomers $\mathrm{CH_2=CHX}$ with benzoyl peroxide as initiator.

**(a) Initiation**
$$\mathrm{(C_6H_5COO)_2 \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2\,C_6H_5COO^{\bullet} \rightarrow 2\,C_6H_5^{\bullet} + 2\,CO_2}\quad(\mathrm{R^\bullet})$$
$$\mathrm{R^{\bullet} + CH_2=CHX \rightarrow R-CH_2-\dot{C}HX}$$

**(b) Propagation** (the radical adds monomer repeatedly)
$$\mathrm{R-CH_2-\dot{C}HX + n\,CH_2=CHX \rightarrow R-[CH_2-CHX]_n-CH_2-\dot{C}HX}$$

**(c) Termination**
- by **coupling (combination)**: $\mathrm{R{\sim}CH_2-\dot{C}HX + {}^{\bullet}CHX-CH_2{\sim}R \rightarrow R{\sim}CH_2-CHX-CHX-CH_2{\sim}R}$
- by **disproportionation** (H transfer): $\mathrm{2\,{\sim}CH_2-\dot{C}HX \rightarrow {\sim}CH_2-CH_2X + {\sim}CH=CHX}$

items.question_md: During dry corrosion, how the nature of oxide film effects the corrosion? Explain in detail.
items.answer_md:
In dry corrosion the metal first forms a surface film of oxide; further attack is possible only if $\mathrm{M^{n+}}$ ions or $\mathrm{O^{2-}}$ ions can diffuse through it. Hence the **nature of the oxide film decides the rate**:

1. **Stable (protective) film:** fine-grained, tightly adhering, non-porous; it acts as a barrier and stops further oxidation. e.g. Al, Sn, Pb, Cu, Cr ($\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$, $\mathrm{Cr_2O_3}$).
2. **Unstable film:** the oxide decomposes back to metal and oxygen ($\mathrm{2M_2O \rightleftharpoons 4M + O_2}$), so no lasting corrosion. e.g. Ag, Au, Pt.
3. **Volatile film:** the oxide evaporates as it forms, exposing fresh metal, so corrosion is rapid and continuous. e.g. $\mathrm{MoO_3}$ on molybdenum.
4. **Porous film:** has pores or cracks through which oxygen reaches the metal, so oxidation continues till the metal is consumed. e.g. alkali and alkaline earth metals (Na, K, Mg, Ca).

**Pilling-Bedworth rule:** $\mathrm{PBR} = \dfrac{V_{oxide}}{V_{metal}}$. If PBR < 1 the film is porous and non-protective (Na 0.58, Mg 0.81); if PBR is about 1 to 2 it is compact and protective (Al 1.29, Cu 1.68); if PBR is much greater than 2 the film is strained, cracks and spalls off (W about 3.4).

items.question_md: Why rapid corrosion of iron (Fe) occurs in dilute nitric acid and not in concentrated nitric acid?
items.answer_md:
**Dilute $\mathrm{HNO_3}$:** it acts mainly as an acid and a mild oxidant. Iron dissolves actively, $\mathrm{Fe \rightarrow Fe^{2+} + 2e^-}$, with reduction of $\mathrm{H^+}$/$\mathrm{NO_3^-}$ at cathodic sites (e.g. $\mathrm{4Fe + 10HNO_3 \rightarrow 4Fe(NO_3)_2 + NH_4NO_3 + 3H_2O}$). The products are soluble, so no protective film forms and corrosion is rapid.

**Concentrated $\mathrm{HNO_3}$:** it is a strong oxidising agent and converts the iron surface into a very thin, compact, non-porous and adherent oxide film (about $\mathrm{Fe_3O_4}$ / $\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}$). The film separates the metal from the acid, and iron becomes **passive** (the metal's potential shifts to a noble value). Further attack practically stops.

So iron corrodes in dilute but not in concentrated nitric acid because of **passivity** caused by the oxidising action of the concentrated acid. (The passive iron does not even displace Cu from $\mathrm{CuSO_4}$ solution until the film is scratched.)

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2021-22 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md:
During wet corrosion which of the following couple will exhibit severe corrosion of Zn: (a) Zn connected with Fe, (b) Zn connected with Cu, (c) Zn connected with Ni and (d) Zn connected with Sn.

Give your answer with proper explanation.
items.answer_md:
**Answer: (b) Zn connected with Cu** shows the most severe corrosion of Zn.

**Reason:** In every couple Zn ($E^\circ = -0.76$ V) is the more active metal, so it is the **anode** and corrodes; the other metal is the cathode. The driving force (EMF) of the galvanic cell is $E^\circ_{cell} = E^\circ_{cathode} - E^\circ_{anode}$, and the greater the separation in the series, the faster the anode corrodes.

| Couple | $E^\circ$ of cathode (V) | $E^\circ_{cell} = E^\circ_{c} - (-0.76)$ (V) |
|---|---|---|
| (a) Zn-Fe | $-0.44$ | 0.32 |
| (c) Zn-Ni | $-0.25$ | 0.51 |
| (d) Zn-Sn | $-0.14$ | 0.62 |
| (b) Zn-Cu | $+0.34$ | **1.10** |

Order of severity of Zn corrosion: **Zn-Cu > Zn-Sn > Zn-Ni > Zn-Fe**.

Anode: $\mathrm{Zn \rightarrow Zn^{2+} + 2e^-}$; cathode (Cu, aerated): $\mathrm{O_2 + 2H_2O + 4e^- \rightarrow 4OH^-}$. Cu is farthest from Zn in the galvanic series, so the potential difference and the corrosion current are largest; Fe is closest, so Zn-Fe corrodes Zn least (this mild sacrificial action is why galvanising protects iron).

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2021-22 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: How relative areas of anode and cathode influence the corrosion? Explain sacrificial anodic protection method.
items.answer_md:
### Effect of relative areas of anode and cathode

Rate of corrosion of the anode $\propto \dfrac{\text{area of cathode}}{\text{area of anode}}$.

The cathodic reaction ($\mathrm{O_2 + 2H_2O + 4e^- \rightarrow 4OH^-}$ or $\mathrm{2H^+ + 2e^- \rightarrow H_2}$) takes up electrons over the whole cathode surface; every one of these electrons must come from the anode ($\mathrm{M \rightarrow M^{n+} + ne^-}$).
- **Small anode, large cathode:** high current density at the anode, so **intense, localised corrosion** (pitting).
- **Large anode, small cathode:** current spread over a large area, so slow, uniform corrosion.

Examples: steel rivets in copper sheet corrode rapidly; copper rivets in steel sheet cause little harm. A scratch in tinned iron (small Fe anode, large Sn cathode) rusts severely. Hence in design the anodic metal should have the larger area, and one should never paint only the anode.

### Sacrificial anodic protection
**Sacrificial anodic protection** (a cathodic protection method): the metal structure to be protected is connected by a wire to a **more active (anodic) metal** such as **Mg, Zn or Al** (or their alloys). The active metal acts as the anode and corrodes ("sacrificed"), while the structure becomes the cathode and is protected.

- Anode reaction: $\mathrm{Mg \rightarrow Mg^{2+} + 2e^-}$; electrons flow to the steel, which acts as cathode: $\mathrm{O_2 + 2H_2O + 4e^- \rightarrow 4OH^-}$.
- The consumed anode is replaced periodically.
- Uses: buried pipelines and cables, ship hulls, water tanks, boilers, marine structures; magnesium blocks in domestic water heaters.

*Diagram (in words):* buried steel pipeline connected by an insulated wire to a buried Mg block in backfill (gypsum + bentonite); $e^-$ arrow from Mg to pipe; Mg labelled anode (corrodes), pipe labelled cathode (protected).

Advantages: no external power, simple, cheap. Disadvantage: anodes must be replaced; limited driving voltage.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2021-22 Sem 2.pdf
items.question_md: A sample of water contains following impurities: $Mg(HCO_3)_2$ = 36.5 mg/l; $CaCl_2$ = 55.5 mg/l; $MgSO_4$ = 30 mg/l; $CaSO_4$ = 68 mg/l. Calculate the quantity of lime and soda (both 90% pure) needed for softening of 10,000 litres of water. [Molecular Weights of $Mg(HCO_3)_2$ = 146; $CaCl_2$ = 111; $MgSO_4$ = 120; $CaSO_4$ = 136]
items.answer_md:
**Given:** volume of water $V$ = 10,000 L; lime purity = 90%, soda purity = 90%.

**To find:** mass of lime $\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2}$ (molar mass 74) and soda $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}$ (molar mass 106) required.

**Step 1: Convert each constituent to $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ equivalent**

$$\text{ppm as CaCO}_3 = \frac{\text{mg/L of salt}\times 100}{\text{molar mass of salt}}$$

| Constituent | Amount (mg/L) | Molar mass | Factor | ppm as $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ | Type | Needs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\mathrm{Mg(HCO_3)_2}$ | 36.5 | 146 | 100/146 | 25 | Temporary Mg | 2L |
| $\mathrm{CaCl_2}$ | 55.5 | 111 | 100/111 | 50 | Permanent Ca | S |
| $\mathrm{MgSO_4}$ | 30 | 120 | 100/120 | 25 | Permanent Mg | L + S |
| $\mathrm{CaSO_4}$ | 68 | 136 | 100/136 | 50 | Permanent Ca | S |

(L = lime, S = soda. Temporary Mg takes 2 lime; permanent Mg takes lime and then soda for the $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ it releases; Na, K salts and $\mathrm{SiO_2}$ cause no hardness and are ignored.)

**Step 2: Formulae**

$$\text{Lime} = \frac{74}{100}\left[2\times\text{Temp Mg}\ (\mathrm{Mg(HCO_3)_2}) + \text{Perm Mg}\ (\mathrm{MgSO_4})\right]\times\frac{V}{10^6}\times\frac{100}{\%\text{ purity}}\ \text{kg}$$

$$\text{Soda} = \frac{106}{100}\left[\text{Perm Ca}\ (\mathrm{CaCl_2}) + \text{Perm Mg}\ (\mathrm{MgSO_4}) + \text{Perm Ca}\ (\mathrm{CaSO_4})\right]\times\frac{V}{10^6}\times\frac{100}{\%\text{ purity}}\ \text{kg}$$

**Step 3: Substitution**

Lime (100% pure) per litre $= \frac{74}{100}[2(25) + 25] = \frac{74}{100}\times 75 = 55.5$ mg/L

Lime (100% pure) for 10,000 L $= 55.5\times 10000 = 555000$ mg $= 0.555$ kg

Lime (90% pure) $= 0.555\times\frac{100}{90} = 0.6167$ kg

Soda (100% pure) per litre $= \frac{106}{100}[50 + 25 + 50] = \frac{106}{100}\times 125 = 132.5$ mg/L

Soda (100% pure) for 10,000 L $= 132.5\times 10000 = 1325000$ mg $= 1.325$ kg

Soda (90% pure) $= 1.325\times\frac{100}{90} = 1.472$ kg

**Result:** Lime required = **616.67 g = 0.6167 kg**; Soda required = **1.472 kg**.

items.topic: Purification of water step by step
items.question_md: Write short note on: Break Point Chlorination
items.answer_md:
**Break-point chlorination** is the addition of chlorine to water just beyond the dose at which all reducing substances, ammonia, chloramines and organic matter have been oxidised; at this **break-point** the residual chlorine is minimum, and any further chlorine appears as **free residual chlorine**, rising in proportion to the dose.

On the curve (residual vs applied chlorine) the residual first rises (chloramine formation), then falls to a minimum (break-point, chloramines destroyed), then rises linearly. Dosing just past the break-point kills all pathogens, removes colour, odour and taste, and leaves 0.1-0.2 ppm free chlorine to protect water in the mains.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2021-22 Sem 2.pdf
items.question_md: Write short note on: Priming and Foaming
items.answer_md:
**Priming** is the carrying over of water droplets with the steam from a boiler, so the steam becomes **wet**. It occurs when steam is produced rapidly and violently.

**Foaming** is the formation of small, **persistent bubbles** (foam) at the water surface in the boiler, which do not break easily. It is caused by oils, grease and alkalis that lower the surface tension of water.

Priming and foaming usually occur together and are jointly called **carry-over**.

**Causes:** priming from high steam velocity, high water level, sudden boiling and poor design; foaming from oils and alkalis. **Effects:** salts deposit on turbine blades and superheaters; wrong water-level reading. **Prevention:** steam purifiers, low water level, soft water for priming; antifoams (castor oil) and oil removal by sodium aluminate for foaming.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2021-22 Sem 2.pdf
items.question_md: Write short note on: Zeolite Process
items.answer_md:
**Zeolite (permutit) process** softens hard water by cation exchange. Zeolite, a hydrated sodium aluminosilicate $\mathrm{Na_2O\cdot Al_2O_3\cdot xSiO_2\cdot yH_2O}$ ($\mathrm{Na_2Ze}$), exchanges its $\mathrm{Na^+}$ for $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$/$\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$:
$$\mathrm{Na_2Ze + Ca(HCO_3)_2 \rightarrow CaZe + 2NaHCO_3}$$
The exhausted bed is regenerated with 10% brine: $\mathrm{CaZe + 2NaCl \rightarrow Na_2Ze + CaCl_2}$. Residual hardness is about 10 ppm and no sludge forms, but turbid or acidic water and $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$/$\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$ spoil the zeolite, and the softened water contains more sodium salts.

items.topic: Sources and specifications of drinking water
items.question_md: What are specifications of drinking water? Which consecutive steps are used to obtain municipal water from raw water (Give name only)? Describe role of Sodium Aluminate and Potash Alum in water purification.
items.answer_md:
**(i) Specifications of drinking water** (WHO / BIS IS 10500):
- Clear, colourless, odourless, pleasant taste; turbidity below 10 ppm.
- pH 6.5-8.5; TDS below 500 ppm; total hardness below about 300 ppm as $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ (IS 10500: 200 mg/L acceptable); chloride below 250 ppm; fluoride about 1-1.5 ppm; nitrate below 45 ppm.
- Free from pathogenic bacteria, toxic metals ($\mathrm{Pb}$, $\mathrm{As}$, $\mathrm{Hg}$) and $\mathrm{H_2S}$; non-corrosive.

**(ii) Steps from raw water to municipal water** (names only):
Screening, then Plain sedimentation, then Coagulation (sedimentation with coagulant), then Filtration, then Disinfection (sterilisation).

**(iii) Role of sodium aluminate and potash alum** (both are **coagulants**): colloidal impurities carry negative charge and do not settle; these chemicals produce gelatinous $\mathrm{Al(OH)_3}$ floc, whose $\mathrm{Al^{3+}}$ neutralises the charge and which entraps the fine particles and bacteria so they settle.

- **Potash alum**, $\mathrm{K_2SO_4\cdot Al_2(SO_4)_3\cdot 24H_2O}$: its aluminium sulphate reacts with the bicarbonate alkalinity of water; effective at pH 6.5-8.5:
$$\mathrm{Al_2(SO_4)_3 + 3Ca(HCO_3)_2 \rightarrow 2Al(OH)_3\downarrow + 3CaSO_4 + 6CO_2}$$
- **Sodium aluminate**, $\mathrm{NaAlO_2}$: hydrolyses to give $\mathrm{Al(OH)_3}$ floc and NaOH; used for **acidic** water (or water with little alkalinity), and the NaOH formed also precipitates some magnesium:
$$\mathrm{NaAlO_2 + 2H_2O \rightarrow Al(OH)_3\downarrow + NaOH}$$
$$\mathrm{MgCl_2 + 2NaOH \rightarrow Mg(OH)_2\downarrow + 2NaCl}$$

items.question_md: What are specifications of a good disinfectant?
items.answer_md:
Specifications of a good disinfectant:

1. It should **kill all pathogenic** micro-organisms quickly at low dose.
2. It should be **non-toxic** to human beings and animals at the dose used.
3. It should not impart any **taste, odour or colour** to the water.
4. It should be **cheap**, easily available, and easy to store, transport and handle.
5. It should be **stable** (should not lose strength on storage).
6. It should leave a small **residual** in water to protect against recontamination in the distribution pipes.
7. Its concentration should be easy to **measure** (simple test for residual).
8. It should act over the normal **pH and temperature** range of water and should not make the water corrosive or harder.

items.question_md: Explain causes and ill effects of Priming and Foaming.
items.answer_md:
**Priming** is carry-over of water droplets with steam (wet steam); **foaming** is the formation of persistent bubbles at the water surface in the boiler.

**Causes of priming**
1. High steam velocity (sudden increase in steam demand).
2. Very high water level in the boiler.
3. Sudden boiling.
4. Faulty boiler design (inadequate steam space).
5. High concentration of dissolved and suspended solids.

**Causes of foaming:** presence of oil, grease and alkalis (and finely divided suspended matter) that reduce the surface tension of water.

**Ill effects**
1. Dissolved salts in the carried-over droplets deposit on superheater tubes and **turbine blades**, reducing their efficiency.
2. Wet steam reduces the heat content and efficiency of the steam; the dissolved salts may corrode the machinery.
3. Foam makes the **water-level reading** in the gauge glass unreliable, risking overheating or damage to the boiler.
4. Machinery parts that use the steam are damaged and their life is shortened.

items.topic: Numericals on calorific value and ultimate analysis
items.question_md:
A coal sample contains 93% carbon, 6% hydrogen and 1% ash. Data obtained after testing it in Bomb Calorimeter is:

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Weight of coal burnt | 0.92 g |
| Weight of water taken | 550 g |
| Water equivalent of bomb and calorimeter | 2200 g |
| Rise in temperature | 2.42 $^\circ C$ |
| Fuse wire correction | 10.0 cal |
| Acid correction | 50.0 cal |

Calculate gross and net calorific value of the coal, assuming the latent heat of condensation of steam as 580 cal/g.
items.answer_md:
**Given**: $x = 0.92$ g, $W = 550$ g, $w = 2200$ g, $\Delta t = 2.42\ ^\circ$C, $t_F = 10.0$ cal, $t_A = 50.0$ cal, H = 6%, $L = 580$ cal/g.

**To find**: GCV and NCV.

**Formulae**
$$\mathrm{GCV} = \frac{(W+w)\,\Delta t - (t_A + t_F)}{x}, \qquad \mathrm{NCV} = \mathrm{GCV} - 0.09\,H \times L$$

**GCV**
$$\mathrm{GCV} = \frac{(550 + 2200)(2.42) - (50 + 10)}{0.92} = \frac{6655 - 60}{0.92} = \frac{6595}{0.92}$$
$$\mathbf{GCV = 7168.48\ cal/g\ (kcal/kg)}$$

**NCV**
$$0.09 \times 6 \times 580 = 313.20\ \text{cal/g}$$
$$\mathrm{NCV} = 7168.48 - 313.20 = \mathbf{6855.28\ cal/g}$$

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2021-22 Sem 2.pdf
items.question_md: Write short note on: Catalytic Cracking
items.answer_md:
**Catalytic cracking** is the decomposition of heavy, high-boiling petroleum fractions (gas oil, heavy oil) into lighter, low-boiling hydrocarbons (mainly petrol) in the presence of a **catalyst**, at lower temperature and pressure than thermal cracking.

- **Catalyst:** artificial clay, zeolite or alumina-silica ($\mathrm{Al_2O_3 + SiO_2}$); conditions about 300-450 °C and 1-5 kg/cm².
- **Mechanism:** carbocation; chains rearrange to branched alkanes and aromatics, so the petrol has a **high octane number**. Example: $\mathrm{C_{10}H_{22} \rightarrow C_5H_{12} + C_5H_{10}}$.
- **Types:** (i) **fixed-bed**: oil vapour passes over a stationary catalyst bed; carbon deposits, so the bed is regenerated by burning off carbon every 8-10 h (process stops); (ii) **fluidised (moving) bed**: powdered catalyst is kept fluidised by oil vapour in the reactor (about 500 °C), sent to a separate **regenerator** where air burns off carbon, and recycled, so the process is continuous.
- **Advantages over thermal cracking:** higher yield and octane number, lower temperature and pressure, less gum, gas and coke, better control of product quality.
