items.question_md:
Give reason why (**Any two**):

b. Plasticizer is used during manufacture of plastics.
items.answer_md:
A **plasticizer** (e.g. dioctyl phthalate, tricresyl phosphate) is a high-boiling liquid of low molecular mass added to the resin because:
- its molecules get **between the polymer chains** and weaken the intermolecular (van der Waals/dipole) forces, so chains slide more easily;
- this **lowers $T_g$** and makes the plastic **soft, flexible and easier to mould** (e.g. rigid PVC becomes flexible PVC for cables, sheets).

It is not a filler: a filler adds bulk or strength, a plasticizer adds flexibility.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2022-23 Sem 1.pdf
items.topic: Composition, setting and hardening of cement
items.question_md:
Give reason why (**Any two**):

c. Gypsum in small amount is absolute necessity in cement.
items.answer_md:
$\mathrm{C_3A}$ reacts with water very fast and exothermically, so cement without gypsum would set almost instantly (**flash set**) and could not be placed and worked.

Gypsum ($\mathrm{CaSO_4\cdot 2H_2O}$, 2 to 3%, added while grinding the clinker) reacts with $\mathrm{C_3A}$ to form insoluble **calcium sulphoaluminate (ettringite)**, which coats the $\mathrm{C_3A}$ grains and **retards** their hydration:
$$\mathrm{3CaO\cdot Al_2O_3 + 3(CaSO_4\cdot 2H_2O) + 26H_2O \rightarrow 3CaO\cdot Al_2O_3\cdot 3CaSO_4\cdot 32H_2O}$$
This gives an initial setting time of at least 30 min. Excess gypsum is avoided because it causes expansion and unsoundness.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2022-23 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md:
Explain the following, with at least two examples each:

(i) Addition polymerization

(ii) Condensation polymerization

Also provide detail mechanism of Addition polymerization.
items.answer_md:
**(i) Addition (chain-growth) polymerisation**: unsaturated monomers add to each other by opening the C=C bond, **without elimination of any molecule**; polymer mass $= n \times$ monomer mass. Fast, needs an initiator.
- Polyethylene: $\mathrm{n\,CH_2=CH_2 \rightarrow -[CH_2-CH_2]_n-}$
- PVC: $\mathrm{n\,CH_2=CHCl \rightarrow -[CH_2-CHCl]_n-}$
- (also polystyrene, Teflon $\mathrm{-[CF_2-CF_2]_n-}$)

**(ii) Condensation (step-growth) polymerisation**: bi- or polyfunctional monomers react through their functional groups with **elimination of a small molecule** ($\mathrm{H_2O}$, HCl, $\mathrm{CH_3OH}$); slow and stepwise.
- Nylon-66: $\mathrm{n\,H_2N(CH_2)_6NH_2 + n\,HOOC(CH_2)_4COOH \rightarrow -[NH(CH_2)_6NHCO(CH_2)_4CO]_n- + 2n\,H_2O}$
- Terylene (PET): $\mathrm{n\,HOCH_2CH_2OH + n\,HOOC-C_6H_4-COOH \rightarrow -[OCH_2CH_2O-CO-C_6H_4-CO]_n- + 2n\,H_2O}$
- (also bakelite from phenol + HCHO)

**Mechanism of addition (free radical) polymerisation**, e.g. ethylene / vinyl monomers $\mathrm{CH_2=CHX}$ with benzoyl peroxide as initiator.

**(a) Initiation**
$$\mathrm{(C_6H_5COO)_2 \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2\,C_6H_5COO^{\bullet} \rightarrow 2\,C_6H_5^{\bullet} + 2\,CO_2}\quad(\mathrm{R^\bullet})$$
$$\mathrm{R^{\bullet} + CH_2=CHX \rightarrow R-CH_2-\dot{C}HX}$$

**(b) Propagation** (the radical adds monomer repeatedly)
$$\mathrm{R-CH_2-\dot{C}HX + n\,CH_2=CHX \rightarrow R-[CH_2-CHX]_n-CH_2-\dot{C}HX}$$

**(c) Termination**
- by **coupling (combination)**: $\mathrm{R{\sim}CH_2-\dot{C}HX + {}^{\bullet}CHX-CH_2{\sim}R \rightarrow R{\sim}CH_2-CHX-CHX-CH_2{\sim}R}$
- by **disproportionation** (H transfer): $\mathrm{2\,{\sim}CH_2-\dot{C}HX \rightarrow {\sim}CH_2-CH_2X + {\sim}CH=CHX}$

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2022-23 Sem 1.pdf
items.topic: Manufacture of Portland cement (wet and dry)
items.question_md: Explain the preparation of Portland cement (with equations). Also give labeled diagram of Rotary kiln.
items.answer_md:
**Raw materials:** calcareous material (limestone, chalk; supplies $\mathrm{CaO}$) and argillaceous material (clay, shale; supplies $\mathrm{SiO_2, Al_2O_3, Fe_2O_3}$) in about **3 : 1** ratio; powdered coal, oil or gas as fuel; 2 to 3% gypsum added at the end.

**Wet process:**
1. Limestone is crushed; clay is washed with water in a **wash mill** to remove flint and organic matter.
2. Both are mixed in about 3 : 1 ratio and ground in a tube mill with water to a **slurry containing 35 to 40% water**.
3. The slurry is corrected for composition in correcting basins and stored in slurry tanks with agitation.
4. It is fed at the upper end of the rotary kiln.

**Dry process:**
1. Limestone and clay are dried, crushed and finely ground separately.
2. They are mixed in the correct proportion (about 3 : 1) as a **dry powder called raw meal**, homogenised by compressed air in blending silos.
3. The raw meal (often made into nodules/pellets with about 12% water, or preheated in a suspension preheater) is fed into the rotary kiln.

**Reactions in the kiln zones:**

1. **Drying zone (upper end, about 400 $^\circ$C):** water of the slurry (or moisture of the raw meal) is evaporated; clay loses its combined water.
$$\mathrm{Al_2O_3\cdot 2SiO_2\cdot 2H_2O \rightarrow Al_2O_3 + 2SiO_2 + 2H_2O}$$
2. **Calcination zone (middle, 700 to 1000 $^\circ$C):** limestone decomposes.
$$\mathrm{CaCO_3 \xrightarrow{\sim 900^\circ C} CaO + CO_2\uparrow}$$
3. **Clinkering (burning) zone (lower end, 1400 to 1500 $^\circ$C):** lime combines with clay oxides; the mass partly fuses into hard greyish balls called **clinker** (3 to 20 mm).
$$\mathrm{2CaO + SiO_2 \rightarrow 2CaO\cdot SiO_2\ (C_2S)}$$
$$\mathrm{3CaO + SiO_2 \rightarrow 3CaO\cdot SiO_2\ (C_3S)}$$
$$\mathrm{3CaO + Al_2O_3 \rightarrow 3CaO\cdot Al_2O_3\ (C_3A)}$$
$$\mathrm{4CaO + Al_2O_3 + Fe_2O_3 \rightarrow 4CaO\cdot Al_2O_3\cdot Fe_2O_3\ (C_4AF)}$$

**Cooling and grinding:** hot clinker is cooled in a rotary cooler (the heated air is used for combustion), then ground in ball/tube mills with **2 to 3% gypsum** ($\mathrm{CaSO_4\cdot 2H_2O}$), which retards setting. Gypsum is added after the kiln, never inside it (it would decompose). The fine powder is Portland cement, stored in silos and packed.

**Labelled diagram of the rotary kiln (draw as described):**
- A long steel cylinder, about 2.5 to 3 m in diameter and 45 to 150 m long, lined inside with **refractory firebricks**, **inclined** slightly (about 1 in 25) and **rotating slowly** (about 1 rpm) on roller supports driven by a gear.
- **Upper end:** inlet for the slurry (wet process) or raw meal (dry process), feed hopper, and the outlet for hot gases to the **chimney** (via dust collector).
- **Lower end:** **burner** where powdered coal, oil or gas is blown in with hot air, and the outlet for **clinker** to the **rotary cooler**.
- Mark the three zones from the top: **drying zone** (about 400 $^\circ$C), **calcination zone** (700 to 1000 $^\circ$C), **clinkering (burning) zone** (1400 to 1500 $^\circ$C) nearest the burner.
- Arrows: charge moves down, hot gases move up (**counter-current**).

```
 slurry/raw meal --> [hopper]
                        \   <- hot gases to chimney
 ___________________________________________________
|  DRYING ZONE   |  CALCINATION ZONE  |  CLINKERING  |<== burner (coal dust
|   ~400 C       |    700-1000 C      |   1400-1500 C|    + hot air)
|________________|____________________|______________|
   firebrick lining, inclined, rotating ~1 rpm          \
                                                         --> clinker to cooler
                                                             --> grind + 2-3% gypsum
```

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2022-23 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: What is Pilling-Bedworth rule? How is it related to the protectiveness of an oxide layer? Explain it by citing various types of oxide layers.
items.answer_md:
**Pilling-Bedworth rule:** The protective nature of an oxide film formed during dry oxidation depends on the ratio of the volume of oxide formed to the volume of metal consumed:

$$\mathrm{PBR} = \frac{V_{oxide}}{V_{metal}} = \frac{M_{oxide}\,\rho_{metal}}{n\,M_{metal}\,\rho_{oxide}}$$

where $M$ = molar mass, $\rho$ = density, $n$ = number of metal atoms in one formula unit of oxide.

**Relation to protectiveness:**

| PBR | Nature of film | Behaviour | Examples (computed from $M$ and $\rho$) |
|---|---|---|---|
| < 1 | Porous, discontinuous (oxide too small to cover metal) | Oxygen reaches the metal through pores; oxidation continues (non-protective) | Na 0.58, Ca 0.65, Mg 0.81 |
| about 1 to 2 | Compact, continuous, adherent, non-porous | Protective; diffusion is very slow, further corrosion stops | Al 1.29, Cu 1.68 |
| >> 2 | Highly stressed (oxide much larger than metal) | Film cracks and flakes off (spalls), fresh metal exposed | Fe ($\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}$) 2.15 is borderline; W ($\mathrm{WO_3}$) 3.4 |

**Types of oxide layers:**
1. **Stable:** fine-grained, tightly adherent (Al, Cr, Cu, Sn, Pb); protective.
2. **Unstable:** decomposes back to metal (Ag, Au, Pt); no oxidation corrosion.
3. **Volatile:** evaporates as formed (Mo forms $\mathrm{MoO_3}$); rapid continuous corrosion.
4. **Porous:** PBR < 1 (alkali and alkaline earth metals); continuous corrosion.

Hence a metal whose oxide occupies a volume equal to or somewhat greater than the metal (PBR about 1 to 2) is protected; very low or very high PBR gives no protection.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2022-23 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md:
Give reason why (**Any two**):

a. Impure metal corrodes faster than pure metal under identical conditions.
items.answer_md: Impurities (e.g. Fe, Cu, Pb in Zn) have a different electrode potential from the base metal. In contact with an electrolyte they form numerous tiny **local galvanic cells**: the base metal acts as anode and the impurity as cathode ($\mathrm{Zn \rightarrow Zn^{2+} + 2e^-}$, $\mathrm{2H^+ + 2e^- \rightarrow H_2}$ on the impurity). Impurities also lower hydrogen overvoltage. A pure metal has no such cells, so it corrodes much more slowly (e.g. 99.999% Zn is hardly attacked by dilute $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$, commercial Zn dissolves fast).

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2022-23 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md:
Give reason why (**Any two**):

b. Small anodic area leads to intense corrosion.
items.answer_md: Rate of corrosion $\propto \dfrac{\text{area of cathode}}{\text{area of anode}}$. The large cathode demands many electrons for the reduction ($\mathrm{O_2 + 2H_2O + 4e^- \rightarrow 4OH^-}$), and all of them must be supplied by oxidation of the small anode ($\mathrm{M \rightarrow M^{n+} + ne^-}$). The current density at the anode is therefore very high and it corrodes intensely, often as deep pits. Example: a steel bolt in a copper sheet, or a scratch on tinned iron.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2022-23 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md:
Give reason why (**Any two**):

c. Rusting of iron is quicker in saline water than in ordinary water.
items.answer_md: Saline water contains dissolved NaCl, which is a strong electrolyte: it greatly **increases the conductivity** of the water, so the corrosion current between anodic and cathodic areas flows easily. Also $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ ions **break down the protective oxide film** on iron and form soluble chlorides. Hence $\mathrm{Fe \rightarrow Fe^{2+} + 2e^-}$ and $\mathrm{O_2 + 2H_2O + 4e^- \rightarrow 4OH^-}$ proceed faster, and rust forms more quickly than in ordinary (poorly conducting) water.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2022-23 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: Explain the mechanism of hydrogen evolution and oxygen absorption in the process of electrochemical corrosion (with figures).
items.answer_md:
In electrochemical corrosion the metal dissolves at the anode ($\mathrm{M \rightarrow M^{n+} + ne^-}$); the electrons are consumed at the cathode by one of two reactions depending on the medium.

### 1. Hydrogen evolution type

Occurs in **acidic, de-aerated** media (acid solutions, industrial wastes). Example: iron in dilute HCl or an iron tank holding acid.

- Anode (large area of the metal): $\mathrm{Fe \rightarrow Fe^{2+} + 2e^-}$
- Electrons flow through the metal to the cathode (small area, e.g. a cathodic impurity or Cu-coated spot): $\mathrm{2H^+ + 2e^- \rightarrow H_2\uparrow}$
- Overall: $\mathrm{Fe + 2H^+ \rightarrow Fe^{2+} + H_2\uparrow}$

In this type the anode is usually large and the cathode small. All metals above hydrogen in the electrochemical series tend to dissolve in acid with $\mathrm{H_2}$ evolution.

*Figure (in words):* iron plate in acid solution; a small cathodic spot (Cu) with $\mathrm{H_2}$ bubbles rising and arrows $\mathrm{2H^+ \rightarrow H_2}$; the rest of the iron surface labelled anode with $\mathrm{Fe \rightarrow Fe^{2+}}$ going into solution; $e^-$ arrow through the metal from anode to cathode.

### 2. Oxygen absorption type

Occurs in **neutral or slightly alkaline, aerated** solutions (moist air, sea water). Example: iron with a crack in its oxide film exposed to aqueous NaCl.

- Anode (small, at the crack): $\mathrm{Fe \rightarrow Fe^{2+} + 2e^-}$
- Cathode (large, oxide-covered surface): $\mathrm{\tfrac12 O_2 + H_2O + 2e^- \rightarrow 2OH^-}$
- $\mathrm{Fe^{2+} + 2OH^- \rightarrow Fe(OH)_2}$; $\mathrm{4Fe(OH)_2 + O_2 + 2H_2O \rightarrow 4Fe(OH)_3}$ (yellow rust, $\mathrm{Fe_2O_3\cdot xH_2O}$); limited $\mathrm{O_2}$ gives black $\mathrm{Fe_3O_4}$.

Here the anode is small and the cathode large, so attack at the crack is intense (pitting).

*Figure (in words):* iron plate with oxide film under NaCl solution; a small crack labelled anode with $\mathrm{Fe \rightarrow Fe^{2+}}$; surrounding film labelled cathode with $\mathrm{O_2}$ entering from air and $\mathrm{OH^-}$ forming; rust deposited between them; $e^-$ arrow through the metal.

| | Hydrogen evolution | Oxygen absorption |
|---|---|---|
| Medium | Acidic, de-aerated | Neutral/alkaline, aerated |
| Cathode reaction | $\mathrm{2H^+ + 2e^- \rightarrow H_2}$ | $\mathrm{O_2 + 2H_2O + 4e^- \rightarrow 4OH^-}$ |
| Area | Large anode, small cathode | Small anode, large cathode |
| Product | Soluble $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ salt, $\mathrm{H_2}$ gas | $\mathrm{Fe(OH)_2}$, then rust |

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2022-23 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: What are 'Impressed Current Cathodic Protection' and 'Sacrificial Anodic Protection' methods of controlling corrosion? Discuss their merits and demerits.
items.answer_md:
Both are **cathodic protection** methods: the structure to be protected is forced to act as the **cathode**, so it does not corrode.

### 1. Sacrificial anodic protection
**Sacrificial anodic protection** (a cathodic protection method): the metal structure to be protected is connected by a wire to a **more active (anodic) metal** such as **Mg, Zn or Al** (or their alloys). The active metal acts as the anode and corrodes ("sacrificed"), while the structure becomes the cathode and is protected.

- Anode reaction: $\mathrm{Mg \rightarrow Mg^{2+} + 2e^-}$; electrons flow to the steel, which acts as cathode: $\mathrm{O_2 + 2H_2O + 4e^- \rightarrow 4OH^-}$.
- The consumed anode is replaced periodically.
- Uses: buried pipelines and cables, ship hulls, water tanks, boilers, marine structures; magnesium blocks in domestic water heaters.

### 2. Impressed current cathodic protection
**Impressed current cathodic protection (ICCP):** a direct current from an external DC source (battery or rectifier) is applied in the opposite direction to the corrosion current, so the structure becomes the **cathode**. The negative terminal is connected to the structure and the positive terminal to an **insoluble (inert) anode** such as graphite, high-silicon iron, scrap iron or platinised Ti, buried in a backfill (coke breeze, gypsum, bentonite) to improve contact. Used for buried pipelines, water tanks, oil and gas lines, transmission towers, ships, marine piers.

*Diagram (in words):* DC source; negative terminal wired to the buried pipeline (cathode); positive terminal wired to a graphite anode buried in backfill some distance away; current flows through the soil from anode to pipe.

### Merits and demerits

| | Sacrificial anode | Impressed current |
|---|---|---|
| External power | Not required | Required (DC source, running cost) |
| Installation/cost | Simple, low initial cost | Higher initial cost; equipment needed |
| Maintenance | Anodes consumed, must be replaced periodically | Inert anodes last long; little replacement |
| Driving voltage / current | Small and fixed; suitable for small structures and low-resistivity media | Large and adjustable; suitable for long pipelines and high-resistivity soils |
| Interference | No stray current problem | Can cause stray-current corrosion of neighbouring structures |
| Control | No control needed | Needs monitoring; over-protection can cause hydrogen embrittlement or coating damage |
| Typical use | Ship hulls, water heaters, short pipelines, offshore platforms | Long buried pipelines, large tanks, mine pipes, marine piers |

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2022-23 Sem 2.pdf
items.topic: Mechanisms of lubrication: thick layer, thin layer, extreme pressure
items.question_md: Discuss the mechanism of *Hydrodynamic* lubrication and compare it with Hydrostatic lubrication giving suitable examples (*two examples for each*).
items.answer_md:
**Mechanism of hydrodynamic lubrication**
- It is a **thick (fluid) film** mechanism: a continuous lubricant film (about 1000 Å or more) completely separates the surfaces.
- At rest the shaft sits on the bearing. On rotation it drags viscous oil into the **converging wedge** between shaft and bearing; the pressure built up in this wedge **lifts the shaft** so it floats on the oil.
- Friction is only the internal friction (**viscosity**) of the oil; $\mu \approx 0.001$-$0.03$. Needs sufficient speed and moderate load.

**Comparison with hydrostatic lubrication**

| Point | Hydrodynamic | Hydrostatic |
|---|---|---|
| Source of film pressure | Relative motion (wedge action) | External **pump** supplies oil under pressure |
| At zero/low speed | No film; contact and wear at start-stop | Full film even at zero speed |
| Load and speed | Moderate load, high speed | Very heavy load, low speed, high precision |
| Equipment and cost | Simple, cheap | Pump, piping, control; costly |
| Examples | (1) Crankshaft/journal bearings of IC engines; (2) Steam-turbine and generator bearings | (1) Bearings of large telescopes; (2) Precision machine-tool spindles and slideways |

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2022-23 Sem 2.pdf
items.question_md: How synthetic lubricants are important in tribology and maintenance, write key points?
items.answer_md:
**Synthetic lubricants** are man-made lubricating fluids (polyalphaolefins, esters, polyglycols, silicones, phosphate esters, fluorocarbons) designed for conditions where petroleum oils fail. Their importance in tribology and maintenance:

1. **Wide temperature range:** high viscosity index, so viscosity changes little; low pour point for cold starts and high thermal stability for hot running (jet engines, turbines).
2. **Oxidation and thermal stability:** little sludge, gum or carbon; longer oil life and **longer drain intervals**, so less downtime and maintenance cost.
3. **Low volatility and high flash point:** less oil loss and lower fire risk; phosphate esters are **fire-resistant** hydraulic fluids.
4. **Reduced friction and wear:** stable film over a range of speeds and loads, giving lower energy use and longer component life.
5. **Chemical inertness:** silicones and fluorocarbons resist chemicals, oxygen and radiation; used in chemical plants and space equipment.
6. **Compatibility:** polyglycols are water-soluble, esters biodegradable, useful for food and environmentally sensitive machines.

Limitation: higher cost, and some (esters) may attack seals and paints, so selection must match the machine.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2022-23 Sem 2.pdf
items.topic: Physical and chemical properties of lubricants and their testing
items.question_md:
A student was given labeled bottles (A) & (B) one of which contains **Single Grade** while other **Multi-grade** lubricant. Student performed viscosity index (V.I) experiment for which the results are presented in the given figure. Find out the bottle which contains **Multi-grade** lubricant with proper justification.

[Figure: Plot of Viscosity (y-axis) vs Temperature (x-axis) with marks at 0°C, 40°C and 100°C. Two straight lines decrease with temperature and cross at 40°C: line (A) falls steeply, line (B) falls gently.]
items.answer_md:
**Bottle (B) contains the multi-grade lubricant.**

**Justification:** Viscosity index (VI) measures how little the viscosity of an oil changes with temperature. A multi-grade oil (e.g. SAE 20W-40) contains VI improvers (polymer additives), so it has a **high VI**: it stays thin enough at low temperature and thick enough at high temperature.

In the figure, line (B) falls **gently**, i.e. its viscosity changes little between 0 $^\circ$C and 100 $^\circ$C, so it has a high VI (multi-grade). Line (A) falls **steeply**, i.e. a large change of viscosity with temperature, low VI, so (A) is the single-grade oil.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2022-23 Sem 2.pdf
items.question_md: What is caustic embrittlement? How does it affect the boilers operation?
items.answer_md:
**Caustic embrittlement** is the brittleness and intercrystalline cracking of boiler metal at stressed parts (rivets, bends, joints) caused by a high concentration of $\mathrm{NaOH}$ in the boiler water; it is a form of stress corrosion.

**Cause.** Boiler feed water softened by the lime-soda process keeps a little residual $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}$. At high pressure it hydrolyses:
$$\mathrm{Na_2CO_3 + H_2O \rightarrow 2NaOH + CO_2}$$
The alkaline water seeps into hair-line cracks and crevices at rivets, bends and joints; water evaporates there and $\mathrm{NaOH}$ becomes highly concentrated.

**Mechanism (concentration cell).**
$$\text{Iron at stressed parts (anode)} \mid \text{conc. NaOH} \parallel \text{dil. NaOH} \mid \text{Iron at plane surface (cathode)}$$
Iron under stress in concentrated $\mathrm{NaOH}$ is the anode and dissolves as **sodium ferroate**:
$$\mathrm{Fe + 2NaOH \rightarrow Na_2FeO_2 + H_2}$$
Sodium ferroate decomposes, depositing magnetite and **regenerating NaOH**, so a small amount of alkali keeps the attack going:
$$\mathrm{3Na_2FeO_2 + 4H_2O \rightarrow 6NaOH + Fe_3O_4 + H_2}$$
The attack runs along the grain boundaries (intercrystalline cracking), so the metal becomes brittle.

**Effect on boiler operation.**
1. Cracks grow along grain boundaries at rivets, joints and bends, so these parts lose strength and become brittle.
2. Leakage of water and steam at joints; the boiler must be shut down for repair, losing output.
3. The weakened shell cannot withstand working pressure, so there is a risk of sudden failure or **boiler explosion**.
4. Because NaOH is regenerated, the damage is continuous and progressive, shortening boiler life.

**Prevention.**
1. Use sodium phosphate instead of sodium carbonate as the softening (conditioning) reagent.
2. Add tannin or lignin, which block the hair-line cracks so NaOH cannot seep in.
3. Add $\mathrm{Na_2SO_4}$, which also blocks the cracks: $\mathrm{Na_2SO_4 : NaOH}$ = 1:1 up to 10 atm, 2:1 up to 20 atm, 3:1 above 20 atm.

items.topic: Purification of water step by step
items.question_md: What do you understand by TDS? How TDS is regulated while purifying water using *domestic/RO* water purifiers.
items.answer_md:
**TDS (Total Dissolved Solids)** is the total amount of inorganic salts ($\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$, $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$, $\mathrm{Na^+}$, $\mathrm{K^+}$, $\mathrm{HCO_3^-}$, $\mathrm{Cl^-}$, $\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}$ ...) and small amounts of organic matter dissolved in water, expressed in mg/L (ppm). The desirable limit for drinking water is 500 mg/L.

**Regulation in domestic RO purifiers**
1. The **RO membrane** removes about 90-99% of dissolved salts, so the permeate has very low TDS (often below 20-30 mg/L) and lacks essential minerals.
2. A **TDS controller (mixing valve)** blends a controlled fraction of water that has passed only through the sediment and carbon / UV-UF stages (not the RO membrane) with the RO permeate, raising the TDS to a desirable level (about 50-150 mg/L).
3. Some purifiers instead add a **mineraliser cartridge** after RO to add back $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ and improve taste.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2022-23 Sem 2.pdf
items.question_md: Suggest use of technology (*any two*) to Reduce/Reuse/Recycle water at domestic level.
items.answer_md:
Any two of the following domestic technologies:

1. **Rooftop rainwater harvesting (Reuse / Recharge)**: rain from the roof is led through pipes and a simple sand-gravel filter into a storage tank for gardening, washing and toilet flushing, or into a recharge pit/borewell to raise the groundwater table. It reduces demand on the municipal supply.
2. **Greywater recycling (Recycle)**: lightly used water from washbasins, bathing and washing machines (not toilets) is passed through a settling tank and sand/charcoal filter and reused for flushing toilets, gardening and floor washing, cutting fresh-water use by about 30-40%.

Other acceptable options: low-flow taps with aerators and dual-flush toilets (Reduce); reuse of RO purifier reject water for mopping or gardening (Reuse).

items.question_md:
A sample of water contains the following data:
$MgCl_2$ - 190 ppm, $CaSO_4$ - 136 ppm, $MgSO_4$ - 180 ppm, $H_2SO_4$ - 49 ppm, $SiO_2$ - 4 ppm. Calculate the amount of lime (90% pure) and soda (96% pure) needed for treating 1 million of water.
items.answer_md:
**Given:** volume of water $V$ = 1 million L ($10^6$ L); lime purity = 90%, soda purity = 96%.

"1 million of water" is taken as 1 million litres; amounts in ppm = mg/L.

**To find:** mass of lime $\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2}$ (molar mass 74) and soda $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}$ (molar mass 106) required.

**Step 1: Convert each constituent to $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ equivalent**

$$\text{ppm as CaCO}_3 = \frac{\text{mg/L of salt}\times 100}{\text{molar mass of salt}}$$

| Constituent | Amount (mg/L) | Molar mass | Factor | ppm as $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ | Type | Needs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\mathrm{MgCl_2}$ | 190 | 95 | 100/95 | 200 | Permanent Mg | L + S |
| $\mathrm{CaSO_4}$ | 136 | 136 | 100/136 | 100 | Permanent Ca | S |
| $\mathrm{MgSO_4}$ | 180 | 120 | 100/120 | 150 | Permanent Mg | L + S |
| $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$ | 49 | 98 | 100/98 | 50 | Free acid ($\mathrm{H^+}$) | L + S |
| $\mathrm{SiO_2}$ | 4 | 60 | - | - | No hardness | none |

(L = lime, S = soda. Temporary Mg takes 2 lime; permanent Mg takes lime and then soda for the $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ it releases; Na, K salts and $\mathrm{SiO_2}$ cause no hardness and are ignored.)

**Step 2: Formulae**

$$\text{Lime} = \frac{74}{100}\left[\text{Perm Mg}\ (\mathrm{MgCl_2}) + \text{Perm Mg}\ (\mathrm{MgSO_4}) + \mathrm{H^+}\ (\mathrm{H_2SO_4})\right]\times\frac{V}{10^6}\times\frac{100}{\%\text{ purity}}\ \text{kg}$$

$$\text{Soda} = \frac{106}{100}\left[\text{Perm Mg}\ (\mathrm{MgCl_2}) + \text{Perm Ca}\ (\mathrm{CaSO_4}) + \text{Perm Mg}\ (\mathrm{MgSO_4}) + \mathrm{H^+}\ (\mathrm{H_2SO_4})\right]\times\frac{V}{10^6}\times\frac{100}{\%\text{ purity}}\ \text{kg}$$

**Step 3: Substitution**

Lime (100% pure) per litre $= \frac{74}{100}[200 + 150 + 50] = \frac{74}{100}\times 400 = 296$ mg/L

Lime (100% pure) for 1 million L ($10^6$ L) $= 296\times 1000000 = 296000000$ mg $= 296$ kg

Lime (90% pure) $= 296\times\frac{100}{90} = 328.89$ kg

Soda (100% pure) per litre $= \frac{106}{100}[200 + 100 + 150 + 50] = \frac{106}{100}\times 500 = 530$ mg/L

Soda (100% pure) for 1 million L ($10^6$ L) $= 530\times 1000000 = 530000000$ mg $= 530$ kg

Soda (96% pure) $= 530\times\frac{100}{96} = 552.08$ kg

**Result:** Lime required = **328.89 kg**; Soda required = **552.08 kg**.

$\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$ (molar mass 98) needs lime to neutralise it and soda for the $\mathrm{CaSO_4}$ formed ($\mathrm{H_2SO_4 + Ca(OH)_2 \rightarrow CaSO_4 + 2H_2O}$), so it appears in both brackets. $\mathrm{SiO_2}$ causes no hardness.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2022-23 Sem 2.pdf
items.question_md: Discuss knocking mechanism in petrol/gasoline and Diesel engines.
items.answer_md:
### Knocking in petrol (SI) engine
- Petrol vapour and air are compressed and ignited by a **spark**; the flame front should travel smoothly through the charge.
- At a high compression ratio the unburnt last portion (**end gas**) is heated and compressed by the advancing flame; hydrocarbons form **peroxides** which decompose explosively, so the end gas **self-ignites before the flame front reaches it**.
- The sudden pressure rise produces a sharp **metallic knocking sound**, loss of power, overheating and damage to pistons and valves.
- Straight-chain alkanes knock most; branched alkanes and aromatics least. Remedy: high octane fuel, antiknock agents.

### Knocking in diesel (CI) engine
- Only air is compressed (ratio 14-22) to a high temperature; fuel is injected and ignites by itself after a short **ignition delay**.
- If the delay is **long**, fuel keeps accumulating in the cylinder and then ignites **all at once**, giving a violent pressure rise: **diesel knock**.
- Fuels that ignite with difficulty (aromatics, branched) knock; straight-chain alkanes (high cetane number) do not. Remedy: high cetane fuel, cetane improvers (ethyl nitrite).

So petrol knock is due to **too early** ignition and diesel knock to **too late** ignition.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2022-23 Sem 2.pdf
items.question_md:
Which of the following (A) and (B) in the given figure are related to octane and cetane numbers and why?

[Figure: Two upward arrows labelled "Slow Burning". Scale (A) reads 100 at top, 90 in the middle, 80 at bottom. Scale (B) reads 80 at top, 90 in the middle, 100 at bottom.]
items.answer_md:
**Scale (A) relates to octane number; scale (B) relates to cetane number.**

- **Scale (A)**: the number increases (80 → 90 → 100) in the direction of **slower burning**. A fuel of higher octane number resists premature self-ignition and burns slowly and smoothly without knocking; iso-octane (slow, smooth burning) is 100 and n-heptane (fast burning, knocks) is 0. So (A) is the octane scale.
- **Scale (B)**: the number decreases (100 → 90 → 80) in the direction of slower burning, i.e. higher numbers mean **faster, easier ignition**. A diesel fuel of high cetane number ignites quickly (short ignition delay); cetane (n-hexadecane) is 100, slow-igniting α-methylnaphthalene is 0. So (B) is the cetane scale.

The two scales run in opposite directions because good petrol (high ON) is a poor diesel (low CN).

items.topic: Gross and net calorific value by bomb calorimeter
items.question_md:
A sample of coal contains 85% C, 8% H, 4% ash and this sample was tested in the Bomb calorimeter for which the observations are given below:

Weight of coal burnt = 0.85 g; Weight of water taken = 700 g; Water equivalent of calorimeter = 2000 g; Rise in temperature = $2.5\,^{\circ}C$; Cooling correction = $0.02\,^{\circ}C$; Fuse wire correction = 10 Cal.; Acid correction = 60 Cal.

Calculate the gross and net calorific values of the fuel. Comment on the experimental validity of the calorific value.
items.answer_md:
**Given**: $x = 0.85$ g, $W = 700$ g, $w = 2000$ g, $\Delta t = 2.5\ ^\circ$C, $t_c = 0.02\ ^\circ$C, $t_F = 10$ cal, $t_A = 60$ cal, H = 8%, C = 85%, ash = 4%. Latent heat of steam $L = 587$ cal/g.

**To find**: GCV and NCV.

**Formulae**
$$\mathrm{GCV} = \frac{(W+w)(t_2 - t_1 + t_c) - (t_A + t_F)}{x}, \qquad \mathrm{NCV} = \mathrm{GCV} - 0.09\,H \times 587$$

**GCV**
$$\mathrm{GCV} = \frac{(700+2000)(2.5 + 0.02) - (60+10)}{0.85} = \frac{2700 \times 2.52 - 70}{0.85} = \frac{6804 - 70}{0.85} = \frac{6734}{0.85}$$
$$\mathbf{GCV = 7922.35\ cal/g\ (kcal/kg)}$$

**NCV**
$$0.09 \times 8 \times 587 = 422.64\ \text{cal/g}$$
$$\mathrm{NCV} = 7922.35 - 422.64 = \mathbf{7499.71\ cal/g}$$

**Comment on experimental validity**
- NCV < GCV as required, and a GCV of about 7900 kcal/kg is typical of a bituminous coal, so the result is reasonable.
- The composition adds to only $85 + 8 + 4 = 97\%$; the remaining 3% (O, N, S) is unreported. Any S and N justify the acid correction of 60 cal.
- The theoretical (Dulong) value from C and H alone is $\frac{1}{100}(8080 \times 85 + 34500 \times 8) = 9628$ kcal/kg; the experimental value is lower, as expected, because part of the H is combined with O and Dulong ignores heat of formation and losses. 8% H is also high for a coal (coals usually have 4-6% H).
- The water equivalent (2000 g) is unusually larger than the mass of water (700 g); with so little water the temperature rise is small, so small reading errors have a large effect.

Overall the calculated values are **acceptable**, but the data have the above limitations.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2022-23 Sem 2.pdf
items.question_md: Discuss thermodynamic criteria for a polymerization process to be feasible.
items.answer_md:
Polymerisation is feasible only if the **Gibbs free energy change is negative**:
$$\Delta G_p = \Delta H_p - T\Delta S_p < 0$$

- **$\Delta S_p$ is negative**: many free monomer molecules become one chain, so translational freedom (disorder) is lost (typically about -100 to -155 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹). The term $-T\Delta S_p$ is therefore positive and opposes polymerisation.
- **$\Delta H_p$ must be negative** (exothermic) and large enough to outweigh it. In addition polymerisation one $\pi$ bond is converted into a stronger $\sigma$ bond, releasing about 35-100 kJ/mol.

Hence polymerisation is favoured at **low temperature**. Above the **ceiling temperature**
$$T_c = \frac{\Delta H_p}{\Delta S_p}$$
$\Delta G_p > 0$ and the polymer depolymerises.

**Examples**
- Ethylene: $\Delta H_p \approx -93$ kJ/mol, $\Delta S_p \approx -155$ J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. At 298 K, $\Delta G_p = -93000 - 298(-155) = -46810$ J/mol $\approx -46.8$ kJ/mol, so it polymerises readily; $T_c = 93000/155 = 600$ K.
- $\alpha$-Methylstyrene: $\Delta H_p \approx -35$ kJ/mol (steric strain lowers it), $\Delta S_p \approx -104$ J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, so $T_c = 35000/104 \approx 337$ K (about 63 °C); it polymerises only at low temperature.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2022-23 Sem 2.pdf
items.question_md: Explain the mechanism of coordination polymerization. Why is it different from ionic polymerization?
items.answer_md:
**Coordination (Ziegler-Natta) polymerisation** (catalyst: $\mathrm{TiCl_4}$ + $\mathrm{Al(C_2H_5)_3}$, monomer: propylene)

1. **Formation of the active site:** the aluminium alkyl alkylates titanium, leaving a Ti atom with a Ti-C bond and a vacant coordination site ($\square$).
$$\mathrm{TiCl_4 + Al(C_2H_5)_3 \rightarrow Cl_3Ti{-}C_2H_5\,(\square) + Al(C_2H_5)_2Cl}$$
2. **Coordination:** the monomer double bond donates its $\pi$ electrons to the vacant site of Ti ($\pi$-complex).
3. **Insertion (propagation):** the monomer is inserted between Ti and the alkyl group; the vacant site is regenerated and the cycle repeats.
$$\mathrm{[Ti]{-}C_2H_5 + CH_2{=}CHCH_3 \rightarrow [Ti]{-}CH_2{-}CH(CH_3){-}C_2H_5}$$
$$\mathrm{[Ti]{-}CH_2{-}CH(CH_3){-}C_2H_5 + n\,CH_2{=}CHCH_3 \rightarrow [Ti]{-}[CH_2{-}CH(CH_3)]_{n+1}{-}C_2H_5}$$
4. **Termination:** by chain transfer with hydrogen (or by $\beta$-hydride elimination).
$$\mathrm{[Ti]{-}CH_2{-}CH(CH_3){\sim} + H_2 \rightarrow [Ti]{-}H + CH_3{-}CH(CH_3){\sim}}$$
Because each monomer is placed in the same orientation on the solid catalyst surface, the product is stereoregular (isotactic polypropylene, linear HDPE) at low pressure and temperature.

### Why it is different from ionic polymerisation
| Coordination | Ionic (cationic/anionic) |
|---|---|
| Growing chain is bonded to a metal (Ti-C bond); no free ion | Growing chain is a free carbocation or carbanion with a counter-ion |
| Monomer coordinates to the catalyst then inserts | Monomer adds directly to the charged chain end |
| Gives stereoregular (isotactic/syndiotactic), linear polymers | Generally poor stereo-control |
| Polymerises simple olefins such as ethylene and propylene | Needs monomers with electron-donating (cationic) or electron-withdrawing (anionic) groups |
| Heterogeneous catalyst, moderate temperature and low pressure | Often very low temperature, polar solvent |

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2022-23 Sem 2.pdf
items.topic: Composition, setting and hardening of cement
items.question_md: What do you understand by setting and hardening of the cement? Write chemical reactions involved in these processes.
items.answer_md:
When cement is mixed with water it forms a plastic paste. The paste first **stiffens (setting)** and then slowly **gains strength (hardening)**. Both result from exothermic hydration and hydrolysis of the four Bogue compounds.

### 1. Setting (stiffening, first 24 h)
- **Initial set** (within minutes to hours): $\mathrm{C_3A}$ hydrates very fast, forming a rigid network of tricalcium aluminate hydrate. Gypsum present reacts with $\mathrm{C_3A}$ to form insoluble calcium sulphoaluminate (ettringite) that coats the grains and slows this reaction, preventing flash set.
- **Final set**: $\mathrm{C_4AF}$ hydrates; $\mathrm{C_3S}$ starts forming tobermorite gel, which fills the pores.
$$\mathrm{3CaO\cdot Al_2O_3 + 6H_2O \rightarrow 3CaO\cdot Al_2O_3\cdot 6H_2O} \quad (+880\ \mathrm{kJ/kg})$$
$$\mathrm{4CaO\cdot Al_2O_3\cdot Fe_2O_3 + 7H_2O \rightarrow 3CaO\cdot Al_2O_3\cdot 6H_2O + CaO\cdot Fe_2O_3\cdot H_2O} \quad (+420\ \mathrm{kJ/kg})$$
$$\mathrm{3CaO\cdot Al_2O_3 + 3(CaSO_4\cdot 2H_2O) + 26H_2O \rightarrow 3CaO\cdot Al_2O_3\cdot 3CaSO_4\cdot 32H_2O}\ \ (\text{ettringite})$$

Also $\mathrm{C_3S}$ begins to hydrate (first equation below) and forms the gel that binds the grains at final set.

### 2. Hardening (strength gain, 1 to 28 days and beyond)
- $\mathrm{C_3S}$ hydrates in 1 to 7 days and gives **early strength**.
- $\mathrm{C_2S}$ hydrates slowly over 7 to 28 days and gives **later (ultimate) strength**.
$$\mathrm{2(3CaO\cdot SiO_2) + 6H_2O \rightarrow 3CaO\cdot 2SiO_2\cdot 3H_2O + 3Ca(OH)_2} \quad (+500\ \mathrm{kJ/kg})$$
$$\mathrm{2(2CaO\cdot SiO_2) + 4H_2O \rightarrow 3CaO\cdot 2SiO_2\cdot 3H_2O + Ca(OH)_2} \quad (+250\ \mathrm{kJ/kg})$$

- The product $\mathrm{3CaO\cdot 2SiO_2\cdot 3H_2O}$ is **tobermorite gel (C-S-H)**, the main binding phase; its interlocking crystals give strength.
- $\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2}$ released makes the paste alkaline (pH about 12.5), which protects steel in RCC.

### Summary
| Stage | Compound | Time | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Initial set | $\mathrm{C_3A}$ (controlled by gypsum) | first minutes to hours | stiffening |
| Final set | $\mathrm{C_4AF}$, start of $\mathrm{C_3S}$ | up to about 10 h | loses plasticity |
| Early hardening | $\mathrm{C_3S}$ | 1 to 7 days | early strength |
| Later hardening | $\mathrm{C_2S}$ | 7 to 28 days | ultimate strength |

IS limits for OPC: initial setting time **not less than 30 min**, final setting time **not more than 600 min (10 h)**.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2022-23 Sem 2.pdf
items.question_md: Write key differences between galvanic and concentrations cells. Suggest appropriate applications of the concentration cell.
items.answer_md:
### Key differences

| Basis | Galvanic cell (corrosion) | Concentration cell (corrosion) |
|---|---|---|
| Electrodes | Two **different** metals in electrical contact | **Same** metal (single piece) |
| Origin of EMF | Difference in standard electrode potentials ($E^\circ_{cell} = E^\circ_{cathode} - E^\circ_{anode}$) | Difference in concentration of electrolyte or of oxygen (aeration) |
| Anode | The more active metal (e.g. Zn in Zn-Cu) | The part in more dilute solution / less aerated region |
| EMF | Generally large (Zn-Cu: 1.10 V) | Small, $E = \frac{0.0591}{n}\log\frac{C_2}{C_1}$ |
| Example | Steel bolts in copper sheet; Zn-Fe couple | Waterline corrosion, pitting, crevice corrosion |

### Applications of the concentration cell
1. **Explaining and predicting corrosion:** differential aeration explains waterline corrosion, pitting, crevice corrosion and corrosion of buried pipelines through soils of different aeration; this guides design (avoid crevices, keep surfaces clean, uniform backfill).
2. **Measurement of solubility product and of unknown ion concentration** from the measured EMF, $E = \dfrac{0.0591}{n}\log\dfrac{C_2}{C_1}$.
3. **Determination of valency of ions and of transport numbers** (concentration cells with transference).
4. **pH measurement** (hydrogen concentration cell) and oxygen sensors (oxygen concentration cell, e.g. zirconia lambda sensor in cars).

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2022-23 Sem 2.pdf
items.question_md: Discuss sacrificial metallic protection from corrosion? What are the advantages and disadvantages of electroplating methods?
items.answer_md:
### Sacrificial metallic protection

The base metal is protected by coating it with (or connecting it to) a metal that is **more anodic (more active)** than itself, e.g. **Zn, Al, Cd on iron**. The coating metal corrodes preferentially and protects the base metal even if the coating is scratched or porous:

At a scratch on galvanised iron: anode $\mathrm{Zn \rightarrow Zn^{2+} + 2e^-}$; electrons flow to the exposed iron, which acts as cathode and is not corroded. Examples: galvanising of iron sheets and pipes (hot-dip Zn at 425 to 450 °C), Mg or Zn blocks attached to ship hulls and buried pipelines. (Contrast: tin on iron is a cathodic coating and protects only while intact.)

### Electroplating

**Advantages**
1. Thin, uniform, adherent coating with controlled thickness.
2. Works at room temperature, so the base metal is not distorted or softened.
3. Gives decorative, bright finish along with corrosion and wear resistance (Ni, Cr, Ag, Au).
4. Little metal is wasted; noble metals can be deposited economically.

**Disadvantages**
1. Requires electricity, rectifiers and careful surface cleaning; slow for thick coats.
2. Coating may be porous; a porous cathodic coating (Ni, Cr) accelerates corrosion of the base at pinholes.
3. Uneven thickness on complex shapes (poor throwing power in recesses).
4. Plating baths (cyanide, chromic acid) are toxic and create effluent problems; hydrogen embrittlement of high-strength steel is possible.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2022-23 Sem 2.pdf
items.question_md: What is the basic difference between paint and varnish? For outdoor metallic protection which of the two (paint/varnish) is more useful and why?
items.answer_md:
| Paint | Varnish |
|---|---|
| Mechanical dispersion of **pigment** + vehicle (drying oil) + thinner, drier, filler, plasticiser | Homogeneous **colloidal solution of a resin** (natural or synthetic) in oil or a volatile solvent; **no pigment** |
| Opaque; gives colour and hides the surface | Transparent; shows the surface underneath |
| Film forms by oxidation and polymerisation of the drying oil | Film forms by evaporation of solvent and/or oxidation of the oil, leaving a hard resin film |
| Thicker, more elastic, weather-resistant film | Thin, hard, glossy film; brittle outdoors |

**For outdoor metallic protection, paint is more useful**, because:
1. Its pigments (e.g. red lead, zinc chromate, $\mathrm{TiO_2}$) are opaque and protect the film and metal from UV light, which degrades a transparent varnish film.
2. Certain pigments actively inhibit corrosion (red lead and zinc chromate passivate steel; zinc dust acts sacrificially).
3. The film is thicker, less permeable to moisture and oxygen and more elastic, so it withstands weathering and temperature changes without cracking; varnish becomes brittle, cracks and peels in sunlight and rain.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2023 Sem 1.pdf
items.topic: Mechanisms of lubrication: thick layer, thin layer, extreme pressure
items.question_md: Discuss the lubrication mechanism in which coefficient of friction decreases to the extent of 0.05 to 0.15.
items.answer_md:
A coefficient of friction of **0.05 to 0.15** is typical of **thin film (boundary) lubrication**.

- It occurs when **load is high, speed is low**, during start-stop, or when oil viscosity is too low; a continuous thick film cannot form and asperities nearly touch.
- A film only a **few molecules thick** is held on each metal surface by **physical or chemical adsorption** of polar molecules (long-chain fatty acids, esters). The adsorbed layers slide over each other and keep the asperities from welding.
- The property that decides performance is **oiliness**, not viscosity.
- **Lubricants:** vegetable and animal oils and their soaps, fatty acids (oleic, stearic), graphite and $\mathrm{MoS_2}$ (alone or in oil).
- **Examples:** gears, cams, rail wheels, slideways, machines at starting.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2023 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: Name the lubricant and its advantages which are used in metal cutting.
items.answer_md:
Lubricants used in metal cutting are called **cutting fluids**. The commonest is **soluble oil**: mineral oil + emulsifier diluted with water to form a milky **oil-in-water emulsion**. For heavy cuts (threading, broaching) **straight cutting oils** (mineral oil with fatty oils and sulphur/chlorine EP additives) are used.

**Advantages**
1. **Cooling:** removes heat from the tool and workpiece, increasing tool life and keeping dimensions accurate.
2. **Lubrication:** reduces friction at the tool-chip interface, lowering power consumption.
3. Prevents **welding of chips** to the tool (built-up edge).
4. **Washes away chips** from the cutting zone.
5. Gives a better **surface finish** and **protects** the freshly cut surface from corrosion.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2023 Sem 1.pdf
items.topic: Mechanisms of lubrication: thick layer, thin layer, extreme pressure
items.question_md: Distinguish clearly between thick film and thin film lubrications.
items.answer_md:
| Point | Thick film (fluid film) lubrication | Thin film (boundary) lubrication |
|---|---|---|
| Film thickness | At least about 1000 Å, more than asperity height | Only a few molecules thick |
| Metal contact | None; surfaces fully separated | Asperities nearly in contact |
| How film is held | Hydrodynamic pressure built by motion | **Adsorption** (physical/chemical) of polar molecules on metal |
| Load and speed | Low load, high speed | High load, low speed, start-stop |
| Property that matters | **Viscosity** | **Oiliness** |
| Coefficient of friction | About 0.001-0.03 | About 0.05-0.15 |
| Lubricants used | Hydrocarbon (mineral) oils of right viscosity with antioxidants | Vegetable/animal oils, fatty acids, soaps, graphite, $\mathrm{MoS_2}$ |
| Examples | Journal bearings, turbines, delicate instruments | Gears, cams, rail axles, slideways |

items.question_md: Explain the significance of octane number and cetane number in petroleum industry.
items.answer_md:
**Significance**

- **Octane number** measures the **antiknock quality of petrol** (spark-ignition engines): % iso-octane (ON 100) in an iso-octane + n-heptane (ON 0) blend that knocks like the fuel. Higher ON allows higher compression ratio, more power and efficiency without knocking; petrol is graded and priced by ON.
- **Cetane number** measures the **ignition quality of diesel** (compression-ignition engines): % n-hexadecane (CN 100) in a cetane + α-methylnaphthalene (CN 0) blend with the same ignition delay. Higher CN means short ignition delay, easy starting and no diesel knock.

The refinery uses them to blend and grade fuels; straight-chain hydrocarbons give high CN but low ON, so good petrol is poor diesel and vice versa.

Example: ON 87 petrol behaves like 87% iso-octane + 13% n-heptane; diesel of CN 50 ignites like 50% cetane + 50% α-methylnaphthalene.

items.topic: Numericals on calorific value and ultimate analysis
items.question_md: A sample of coal contained C-84%, $H_2$-4%, $O_2$= 2% and $N_2$= 1%. Estimate the minimum quantity of the air required for combustion of 1kg of the sample. Find the percentage of dry products formed if 20% excess air is supplied.
items.answer_md:
**Given** (per kg coal): C = 0.84 kg, H = 0.04 kg, O = 0.02 kg, N = 0.01 kg (rest ash/moisture, needs no oxygen). Air contains 23% $\mathrm{O_2}$ and 77% $\mathrm{N_2}$ by mass. Excess air 20%.

**To find**: minimum air per kg; % composition of dry products with 20% excess air.

### Oxygen required
| Reaction | $\mathrm{O_2}$ (kg) |
|---|---|
| $\mathrm{C + O_2 \rightarrow CO_2}$: $0.84 \times \frac{32}{12}$ | 2.24 |
| $\mathrm{2H_2 + O_2 \rightarrow 2H_2O}$: $0.04 \times 8$ | 0.32 |
| Total | 2.56 |
| Less O present in coal | $-0.02$ |
| **Net $\mathrm{O_2}$ required** | **2.54** |

### Minimum air
$$\text{Minimum air} = 2.54 \times \frac{100}{23} = \mathbf{11.04\ kg\ per\ kg\ coal}$$

### Air with 20% excess
$$\text{Air supplied} = 11.04 \times 1.20 = 13.25\ \text{kg}$$

### Dry products (water vapour excluded)
| Product | Calculation | Mass (kg) | % by mass |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\mathrm{CO_2}$ | $0.84 \times \frac{44}{12}$ | 3.080 | **22.32** |
| $\mathrm{N_2}$ | $0.01 + 0.77 \times 13.252$ | 10.214 | **74.00** |
| $\mathrm{O_2}$ (excess) | $0.20 \times 2.54$ | 0.508 | **3.68** |
| Total | | 13.802 | 100.00 |

**Result**: minimum air = **11.04 kg/kg**; dry products by mass: $\mathrm{CO_2}$ **22.32%**, $\mathrm{N_2}$ **74.00%**, $\mathrm{O_2}$ **3.68%**.

(By volume, dividing each mass by its molar mass: $\mathrm{CO_2}$ 15.53%, $\mathrm{N_2}$ 80.94%, $\mathrm{O_2}$ 3.53%.)

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2023 Sem 1.pdf
items.topic: Gross and net calorific value by bomb calorimeter
items.question_md: Which one of the two (Gross caloric value and Net calorific value) is easy to determine with proper justification.
items.answer_md:
**Gross calorific value (GCV) is easier to determine.**

**Justification**
1. In the **bomb calorimeter** (and Boys' gas calorimeter) the fuel burns in a closed vessel and the products cool to near room temperature, so the steam formed **condenses** and gives up its latent heat to the water. The measured heat is therefore directly the GCV:
$$\mathrm{GCV} = \frac{(W+w)(t_2-t_1)}{x}$$
2. To measure NCV directly the steam would have to be kept uncondensed and its latent heat excluded, which is not possible in a simple calorimeter.
3. Hence NCV is **not measured** but **calculated** from the GCV and the hydrogen content:
$$\mathrm{NCV} = \mathrm{GCV} - 0.09\,H \times 587\ \text{cal/g}$$

So GCV is obtained directly by experiment, while NCV needs GCV plus %H from ultimate analysis.

items.topic: Purification of water step by step
items.question_md: What is the physical significance of break point chlorination? What kind of information can be drawn out of it?
items.answer_md:
**Physical significance.** The break point is the chlorine dose at which all chlorine-consuming substances in the water (reducing agents, ammonia, organic matter, micro-organisms) have been completely oxidised. Any chlorine added beyond it remains as **free residual chlorine**. So it marks the minimum dose that guarantees complete disinfection.

**Curve (residual chlorine vs chlorine added):** no residual at first (reducing agents consume $\mathrm{Cl_2}$); residual rises (chloramines formed); residual falls to a minimum, the **break point** (chloramines and organics destroyed); then free residual rises linearly.

**Information drawn from it**
1. The **chlorine demand** of the water: the dose needed to reach the break point.
2. The correct **dose** to apply: just beyond the break point, giving a small free residual (about 0.1-0.2 ppm).
3. The amount of **ammonia and organic matter** present: a higher, later hump means more chloramine-forming impurities.
4. Whether the water is truly safe: free residual chlorine indicates complete oxidation of pathogens, taste and odour causing compounds, and protection against recontamination in the mains.

items.question_md:
A sample of water gave the following data:

Total alkalinity = 320 ppm as $CaCO_3$

Calcium Hardness = 252 ppm as $CaCO_3$

Magnesium Hardness = 70 ppm as $CaCO_3$

Calculate the lime and soda required to soften the 1 million liters of this water sample. Comment on the validity of the data.
items.answer_md:
**Given:** total alkalinity = 320 ppm, Ca hardness = 252 ppm, Mg hardness = 70 ppm (all as $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$); $V = 10^6$ L. Purity not stated, so 100% pure lime and soda are assumed.

**To find:** lime and soda for $10^6$ L; validity of data.

**Step 1: Split the hardness.** Total hardness $= 252 + 70 = 322$ ppm. Taking the alkalinity as bicarbonate ($\mathrm{HCO_3^-}$) alkalinity, it is the carbonate (temporary) hardness, and it is assigned first to Ca, then to Mg:

| Component | ppm as $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ | Needs |
|---|---|---|
| Temporary Ca (all Ca hardness, 252 < 320) | 252 | L |
| Temporary Mg = 320 - 252 | 68 | 2L |
| Permanent Mg = 70 - 68 | 2 | L + S |
| Permanent Ca | 0 | S |

**Step 2: Formulae and substitution**
$$\text{Lime} = \frac{74}{100}[\text{Temp Ca} + 2\times\text{Temp Mg} + \text{Perm Mg}] = \frac{74}{100}[252 + 2(68) + 2] = \frac{74}{100}\times 390 = 288.6\ \text{mg/L}$$
$$\text{Soda} = \frac{106}{100}[\text{Perm Ca} + \text{Perm Mg}] = \frac{106}{100}[0 + 2] = 2.12\ \text{mg/L}$$

For $10^6$ L: lime $= 288.6\times 10^6$ mg $= 288.6$ kg; soda $= 2.12\times 10^6$ mg $= 2.12$ kg.

**Result:** Lime = **288.6 kg**, Soda = **2.12 kg** for 1 million litres.

**Validity of data:** The data are valid. Total hardness (322 ppm) is greater than total alkalinity (320 ppm), so all the alkalinity can be accounted for as bicarbonates of Ca and Mg and no $\mathrm{NaHCO_3}$ is present (that would require alkalinity > total hardness). Hence carbonate hardness = 320 ppm and non-carbonate hardness = 2 ppm. Since bicarbonate and hydroxide alkalinity cannot coexist, the alkalinity is taken as wholly $\mathrm{HCO_3^-}$; nearly all the hardness is temporary, so the water needs mostly lime and very little soda.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2023 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: Which one of the two (cold lime soda & hot lime soda) is most preferred method for water purification? Justify by writing chemical equations involved in that particular method?
items.answer_md:
The **hot lime-soda process** is the preferred method.

**Justification**
1. At 80-150 °C the reactions are fast (about 15 minutes), so plant output is high.
2. The precipitate is coarse and settles quickly; **no coagulant** is required.
3. Dissolved $\mathrm{CO_2}$ and air are driven out, reducing corrosion.
4. Residual hardness is **15-30 ppm** against 50-60 ppm in the cold process, and less lime and soda are used.

```
  Raw water   Lime + soda    Steam
      |           |            |
      v           v            v
   +-------------------------------+
   |  REACTION TANK (80-150 °C,     |
   |  chemicals and water mixed)    |
   +---------------+---------------+
                   v
         +-------------------+
         |  CONICAL          |   softened water ---> +-------------+
         |  SEDIMENTATION    |---------------------> | SAND FILTER |--> Softened
         |  TANK             |                       | fine sand / |    water
          \                 /                        | coarse sand/|
           \_______________/                         | gravel      |
                   |                                 +-------------+
             Sludge outlet
```

**Chemical equations involved**

**Reactions with lime** $\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2}$ (temporary hardness, Mg salts, acids, $\mathrm{CO_2}$, Fe and Al salts):
$$\mathrm{Ca(HCO_3)_2 + Ca(OH)_2 \rightarrow 2CaCO_3\downarrow + 2H_2O}$$
$$\mathrm{Mg(HCO_3)_2 + 2Ca(OH)_2 \rightarrow 2CaCO_3\downarrow + Mg(OH)_2\downarrow + 2H_2O}$$
$$\mathrm{MgCl_2 + Ca(OH)_2 \rightarrow Mg(OH)_2\downarrow + CaCl_2}$$
$$\mathrm{MgSO_4 + Ca(OH)_2 \rightarrow Mg(OH)_2\downarrow + CaSO_4}$$
$$\mathrm{CO_2 + Ca(OH)_2 \rightarrow CaCO_3\downarrow + H_2O}$$
$$\mathrm{2HCl + Ca(OH)_2 \rightarrow CaCl_2 + 2H_2O};\quad \mathrm{H_2SO_4 + Ca(OH)_2 \rightarrow CaSO_4 + 2H_2O}$$
$$\mathrm{FeSO_4 + Ca(OH)_2 \rightarrow Fe(OH)_2\downarrow + CaSO_4};\quad \mathrm{4Fe(OH)_2 + O_2 + 2H_2O \rightarrow 4Fe(OH)_3\downarrow}$$
$$\mathrm{Al_2(SO_4)_3 + 3Ca(OH)_2 \rightarrow 2Al(OH)_3\downarrow + 3CaSO_4}$$
$$\mathrm{2NaHCO_3 + Ca(OH)_2 \rightarrow CaCO_3\downarrow + Na_2CO_3 + 2H_2O}$$

**Reactions with soda** $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}$ (calcium permanent hardness, original and that produced by lime):
$$\mathrm{CaCl_2 + Na_2CO_3 \rightarrow CaCO_3\downarrow + 2NaCl}$$
$$\mathrm{CaSO_4 + Na_2CO_3 \rightarrow CaCO_3\downarrow + Na_2SO_4}$$

items.question_md: What is vulcanization of rubber in plastic industry? Is it advisable to burn the vulcanized rubber? Justify your answer.
items.answer_md:
**Vulcanisation** (Goodyear, 1839) is the process of heating raw rubber with **sulphur** (or $\mathrm{S_2Cl_2}$, peroxides) at about 100-140 °C, usually with an accelerator (e.g. mercaptobenzothiazole) and activator (ZnO), so that **-S-S- cross-links** form between polyisoprene chains at the C=C / allylic positions, converting soft plastic rubber into a strong, elastic, three-dimensional network.

$$\mathrm{[-CH_2-C(CH_3)=CH-CH_2-]_n} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{S}} \text{chains joined by } \mathrm{-S-S-} \text{ bridges}$$

The cross-links make rubber stronger, elastic, non-sticky and resistant to solvents and wear.

**Is it advisable to burn vulcanised rubber? No.**
1. Being cross-linked (thermoset-like), it **cannot be melted** and reshaped, and burns only incompletely with thick smoke.
2. The combined sulphur burns to **$\mathrm{SO_2}$** (with some $\mathrm{H_2S}$/$\mathrm{CS_2}$): $\mathrm{S + O_2 \rightarrow SO_2}$, which is toxic and causes **acid rain** ($\mathrm{SO_2 \rightarrow SO_3 \xrightarrow{H_2O} H_2SO_4}$).
3. Incomplete combustion releases **CO, soot and carcinogenic polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons**, plus ZnO and additive fumes.

So open burning is harmful; old rubber should instead be **reclaimed** (devulcanised), ground into crumb rubber for roads/mats, or pyrolysed in controlled plants.

items.topic: Composition, setting and hardening of cement
items.question_md: Explain setting and hardness of Portland cement by writing all the chemical equations involved in the process.
items.answer_md:
When cement is mixed with water it forms a plastic paste. The paste first **stiffens (setting)** and then slowly **gains strength (hardening)**. Both result from exothermic hydration and hydrolysis of the four Bogue compounds.

### 1. Setting (stiffening, first 24 h)
- **Initial set** (within minutes to hours): $\mathrm{C_3A}$ hydrates very fast, forming a rigid network of tricalcium aluminate hydrate. Gypsum present reacts with $\mathrm{C_3A}$ to form insoluble calcium sulphoaluminate (ettringite) that coats the grains and slows this reaction, preventing flash set.
- **Final set**: $\mathrm{C_4AF}$ hydrates; $\mathrm{C_3S}$ starts forming tobermorite gel, which fills the pores.
$$\mathrm{3CaO\cdot Al_2O_3 + 6H_2O \rightarrow 3CaO\cdot Al_2O_3\cdot 6H_2O} \quad (+880\ \mathrm{kJ/kg})$$
$$\mathrm{4CaO\cdot Al_2O_3\cdot Fe_2O_3 + 7H_2O \rightarrow 3CaO\cdot Al_2O_3\cdot 6H_2O + CaO\cdot Fe_2O_3\cdot H_2O} \quad (+420\ \mathrm{kJ/kg})$$
$$\mathrm{3CaO\cdot Al_2O_3 + 3(CaSO_4\cdot 2H_2O) + 26H_2O \rightarrow 3CaO\cdot Al_2O_3\cdot 3CaSO_4\cdot 32H_2O}\ \ (\text{ettringite})$$

Also $\mathrm{C_3S}$ begins to hydrate (first equation below) and forms the gel that binds the grains at final set.

### 2. Hardening (strength gain, 1 to 28 days and beyond)
- $\mathrm{C_3S}$ hydrates in 1 to 7 days and gives **early strength**.
- $\mathrm{C_2S}$ hydrates slowly over 7 to 28 days and gives **later (ultimate) strength**.
$$\mathrm{2(3CaO\cdot SiO_2) + 6H_2O \rightarrow 3CaO\cdot 2SiO_2\cdot 3H_2O + 3Ca(OH)_2} \quad (+500\ \mathrm{kJ/kg})$$
$$\mathrm{2(2CaO\cdot SiO_2) + 4H_2O \rightarrow 3CaO\cdot 2SiO_2\cdot 3H_2O + Ca(OH)_2} \quad (+250\ \mathrm{kJ/kg})$$

- The product $\mathrm{3CaO\cdot 2SiO_2\cdot 3H_2O}$ is **tobermorite gel (C-S-H)**, the main binding phase; its interlocking crystals give strength.
- $\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2}$ released makes the paste alkaline (pH about 12.5), which protects steel in RCC.

### Summary
| Stage | Compound | Time | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Initial set | $\mathrm{C_3A}$ (controlled by gypsum) | first minutes to hours | stiffening |
| Final set | $\mathrm{C_4AF}$, start of $\mathrm{C_3S}$ | up to about 10 h | loses plasticity |
| Early hardening | $\mathrm{C_3S}$ | 1 to 7 days | early strength |
| Later hardening | $\mathrm{C_2S}$ | 7 to 28 days | ultimate strength |

IS limits for OPC: initial setting time **not less than 30 min**, final setting time **not more than 600 min (10 h)**.

items.question_md: What are the typical conditions when polymerization occurs through ionic mechanism? Illustrate the general mechanism of anionic polymerization.
items.answer_md:
**Typical conditions for ionic polymerisation:**
- **Monomer type:** electron-donating groups (e.g. isobutylene, vinyl ethers) favour **cationic**; electron-withdrawing groups (e.g. acrylonitrile, styrene, methyl methacrylate) favour **anionic**.
- **Catalyst:** Lewis acid with co-catalyst ($\mathrm{BF_3/H_2O}$, $\mathrm{AlCl_3}$) for cationic; strong base or organometallic ($\mathrm{KNH_2}$ in liquid $\mathrm{NH_3}$, n-BuLi, Na) for anionic.
- **Low temperature** (about $-80$ to $-100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ for cationic) to suppress side reactions; reactions are very fast.
- Solvent of suitable polarity; **dry, pure, oxygen-free** system (traces of water or $\mathrm{CO_2}$ kill carbanions).

**Anionic polymerisation** (initiator: $\mathrm{KNH_2}$ in liquid $\mathrm{NH_3}$, monomer: acrylonitrile; favoured by electron-withdrawing groups such as $-\mathrm{CN}$, $-\mathrm{COOR}$, $-\mathrm{C_6H_5}$)

1. **Initiation:** the amide ion adds to the monomer and forms a carbanion.
$$\mathrm{KNH_2 \rightarrow K^+ + NH_2^-}$$
$$\mathrm{NH_2^- + CH_2{=}CHCN \rightarrow H_2N{-}CH_2{-}CH(CN)^-}$$
2. **Propagation:** the carbanion adds monomer.
$$\mathrm{H_2N{-}CH_2{-}CH(CN)^- + n\,CH_2{=}CHCN \rightarrow H_2N{-}[CH_2{-}CH(CN)]_n{-}CH_2{-}CH(CN)^-}$$
3. **Termination:** the carbanion takes a proton from the solvent (or from added water/acid); with no proton source the chain stays active (living polymer).
$$\mathrm{{\sim}CH_2{-}CH(CN)^- + NH_3 \rightarrow {\sim}CH_2{-}CH_2(CN) + NH_2^-}$$

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2023 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: What do you understand by dry corrosion? How it is different from wet corrosion? Explain with suitable illustration.
items.answer_md:
**Dry (chemical) corrosion** is the direct chemical attack of a metal by dry gases such as $\mathrm{O_2}$, $\mathrm{Cl_2}$, $\mathrm{H_2S}$ or $\mathrm{SO_2}$, usually at high temperature, **in the absence of a liquid electrolyte**. The metal surface reacts with the gas and a layer of corrosion product (oxide, sulphide, halide) forms on it.

**Illustration (oxidation corrosion):**

$$\mathrm{2M \rightarrow 2M^{n+} + 2n\,e^-}\ \text{(at metal surface)},\qquad \mathrm{\tfrac{n}{2}O_2 + 2n\,e^- \rightarrow n\,O^{2-}}$$
$$\mathrm{2M + \tfrac{n}{2}O_2 \rightarrow 2M^{n+} + n\,O^{2-} \ (= M_2O_n)}$$

e.g. $\mathrm{4Fe + 3O_2 \rightarrow 2Fe_2O_3}$ when iron is heated in air. The oxide film forms at the metal/air interface; further attack needs metal ions to diffuse outward or $\mathrm{O^{2-}}$ to diffuse inward through it, so the nature of the film (stable, porous, volatile, unstable) controls the rate.

*Diagram in words:* a metal block with a thin oxide layer on top; arrows show $\mathrm{M^{n+}}$ moving outward and $\mathrm{O^{2-}}$ moving inward through the layer, with $\mathrm{O_2}$ gas above.

**Wet (electrochemical) corrosion** occurs when the metal is in contact with a conducting liquid (moisture, sea water, acid). Separate anodic and cathodic areas form; e.g. rusting of iron: anode $\mathrm{Fe \rightarrow Fe^{2+} + 2e^-}$, cathode $\mathrm{O_2 + 2H_2O + 4e^- \rightarrow 4OH^-}$, then $\mathrm{Fe^{2+} + 2OH^- \rightarrow Fe(OH)_2 \rightarrow Fe_2O_3\cdot xH_2O}$ (rust).

| Basis | Dry corrosion | Wet corrosion |
|---|---|---|
| Medium | Dry gases, no electrolyte | Liquid electrolyte (moisture, solution) needed |
| Mechanism | Direct chemical reaction (adsorption/absorption of gas) | Electrochemical: formation of galvanic cells, current flows |
| Anode/cathode | No separate anodic and cathodic areas | Distinct anodic and cathodic areas |
| Site of attack | Uniform over the exposed surface | Only at the anode, often localised (pits) |
| Product location | Product forms where the attack occurs | Metal dissolves at the anode; product deposits near the cathode |
| Temperature | Usually high temperature | Ordinary temperature |
| Rate | Governed by diffusion through the film | Governed by cell potential, conductivity, area ratio |
| Example | Fe heated in air forming $\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}$; Ag tarnishing in $\mathrm{H_2S}$ | Rusting of iron in moist air; corrosion of Zn in dilute $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$ |

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2023 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: Can the corrosion be prevented by the design and selection of material, discuss with suitable example?
items.answer_md:
**Yes.** Corrosion needs anode, cathode, electrolyte and contact; good design and choice of material remove or weaken these conditions.

### Selection of material
1. Use **noble metals** (Au, Pt) for critical small parts, or **passive alloys** (stainless steel, Ti, Al) in aggressive media.
2. Use **pure metals** where possible, because impurities form local cells.
3. Avoid coupling metals that are **far apart in the galvanic series**; if unavoidable, choose metals close together (e.g. Cu with brass, not Cu with steel).
4. Choose alloys suited to the environment: Cu-Ni alloys for sea water, stainless steel for food and chemical plants.

### Proper design
1. **Area ratio:** keep the anode large and the cathode small. Example: steel plates joined with copper rivets corrode slowly; copper plates with steel rivets corrode the rivets rapidly.
2. **Insulate dissimilar metals** with rubber/plastic washers where they must be joined.
3. **Avoid crevices, sharp corners and stagnant pockets**: prefer welding to riveting or bolting; give tanks a sloping bottom and drain holes so water does not collect.
4. Ensure **uniform aeration** and flow, avoid differential aeration.
5. Make the structure easy to inspect, clean and repaint; avoid residual stress (stress relief annealing).

Example: a water tank designed with a sloping, fully drainable bottom and welded joints suffers far less pitting and crevice corrosion than one with a flat bottom and riveted seams.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2023 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: Explain the major difference between galvanic and concentrations cells. How the concentration difference leads to corrosion of materials.
items.answer_md:
| Basis | Galvanic cell (corrosion) | Concentration cell (corrosion) |
|---|---|---|
| Electrodes | Two **different** metals in electrical contact | **Same** metal (single piece) |
| Origin of EMF | Difference in standard electrode potentials ($E^\circ_{cell} = E^\circ_{cathode} - E^\circ_{anode}$) | Difference in concentration of electrolyte or of oxygen (aeration) |
| Anode | The more active metal (e.g. Zn in Zn-Cu) | The part in more dilute solution / less aerated region |
| EMF | Generally large (Zn-Cu: 1.10 V) | Small, $E = \frac{0.0591}{n}\log\frac{C_2}{C_1}$ |
| Example | Steel bolts in copper sheet; Zn-Fe couple | Waterline corrosion, pitting, crevice corrosion |

**Concentration cell corrosion** occurs on a single metal when its parts are exposed to electrolyte of different concentration or different aeration, which creates a potential difference between them.

- **Differential aeration (most common):** the **less aerated part is anodic** and corrodes: $\mathrm{M \rightarrow M^{n+} + ne^-}$; the more aerated part is cathodic: $\mathrm{O_2 + 2H_2O + 4e^- \rightarrow 4OH^-}$.
- **Metal-ion concentration cell:** the part in the more dilute solution of its own ions is anodic ($E = \frac{0.0591}{n}\log\frac{C_2}{C_1}$).

Examples: Zn rod partly immersed in NaCl (immersed portion corrodes), waterline corrosion, pitting under dust/drops, crevice corrosion under bolts, buried pipes passing through clay and sand.

Mechanism of Wet corrosion by Oxygen Absorption

```
            O2 (air)        O2 (air)
```

Give Detailed Labelled Diagram (only) of the following process. **(Do not explain in words)**

Ion-exchange Process for Softening of Water
items.answer_md:
**Ion-exchange (demineralisation) process: labelled diagram**

items.topic: Physical and chemical properties of lubricants and their testing
items.question_md:
State whether the following statement is **True** or **False**. Give reasons in support of your answer.

Oils having high viscosity need not to have high viscosity-index.
items.answer_md:
**True.**

- **Viscosity** is the resistance to flow **at a given temperature**; it says how thick the oil is.
- **Viscosity index (VI)** measures the **rate of change of viscosity with temperature**: high VI means viscosity changes little on heating or cooling. $\mathrm{VI} = \dfrac{L-U}{L-H} \times 100$ (Dean and Davis).
- The two are independent. A heavy **naphthenic** (Gulf coast type) oil can be very viscous yet its viscosity falls steeply on heating, so it has a **low VI** (about 0). A **paraffinic** (Pennsylvanian) oil of lower viscosity can have a **high VI** (about 100).

So a high-viscosity oil need not have a high viscosity index.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2024 Sem 2.pdf
items.question_md:
State whether the following statement is **True** or **False**. Give reasons in support of your answer.

All simple organic molecules cannot produce polymers.
items.answer_md:
**True.** Not every simple organic molecule can form a polymer.

**Reasons**
1. **Functionality must be at least 2.** A monomer must have at least two bonding sites: a multiple bond (C=C counts as 2, e.g. ethylene, vinyl chloride) or two reactive functional groups (diol, diacid, diamine, amino acid). Molecules with functionality 1 can join only once and then stop.
   - Examples that **cannot** polymerise: methane, ethane (saturated, functionality 0); ethanol, acetic acid, methylamine (functionality 1). Ethanol + acetic acid stop at ethyl acetate:
   $$\mathrm{CH_3COOH + C_2H_5OH \rightarrow CH_3COOC_2H_5 + H_2O}$$
   (no further groups left to react)
   - Examples that **can**: ethylene (bifunctional), ethylene glycol + terephthalic acid (both bifunctional) give terylene.
2. **Thermodynamics must allow it**: $\Delta G_p = \Delta H_p - T\Delta S_p < 0$, i.e. the reaction must be sufficiently exothermic and below the ceiling temperature.
3. Steric hindrance can prevent it even with a double bond (e.g. 1,2-disubstituted alkenes such as stilbene hardly polymerise).

Hence only molecules satisfying these conditions act as monomers.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2024 Sem 2.pdf
items.question_md:
State whether the following statement is **True** or **False**. Give reasons in support of your answer.

Large anodic area results in intense corrosion.
items.answer_md:
**False.**

The rate of corrosion is proportional to $\dfrac{\text{area of cathode}}{\text{area of anode}}$. The cathodic reaction (e.g. $\mathrm{O_2 + 2H_2O + 4e^- \rightarrow 4OH^-}$) demands electrons in proportion to the cathode area, and all of them must come from the anode ($\mathrm{M \rightarrow M^{n+} + ne^-}$).

- **Large anode, small cathode:** the electron demand is spread over a large anodic area, so current density at the anode is low and corrosion is mild and uniform.
- **Small anode, large cathode:** the same or greater current is drawn from a tiny area, so the anode corrodes **intensely** (deep pits).

Example: a copper rivet in a large steel plate causes little corrosion, but a steel rivet in a large copper plate corrodes rapidly. So it is a **small** anodic area that gives intense corrosion.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2024 Sem 2.pdf
items.question_md:
State whether the following statement is **True** or **False**. Give reasons in support of your answer.

Catalytic Cracking is superior as compared to Thermal Cracking.
items.answer_md:
**True.** Catalytic cracking is superior to thermal cracking.

**Reasons**
1. **Higher octane number** petrol (about 80-90 vs 65-70), because the carbocation mechanism produces branched and aromatic hydrocarbons that resist knocking.
2. **Higher yield** of petrol and better control of products.
3. Needs **lower temperature (300-450 °C) and pressure (1-5 kg/cm²)** than thermal cracking (475-650 °C, up to 100 kg/cm²), saving energy.
4. Less gum and unstable dienes; less gas and coke formed.
5. **Lower sulphur** in the product, since S compounds are removed as $\mathrm{H_2S}$ on the catalyst.
6. In fluidised-bed units the process is continuous and the heat from burning off coke in the regenerator is reused.

Example: $\mathrm{C_{10}H_{22} \xrightarrow{\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3/\text{SiO}_2} C_5H_{12} + C_5H_{10}}$

items.question_md:
Distinguish between the following in **Point-wise** manner:

Chemical and Electrochemical Mechanism of Corrosion.
items.answer_md:
| No. | Chemical (dry) mechanism | Electrochemical (wet) mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Direct reaction of the metal with dry gases ($\mathrm{O_2}$, $\mathrm{Cl_2}$, $\mathrm{H_2S}$) | Takes place in presence of a conducting liquid (electrolyte) |
| 2 | No anodic and cathodic areas; no flow of current | Numerous anodic and cathodic areas; electrons flow from anode to cathode |
| 3 | Corrosion is uniform over the surface | Occurs only at anodic areas, often localised |
| 4 | Corrosion product forms at the site of attack | Metal dissolves at the anode, product deposits near the cathode |
| 5 | Usually at high temperature; rate governed by diffusion through the oxide film | At ordinary temperature; rate governed by EMF, conductivity, area ratio |
| 6 | Self-controlled if the film is protective | Continues as long as the electrolyte and cathodic reactant are present |
| 7 | e.g. $\mathrm{4Fe + 3O_2 \rightarrow 2Fe_2O_3}$ on heating | e.g. rusting: $\mathrm{Fe \rightarrow Fe^{2+} + 2e^-}$; $\mathrm{O_2 + 2H_2O + 4e^- \rightarrow 4OH^-}$ |

items.topic: Physical and chemical properties of lubricants and their testing
items.question_md:
Give proper reasoning of following:

Lubricating oils should have low Steam Emulsification Number.
items.answer_md:
**Steam emulsion number (SEN)** is the time in seconds in which an oil-water emulsion (formed by passing steam through the oil) separates into layers.

A **low SEN** means water separates out quickly (good demulsibility). If oil forms a stable emulsion, it lubricates poorly, traps dirt and forms sludge, and the water promotes corrosion. Oils in contact with water or steam (steam turbines, marine engines) must therefore have a low SEN.

items.path: library/archive/CY1107/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2024 Sem 2.pdf
items.question_md:
Give proper reasoning of following:

PVC is soft and flexible whereas Bakelite is hard and brittle.
items.answer_md:
- **PVC** is a **thermoplastic**: linear $\mathrm{-[CH_2-CHCl]_n-}$ chains held only by weak van der Waals and dipole forces, so chains can slide over each other. With added plasticizer (e.g. dioctyl phthalate) these forces are weakened further, $T_g$ falls, and PVC is soft and flexible.
- **Bakelite** is a **thermoset**: phenol units are joined in all directions by covalent $\mathrm{-CH_2-}$ bridges into a rigid **3-D cross-linked network**. No chain can move relative to another, so it is hard; under stress bonds break instead of chains sliding, so it is brittle.

items.question_md:
Give proper reasoning of following:

Iron corrodes faster than Aluminum, even though Iron is placed below Aluminum in the electrochemical series.
items.answer_md: Al ($E^\circ = -1.66$ V) is more active than Fe ($E^\circ = -0.44$ V), but on exposure to air Al instantly forms a thin, compact, adherent, non-porous and self-healing film of $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$ ($\mathrm{4Al + 3O_2 \rightarrow 2Al_2O_3}$; PBR about 1.29, protective). This makes Al **passive**, so it behaves as a noble metal. Iron forms porous, non-adherent rust ($\mathrm{Fe_2O_3\cdot xH_2O}$) that flakes off and exposes fresh metal, so iron keeps corroding.

items.topic: Scale and sludge: internal and external treatment
items.question_md:
Give proper reasoning of following:

Calgon treatment prevents scale formation in the boilers.
items.answer_md:
**Calgon** is sodium hexametaphosphate, $\mathrm{Na_2[Na_4(PO_3)_6]}$. In the boiler it reacts with the scale-forming $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ salts to form a **soluble complex**:
$$\mathrm{2CaSO_4 + Na_2[Na_4(PO_3)_6] \rightarrow Na_2[Ca_2(PO_3)_6] + 2Na_2SO_4}$$
Since $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ is held in solution as a soluble complex, $\mathrm{CaSO_4}$ cannot precipitate on the hot surfaces; hence **neither scale nor sludge** forms.
